# Evert Calderon / Mesa Group Consulting: How SuperMoney and Novae Fit Into His Business

## Executive Summary

Evert Calderon is using SuperMoney and Novae as two complementary affiliate/referral partners that let his Bakersfield credit repair firm, Mesa Group Consulting, monetize clients across their entire financial lifecycle without building or licensing any of the underlying products himself. SuperMoney supplies embedded loan and credit card comparison offers (commissioned lead generation); Novae supplies fulfillment for debt settlement, estate planning, life insurance, and business credit products via a direct-selling affiliate program with per-sale commissions. This is confirmed not just by the Miro board you found, but by Mesa Group's own live website, which names both companies as "strategic partnerships" and publishes an FTC-compliant affiliate disclosure describing exactly these relationships.

---

## 1. The Companies

### SuperMoney (SuperMoney LLC) — the affiliate offer engine

SuperMoney is a private fintech company headquartered in Santa Ana, California, founded June 18, 2013 by Miron Lulic — the same founding team behind Optima Tax Relief and the lender LoanNow (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SuperMoney, https://www.crunchbase.com/organization/supermoney, https://finovate.com/supermoney-brings-kayak-like-ux-online-borrowing-process/). It operates a "KAYAK-like" comparison marketplace for financial products across 50+ categories: credit cards, personal loans, auto loan refinancing, student loan refinancing, debt consolidation, mortgages, insurance, banking, and more. Its multi-lender offer engine has processed over $5 billion in loan requests since 2017 (https://www.supermoney.com/supermoney-surpasses-5-billion-in-loan-requests-with-transparent-access-to-financing).

Crucially for this research, SuperMoney's consumer site is free; the company gets paid by lenders and issuers for referrals — and it shares that revenue with publishers through its "Monetize" partner program (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize, https://help.supermoney.com/article/33-how-can-i-partner-with-supermoney). The program offers three tools:

- **Super Links** — tracked referral links that send a publisher's users to any of SuperMoney's 50+ verticals, plus turnkey co-branded pages listing related offers so the publisher "earns commission on those alternative offers" even when the primary product isn't monetized (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize/super-links).
- **Money Marketplace** — a white-label comparison experience embedded in the publisher's own site under the publisher's brand.
- **Pre-Qualification Platform** — an embedded widget where a consumer submits one form and gets real-time pre-qualified offers from dozens of lenders with only a soft credit pull, without leaving the publisher's site. SuperMoney markets this specifically to credit-adjacent businesses; its case study describes a credit-counseling organization embedding the platform so call-center reps can pre-populate applications and review offers with clients (https://www.supermoney.com/monetize/prequalification-platform).

Affiliates typically earn per qualified lead rather than waiting for a funded loan ("Commissionable Direction – Earn commissions per qualified lead," https://www.flexoffers.com/affiliate-programs/supermoney-affiliate-program/), and the program is also distributed through networks like FlexOffers and Takeads (up to 30% per sale, https://takeads.com/merchants/supermoney-us/).

### Novae (Novae LLC) — the product fulfillment and high-ticket commission partner

Novae is a Black-owned fintech based in Conyers, Georgia, founded in 2014, led by CEO Reco McCambry, serving all 50 states and Puerto Rico (https://novaemoney.com/). It is a member of the Direct Selling Association and distributes its products through a multi-level affiliate marketing program rather than traditional retail (https://novaemoney.com/life-insurance/, https://novaemoney.com/common/terms_conditions.asp). Its product lines map almost one-for-one onto your Miro board:

- **Credit tools:** myNovaeDisputes, an AI-powered DIY credit dispute platform ("Novae is not a credit repair company," https://www.mynovaedisputes.com/), plus myNovaeCredit monitoring and credit-builder programs.
- **Debt relief (consumer):** the "Debt Help" program launched in 2023 — a debt settlement service for unsecured debts ($10,000 minimum) promising reduced payments, resolution in 20–48 months, and fees collected only after settlement per FTC rules (https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/novae-becomes-first-fintech-company-to-offer-debt-help-to-struggling-americans-301870118.html, https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/debt-help).
- **Business debt relief:** negotiation/settlement of merchant cash advances, business credit cards, loans, leases, judgments and lawsuits ($15,000 minimum; marketing claims of payment reductions averaging 80%, up to 90%) (https://novaemoney.com/business-debt-help/, https://novaedebthelp.com/for-businesses).
- **Business credit:** the "Lendavo" business credit building program, sold at $2,495 one-time (or payment plans) with a "$50K funding opportunities guarantee" (https://novaemoney.com/business-credit/).
- **Trust & will plans:** white-label online estate planning — will-based and trust-based packages with state-specific documents, pour-over wills, powers of attorney, etc. (https://novaemoney.com/willcan/trusts, https://novaemoney.com/trsolutions/wills). Novae also runs a "Novae Trust Program" listed in its affiliate enrollment materials.
- **Life insurance:** offered through a partnership with Policygenius, the national insurance marketplace (https://novaemoney.com/life-insurance/).

The affiliate program itself is structured like classic direct sales: enrollment tiers of roughly $99 + $49/month (Basic), $299 + $69/month (Plus), and $499 + $99/month (Pro), with personal commissions, customer acquisition bonuses, and team override commissions paid through ten generations of recruited affiliates (https://novaemoney.com/become-an-affiliate/, https://novaemoneytraining.com/wp-content/uploads/Affiliate_Enrollment_Agreement.pdf, https://novaepays.com/sales-commissions/). Novae advertises "up to $3,000+ per referral" on high-end programs (https://novaemoney.com/become-an-affiliate/) and "up to $4,000/customer" at the Pro tier (enrollment agreement PDF). For context and caution: Novae's own income disclosure states the average participant earned just $1,408 in 2023, so large payouts are the exception, not the norm.

### Mesa Group Consulting (MESA & CO CONSULTING LLC)

Mesa Group is a small financial services firm founded in 2023 at 5001 California Ave, Suite 219, Bakersfield, CA, with 1–10 employees (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/, https://linkedin.com/in/evertcalderon). Evert Jafet Calderon is its public face and operator — his LinkedIn title is "Visionary Operations Officer," and the site calls him senior writer/spokesperson. He is a Credit Consultants Association "Credit Score Certified" consultant trained by the American Credit Repair Academy, and has appeared on local TV (KGET Studio 17) promoting the firm (https://ccasite.org/members/score-certified/organization/Mesa+Group+Consulting/, https://www.kget.com/studio17live/studio-17-take-control-of-your-credit-with-mesa-group-consulting/). Mesa's core revenue services are CROA-compliant credit repair ("Mesa360"), credit consulting, business funding brokering, a DIY credit platform ("Creditily"), and a "Mesa Financial Concierge" membership bundled with a SmartCredit monitoring subscription. The firm markets in English, Spanish, and Punjabi to Bakersfield's immigrant communities.

---

## 2. What Evert Is Using SuperMoney For

Evert is a **publisher affiliate of SuperMoney, not an advertiser and not a customer**. His own affiliate disclosure — written to comply with FTC 16 CFR Part 255 — states it verbatim: SuperMoney is his "financial product comparison platform offering personal loans, auto loan refinancing, student loan refinancing, debt consolidation loans, and credit card comparisons," and Mesa "may receive a commission when you use SuperMoney and select financial products" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure). Those five products are exactly the five "new page - supermoney affiliate" items on the Miro board.

The mechanics are visible on the live site. Mesa's homepage features a "Mesa Marketplace" section with links for Credit Cards, Personal Loans, Auto Loan Refi, Student Loan Refi, Debt Consolidation, Debt Relief, Trust & Will, and Life Insurance — the Miro board, built. The credit cards page invites visitors to "See My Pre-Qualified Offers" via embedded "Powered by" widgets, promises "no hard inquiry" pre-qualification and "400+ cards from top issuers," and discloses "we may earn a referral fee if you're approved, at no extra cost to you" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/credit-cards). That is the pattern of SuperMoney's embedded Pre-Qualification Platform / co-branded offer engine: the client never leaves Mesa's branded environment, applies with a soft pull, and SuperMoney pays Mesa per qualified lead.

Why this matters to his business model:

1. **Monetizing the post-repair client.** Mesa's core service raises credit scores. A client whose score jumps from 512 to 762 (a real testimonial on the site) immediately becomes eligible for cards, refis, and consolidation loans. The SuperMoney pages are the monetization layer for that newly creditworthy audience — the site's own copy walks clients from repair into "consolidated that debt at a fraction of the interest" and "6.9%, not 18%" auto financing.
2. **SEO capture.** Each "new page" is a standalone, keyword-targeted landing page ("personal loans," "auto loan refi," etc.) designed to rank and convert organic/local search traffic through tracked affiliate links — standard affiliate site architecture, wrapped in Mesa's local, trilingual brand.
3. **No licensing burden.** As the pages repeatedly state, "Mesa Group Consulting is not a lender and does not make credit decisions." SuperMoney's lender network provides the products, compliance, and underwriting; Mesa just refers and collects commissions.

## 3. What Novae Does and How Evert Uses It

Novae is the fulfillment partner for everything SuperMoney doesn't cover — the service products on the right half of the Miro board. Mesa's affiliate disclosure again confirms the relationship directly: "Novae: Business funding and debt relief services (business and personal)… Mesa Group receives a commission when you secure funding or enroll in debt relief services through Novae" (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure). Mapping the board to Novae's catalog:

| Miro board item | Novae product | How Mesa earns |
|---|---|---|
| Debt relief | Consumer Debt Help (debt settlement, $10k+ unsecured) | Per-enrollment commission |
| Trust & will plan | Will-Based / Trust-Based Estate Plans (white-label docs) | Per-sale commission |
| Life insurance | Life insurance via Novae's Policygenius partnership | Per-policy commission |
| Business debt relief | Business Debt Help (MCA/business debt settlement, $15k+) | High-ticket commission (Novae advertises up to $3,000+/referral) |
| Business credit | Lendavo business credit building program ($2,495 retail) | Per-sale commission |

Two nuances worth knowing:

- **Novae is itself partly a middleman.** Its life insurance is fulfilled by Policygenius, and its trust/will documents are white-labeled estate planning software. Notably, Mesa's own affiliate disclosure separately names Policygenius (life insurance) and Trust & Will, the direct-to-consumer estate planning company (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure). So Evert may be going through Novae for these, or directly to the same underlying providers Novae uses — the Miro board attributes them to Novae, but the disclosure hedges both ways. Either way, the fulfillment stack is identical.
- **The strategic fit is a "no wrong door" funnel.** Credit repair only works for inaccurate/outdated items; consumers who legitimately owe unaffordable debt are poor candidates for it. Novae's debt settlement programs (consumer and business) let Mesa still serve — and earn from — those leads. Similarly, business owners who don't qualify for funding can be routed into Novae's business credit building program, and families completing credit repair get cross-sold estate plans and life insurance ("protecting your legacy," as the homepage puts it). Novae essentially gives a 10-person local shop a national product catalog, with Novae handling "customer service, product and service delivery, billing" per its own comp plan document (https://www.novaemoneytraining.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/NM_CompPlan_0619.pdf).

## 4. The Overall Strategy

Putting it together, Evert is building Mesa Group into a vertically layered affiliate marketing operation on top of a local credit repair storefront:

- **Layer 1 — Services sold directly:** credit repair (Mesa360), consulting, Concierge membership, SmartCredit monitoring (recurring affiliate revenue; his disclosure flags recurring commissions as a stated conflict-of-interest risk).
- **Layer 2 — SuperMoney pages:** low-friction, high-volume lead-gen commissions on lending products, especially as the natural "next step" for repaired credit files.
- **Layer 3 — Novae pages:** lower-volume but much higher-ticket commissions (debt settlement enrollments, $2,495 business credit programs, estate plans, insurance policies), covering customer segments credit repair can't.

The entire model is disclosed with unusual thoroughness: Mesa's affiliate disclosure names every partner (SmartCredit, SuperMoney, Novae, PolicyGenius, Trust & Will, Ava, CreditStrong, Self, and rent-reporting services), explains pay-per-enrollment/pay-per-funding/revenue-share/recurring structures, and even acknowledges the conflicts of interest inherent in commission-driven recommendations (https://www.mesagroupconsulting.com/affiliate-disclosure).

## 5. Uncertainties and Caveats

- **Exact payouts are confidential.** Mesa's disclosure explicitly cites NDAs with partners. Novae publishes ranges ("up to $3,000+ per referral," "up to $4,000/customer" at Pro tier), but what Evert actually earns depends on his affiliate tier and volume — and Novae's own disclosure shows the average affiliate made $1,408 in 2023. SuperMoney payouts are per qualified lead and vary by vertical.
- **Whether Evert pays for a Novae affiliate tier** (Basic/Plus/Pro at $49–$99/month) versus a lighter referral arrangement is not publicly visible. The Miro board only proves he routes products through Novae, not his enrollment level.
- **Life insurance and estate planning have dual paths** (Novae vs. direct Policygenius/Trust & Will relationships per his disclosure), so the "novae" label on the Miro board may reflect either the fulfillment channel or simply who he signed up through.
- **Novae's MLM structure** (10-generation overrides, paid enrollment tiers) is legal direct selling — DSA member — but it is a recruitment-based model with a low documented average income, which is relevant context if you are evaluating the relationship.
- The Miro board is a plan, but it has been substantially executed: the Mesa Marketplace pages are live on mesagroupconsulting.com today with the exact categories listed.

# Maternal Mortality and Prenatal Care Access: Rohingya Refugees in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh vs. Karen Refugees in Mae La Camp, Thailand, 2017–2023

## 1. Executive Summary

Between 2017 and 2023, the Rohingya camps of Cox's Bazar and Mae La camp in Thailand represented two contrasting models of refugee maternal healthcare. Cox's Bazar, a mass-influx emergency setting of ~900,000 people served by a fragmented network of NGO-operated health posts, field hospitals, and 24/7 basic emergency obstetric care (BEmONC) facilities, entered the period with a maternal mortality ratio (MMR) of 179 per 100,000 live births and only ~12–35% facility-based delivery; by 2023 it had pushed facility-based deliveries to ~85% and reduced maternal deaths from 83 (2022) to 57 (2023). Mae La, a protracted camp of ~39,000 with a mature, single-provider obstetric model built over three decades (Shoklo Malaria Research Unit, SMRU) and referral integration with Thai public hospitals, maintained skilled birth attendance at 95–96%, antenatal care (ANC) coverage above 90%, neonatal mortality of 6–8 per 1,000 live births, and zero reported maternal deaths in 2018. The 2021 UK-driven UNFPA funding cut (~85% to UNFPA Supplies) materially threatened commodity and midwifery continuity in Cox's Bazar, where UNFPA is the lead sexual and reproductive health (SRH) agency; there is no evidence it affected Mae La, where UNFPA is not an operational actor — an important asymmetry that corrects the premise of uniform impact.

## 2. Data Sources and Caveats

**Cox's Bazar:** UNFPA Maternal and Perinatal Mortality Surveillance and Response (MPMSR) annual reports (2020–2023), the CDC/UNFPA Reproductive Age Mortality Study (RAMOS, Aug 2017–Aug 2018), UNFPA Sexual and Reproductive Health Working Group (SRH WG) bulletins (2021–2023), WHO/Health Sector bulletins, UNHCR public health factsheets, a prospective neonatal mortality surveillance study (BMJ Global Health, 2022), and an MSF qualitative study on home births (Hadiuzzaman et al., 2022).

**Mae La:** UNHCR Health Information System (HIS/iRHIS) site reports (2017, 2018), SMRU-associated peer-reviewed studies (Hoogenboom et al. 2015; ALSO/PPH cohort study 2016; PLOS One neonatal intensive care study; contraception cohort 1996–2015), and a Cambridge/PHCR&D retrospective analysis of two Thai-border camps (2000–2018).

**Key caveats:** (1) Mae La HIS site data are most complete through 2018; site-level HIS reporting for 2019–2023 is thin in the public domain, so Mae La's 2019–2023 picture relies on the long-run retrospective literature and organizational records. (2) Cox's Bazar indicators come from overlapping systems (DHIS2, CHW Working Group, EWARS/MPMSR) that sometimes contradict each other — e.g., WHO concurrent monitoring in 2023–24 suggested only 43% facility delivery versus >80% in CHW-WG/4W data (https://rohingyaresponse.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/CXB-Health-Sector-Bulletin-Feb-2024-1.pdf). (3) Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) *incidence* is not published as a clean population rate in either setting; cause-of-death shares and complication rankings are used as proxies.

## 3. Indicator Comparison

| Indicator | Cox's Bazar (Rohingya) | Mae La (Karen) |
|---|---|---|
| MMR | 179/100,000 live births (95% CI 130–228), RAMOS 2017–18 (https://healthynewbornnetwork.org/hnn-content/uploads/Preliminary-Report-RAMOS-Cox_s-Bazar-1.pdf); vs. Bangladesh national 115 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12613593/) | 126.5/100,000 across 2000–2018 in two border camps (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/primary-health-care-research-and-development/article/.../5A2A03E5B33226D61F84A028BB229992); 0 maternal deaths in Mae La in 2018, 1 in 2017 (HIS site reports) |
| ANC 4+ visits | Facility-reported 4th-visit coverage only 16–21% (monthly, Jan–Aug 2022; 17% average) per Health Sector DHIS2 (https://reliefweb.int/attachments/2f6538fb-4542-4e83-a285-13c3c0174db8/final_health_sector_bulletin_august_2022.pdf); women completing 4+ ANC rose 26,965 (2020) → 39,307 (2021), +45.7% (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/srh_working_group_annual_bulletin_2021.pdf); ANC4 reported at 75–85% of facility births by 2023 (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/srh_wg_bulletin_annual_bulletin_2023_final_1.pdf); an April 2023 survey found 47% received no ANC at all in their last pregnancy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10835278/) | >90% of pregnant women attended SMRU ANC; >90% completed 4+ visits over 2000–2018 (Cambridge study); ANC coverage 89% (2017) and 91% (2018) in UNHCR HIS (https://reliefweb.int/attachments/39ea9ee8-f0f1-3911-a9c5-b75ce55bc944/Thailand_2017_Maela.pdf; https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/TH/Thailand_2018_Maela.pdf) |
| Skilled birth attendance / facility delivery | Home deliveries: 88% (2018) → 59% (2019) → 42% (2020) → 30% (Q1 2021) (https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/searo/bangladesh/bangladesh---rohingya-crisis---pdf-reports/health-sector-bulletin/2021/health-sector-cox-s-bazar-bulletin-no-14-(-jan-mar)-2021.pdf); facility-based deliveries 58% (2020) → 70% (2021) (SRH WG 2021); ~75% (2022); 85% by Dec 2023 (SRH WG 2023); only 35% facility-based in June 2019 per MSF (https://scienceportal.msf.org/api/assets/7744/download/13930) | 96% (2017), 95% (2018) of all births attended by skilled personnel (UNHCR HIS); ~80% SBA average 2000–2018; SMRU facility share of live births rose from 54.1% (2000–07) to 74.2% (2008–13) (ALSO study, https://exa.ai/library/publication/ndzbxd6l13c) |
| PPH | Leading obstetric complication managed at facilities and leading cause of maternal death: 44% of 83 deaths in 2022 (≈36–37 hemorrhage deaths), 31% hypertensive disorders (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/mpmsr_annual_report_2022.pdf.pdf); 35% of 57 deaths in 2023 (n=20) (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/2024-09/MPMSR%20Annual%20Report%202023%20Final.docx.pdf); managed complications fell 4.8% in 2022 (SRH WG 2022) | PPH the most common intrapartum complication in SMRU's 2007–08 WHO Safe Motherhood audit (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25652646/); PPH-attributable MMR among SMRU facility deliveries fell from 59.3/100,000 (2000–07) to 0 (2008–15) after ALSO training — a significant risk difference of −59.3 (p=0.0065) (ALSO study) |
| Neonatal mortality (≤28 days) | 27.0/1,000 live births (95% CI 22.3–31.8), prospective surveillance Sep 2017–Dec 2018; stillbirth 15.2/1,000 total births; 76.3% of neonatal deaths at home/community (https://gh.bmj.com/content/7/4/e008110); RAMOS-derived NMR 18/1,000 | 8/1,000 (2017), 6/1,000 (2018) per UNHCR HIS site reports; long-run decline driven by SMRU neonatal care introduced 2008–2011 (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0072721&type=printable) |

**Quantitative cross-checks:** (a) Cox's Bazar 2017–18 neonatal mortality was 27.0/1,000 vs. Mae La's 6/1,000 in 2018 — a rate ratio of ~4.5. (b) The 2021 rise in 4+ ANC completers: (39,307 − 26,965)/26,965 = 45.8%, matching the SRH WG's reported 45.7%. (c) 44% of 83 deaths = 36.5 hemorrhage-attributed deaths in 2022; the 2023 figure of 20 hemorrhage deaths among 57 implies a ~45% absolute reduction in hemorrhage deaths year-on-year, coincident with EmONC/QoC investments. (d) Cox's Bazar C-section rate was 5.7–7.6% of facility deliveries (2022–2023), near the low end of the WHO 5–15% band; Mae La reported 13% in 2018 (within band) and a long-run average of 3.7% (2000–2018).

## 4. Cox's Bazar: Trajectory and Service Model 2017–2023

The acute influx began August 2017. Baseline mortality was high: RAMOS found an MMR of 179/100,000 and a pregnancy-related death ratio of 282/100,000, with 50% of pregnancy-related deaths at home and 6% in transit; 26% of families sought no treatment before death, nearly half judging it unimportant (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/Final%20RAMOS%20Summary%20Report%20for%20circulation_0.pdf). The delivery model that emerged was NGO-operated and fragmented: ~200 health facilities run by >100 health-sector partners (health posts, primary health centers, NGO field hospitals such as HOPE Foundation and MSF facilities), coordinated by a WHO-led Health Sector with UNFPA leading the SRH Working Group; UNHCR directly supported 28 healthcare facilities (https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/download/100119). Facilities provide 24-hour BEmONC with referral to tertiary care; comprehensive EmONC (surgery, blood transfusion) depends on referral outside the camps.

Progress was real but uneven. Facility-based delivery climbed from ~12% (2018) to 85% (Dec 2023); facility deliveries rose from 27,240 (2022) to 33,854 (2023), 70.9% of them Rohingya (SRH WG 2023 bulletin). Yet DHIS2-based ANC4 completion among all deliveries was only ~17% in 2022 — flagged by the Health Sector as a priority gap — and MPMSR audits found that among 96 pregnancy-related deaths in 2021, 35.7% of those with any ANC had fewer than 4 visits (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/mpmsr_annual_report_2021.pdf). Maternal deaths numbered 96 (2021), 83 (2022), 57 (2023); 71–75% occurred at facilities or in referral transit, indicating quality-of-care and referral delays rather than access alone (MPMSR 2022, 2023). Documented avoidable factors: preference for informal providers, poor referral and surgical-consent counseling, lack of equipment/medicines (MPMSR 2022). Camps nearer a secondary facility had significantly lower neonatal mortality (p<0.01), while the raw number of in-camp facilities did not correlate — evidence that EmONC proximity, not clinic count, drives newborn survival (https://gh.bmj.com/content/7/4/e008110).

## 5. Mae La: Trajectory and Service Model

Mae La (population 39,061 in 2018; site open since 1984) operated a consolidated model: SMRU was the sole ANC and delivery provider from 1997 until it withdrew from the camps at end-2016, after which general healthcare passed from MSF (pre-2005) → PU-AMI (to 2015) → the American Refugee Committee → the International Rescue Committee (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0172007; https://wellcomeopenresearch.org/articles/11-21/v2). Critically, this is not a full Thai Ministry of Public Health (MOPH) integration model *inside* the camp — care remains NGO/charitable-actor delivered — but it is *referral-integrated* with the Thai public system: complicated cases and procedures (e.g., tubal ligation by mini-laparotomy) go to Thai public hospitals (Mae Sot), a standby emergency car was documented in the facility assessment, and EmOC was available 24/7 in most border sites (https://www.womensrefugeecommission.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/th_rha.pdf). Outcomes reflect three decades of maturation: a six-fold reduction in maternal deaths among ANC users (1986–2010) (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0040244), elimination of PPH deaths at the facility after ALSO training, infant mortality falling from 183/1,000 (1987) to single digits, and NMR of 6–8/1,000 in 2017–2018 — below Thailand's 2012 national rate of 8/1,000. The 2018 HIS report shows a thin but dense workforce: 3 doctors (1:13,020 population), 72 qualified nurses (1:543), 64 CHWs, 62,085 consultations/year, hospitalization rate 138 (https://his.unhcr.org/ar2018/files/TH/Thailand_2018_Maela.pdf). Known quality gaps persisted: high nulliparous episiotomy rate (49%), inconsistent controlled cord traction and hand hygiene, and slow recognition of PPH severity in observed practice (Hoogenboom et al. 2015).

## 6. Structural Correlates of the Outcome Gap

**Midwife/birth-attendant density and production.** Cox's Bazar had to create a midwifery cadre from scratch: UNFPA supported 283 midwives in 2023 — over 60% of the response's midwifery workforce — implying a total of roughly 470 midwives, or ~1:1,950 total population (≈1:390 women of reproductive age) for ~919,000 Rohingya, plus 2 international midwife mentors and 3 national coordinators conducting 151 mentoring visits (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/srh_wg_bulletin_annual_bulletin_2023_final_1.pdf; https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/UNFPA%20Bangladesh%20Situation%20Report%20April-June%202022.pdf). Mae La instead relied on a stable, locally trained SBA cadre built through accelerated, competency-based training programs with expatriate obstetric/pediatric supervision (https://exa.ai/library/publication/pdkfffntrv9), achieving near-universal ANC documentation quality (>90% of essential elements).

**EmONC within a 2-hour radius.** In Cox's Bazar, in-camp facilities are BEmONC-only; comprehensive care requires external referral, mitigated from 2022 by UNFPA's 24/7 Emergency Response and Transport System — 8 ambulances across 34 camps, managing 1,554 emergency obstetric referrals in a single quarter (Apr–Jun 2022) — yet MPMSR audits still cite referral delay as a leading avoidable factor. In Mae La, the birthing unit plus standby vehicle and the Thai hospital referral corridor put surgical obstetrics reliably within reach; the comparative literature confirms camps proximate to secondary care had significantly lower NMR on the Bangladesh side, underscoring what Mae La's referral integration achieves.

**Cultural mediation of traditional birth attendants (TBAs).** This is the sharpest behavioral divergence. Among Rohingya, TBAs commanded higher trust than formally trained midwives; home birth was normalized practice from Myanmar, and facility aversion was driven by unfamiliarity with midwives, perceived loss of autonomy, disregard for practices such as birthing ropes, privacy concerns, movement-permission barriers, and distance (https://scienceportal.msf.org/api/assets/7744/download/13930). The Cox's Bazar response compensated through a 1,440+ strong CHW network (42,969 ANC/facility-delivery referrals in Q1 2021 alone), midwife-led birthing centers, and community engagement — rather than formal TBA integration, which Bangladeshi policy discourages. In the Karen setting, TBAs were historically *absorbed into* the health system (e.g., Backpack Health Worker Teams pairing medical assistants with TBAs; SMRU's locally trained Karen SBAs), converting cultural trust into a referral asset rather than a competitor (https://www.womensrefugeecommission.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/th_rha.pdf). The outcome correlation is consistent: where TBA trust was institutionalized (Mae La), SBA coverage exceeded 90%; where it was not (Cox's Bazar), the system spent 2017–2023 climbing from 12% to 85% facility delivery, with hemorrhage — the complication least survivable at home — remaining the top killer throughout.

## 7. The 2021 UNFPA Funding Reduction: Differential Impact

In April 2021 the UK announced an ~85% cut to UNFPA Supplies (expected £154M/$211M reduced to ~£23M/$32M) plus £12M ($17M) from core funds; UNFPA estimated the withdrawn funds would have prevented ~250,000 maternal and child deaths globally (https://www.unfpa.org/press/statement-uk-government-funding-cuts; https://news.un.org/en/story/2021/04/1090892). IPPF projected 2.4 million additional unintended pregnancies and 7,447 maternal deaths across its services alone by end-2021 absent replacement funding (https://w03.ippf.org/news/aid-cuts-could-lead-more-two-million-unintended-pregnancies-end-year-continued-blow-women-and).

**Cox's Bazar (direct exposure):** UNFPA is the lead SRH agency and principal contraceptive-commodity pipeline for the response, so the cut struck the core of the supply chain precisely when COVID-19 had already depressed services. Measurable 2021 stress signals: facility-based deliveries dipped sharply April–June 2021 during the COVID spike compounded by resource strain (SRH WG 2021 annual bulletin); the IRC documented a 2020 ANC collapse followed by a protocol reduction from 8 to 4 recommended ANC visits "to decrease visits to health facilities" (https://reliefweb.int/attachments/695fbdb6-2f22-4b0c-bd64-e833a0870407/srh-bangladesh.pdf). Continuity was preserved through three mechanisms: (1) the January 2021 World Bank–financed US$38.8M Health and Gender Support Project signed by UNFPA with the Government of Bangladesh (https://bangladesh.unfpa.org/en/news/strengthening-health-and-gender-services-coxs-bazar-district-us388-million-through-world-bank); (2) aggressive community outreach that still raised 4+ ANC completion 45.7% and PNC visits 40.2% in 2021; and (3) the ERTS ambulance network. Nonetheless, the persistently low DHIS2 ANC4 completion (~17% in 2022) and 96 maternal deaths in 2021 indicate the continuity achieved was quantitative (visits) more than qualitative (completed care packages), a gap MPMSR audits tie to equipment/medicine shortages — exactly the commodity category the UNFPA Supplies cut targeted.

**Mae La (no direct exposure):** There is no evidence the 2021 UNFPA reduction affected Mae La's maternal services. UNFPA is not an operational maternal-health provider in the Thai camps; financing flows through the Thai-border NGO consortium (IRC for health; The Border Consortium for food/shelter) and research-philanthropic funding (Wellcome for SMRU). Mae La's relevant financing shocks were earlier (PU-AMI's 2015 departure and SMRU's end-2016 camp withdrawal, forcing handover of ANC/delivery to IRC) and later (the 2025 USAID collapse, which prompted SMRU's re-engagement — outside this report's window). The contrast is instructive: Cox's Bazar's dependence on a single UN agency's commodity line created a single point of failure in 2021, whereas Mae La's diversified, long-tenure provider base buffered it from that specific shock — though it proved equally vulnerable to its own donor shocks in other years.

## 8. Limitations

Mae La site-level HIS data beyond 2018 were not retrievable within this review; 2019–2023 inferences rest on the 2000–2018 retrospective record. Cox's Bazar MMR is survey-based (RAMOS) with wide confidence intervals; MPMSR death counts (57–96/year) are surveillance minima, and applying them to ~27,000–34,000 annual facility deliveries implies facility-observed ratios whose denominators undercount home births — hence no single post-2018 MMR point estimate is defensible. PPH incidence (per 100 deliveries) is unpublished for both settings; cause-of-death proportions are used instead. The two settings' "ANC 4+" figures use different denominators (all estimated deliveries vs. facility births), and Cox's Bazar figures carry documented inter-system discrepancies (43% vs. >80% facility delivery in 2023 concurrent-monitoring vs. CHW-WG data).

## 9. Conclusion

From 2017–2023, Mae La demonstrated what a protracted, consolidated, referral-integrated refugee obstetric system can achieve: ≥95% skilled attendance, >90% ANC coverage, zero PPH facility deaths, and neonatal mortality at or below the Thai national rate. Cox's Bazar demonstrated both the speed and the ceiling of emergency response: facility deliveries rose seven-fold in six years and maternal deaths fell ~40% from 2021 to 2023, yet hemorrhage-dominant facility mortality, ~17–47% genuine ANC4 completion depending on the data system, and neonatal mortality 4.5 times Mae La's level persisted. The correlates are structural, not merely financial: midwife density built over decades vs. years, surgical obstetrics within a reliable transport corridor vs. across a congested referral chain, and TBA trust institutionalized vs. competed with. The 2021 UNFPA cut tested Cox's Bazar's single-pipeline dependency and exposed continuity as visit-volume maintained at the expense of completed care; Mae La, outside UNFPA's operational footprint, was untouched by that shock — a reminder that in refugee maternal health, who funds the commodity line is as determinative as who staffs the delivery room.

- ANC4: Mae La >90% vs Cox's Bazar 17% (2022 DHIS2 facility-reported) — but note definitional differences; CHW-WG data shows ~77-85% coverage in 2023; WHO concurrent monitoring suggested only 43% facility delivery — data quality caveats.

Structure the report:
1. Executive summary
2. Data sources & caveats
3. Indicator comparison table
4. Cox's Bazar trajectory 2017-2023
5. Mae La profile

Note caveats: Mae La HIS data mostly through 2018; 2019-2023 thin; SMRU departure 2016, handover to PU-AMI then ARC/IRC; UNFPA not present in Mae La so 2021 cut asymmetry; PPH incidence rates not directly comparable.

Compute some numbers via mental math:
- 83 deaths × 0.44 = 36.5 hemorrhage deaths in 2022 Cox's Bazar.
- 57 × 0.35 = 20 (matches n=20).
- Facility delivery trend: home delivery 88% (2018) → 30% (Q1 2021) = facility 12% → 70%.
- ANC4 increase: 26,965 → 39,307 = +45.7% (matches).
- Mae La 2018: 1,200 deliveries/yr, ~95% SBA.
- Midwife ratio Cox's: 283 midwives / ~919,000 Rohingya = 1:3,247. If 283 is 60% → total ~470 midwives → 1:1,955. WRA ~20% → ~184k WRA → 1:392 WRA.
- Mae La nurses: 72/39,061 = 1:543.

Write final report now. Be honest about uncertainty and data gaps, and correct premise where needed (e.g., "UNFPA funding reduction affected both locations" — evidence only supports Cox's Bazar; Mae La unaffected directly since UNFPA doesn't operate there; also Mae La's major funding shock was 2015-2016 transition and later USAID 2025 freeze which is outside window).

# Medical-Grade Vaccine Refrigeration Procurement Analysis
## 200-Bed Hospital Network — 8 Rural Clinic Sites in Montana & Wyoming

---

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY — CRITICAL FINDINGS FIRST

**1. One of your three shortlisted products must be disqualified immediately.** The Panasonic MDF-DU702VH-PA is **not a refrigerator**. It is a -40°C to -86°C ultra-low temperature (ULT) freezer (729 L, 220V, NEMA 6-15P), designed for biorepositories and -80°C storage such as Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine ultra-cold requirements (https://www.phchd.com/us/biomedical/preservation/ultra-low-freezers/mdf-du702vhpa; https://markitbiomedical.com/knowledge-center/files/11559_3_PHCBI_MDF_DU702VH_technical_spec_vf.pdf). It cannot hold the +2°C to +8°C range required for routine refrigerated vaccines, is not certified to NSF/ANSI 456, draws 2-6x the energy of the refrigerator candidates, and costs roughly $24,300-$24,500 per unit (https://www.graylinemedical.com/products/panasonic-vip-eco-series-ultralow-temperature-freezers-freezer-25-7cf-86c-vip-eco-natural-230v-mdf-du702vh-pa). The correct PHCbi/Panasonic comparators for this application would be the MPR-S300H-PA (12.2 cu ft, +2°C to +14°C, marketed as "designed to meet CDC requirements for vaccine and biologics storage... where power brown-outs or outages are common") or MPR-722-PA (https://www.phchd.com/us/biomedical/preservation/pharmaceutical-refrigerators/mpr-s300h-pa; https://daiscientific.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/PHC_MPR-S300H-Product-Sheet.pdf). I recommend correcting the specification. The ULT is analyzed below only for completeness.

**2. No candidate — and no conventional medical-grade refrigerator — will survive a 6-12 hour outage on thermal mass alone.** Published evidence indicates pharmaceutical-grade refrigerators "can warm to 8 °C in less than one hour after the power is discontinued" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4896515/). Thermo Fisher's own factory test data shows an unloaded TSX 12 cu ft unit warming from 5°C to 15°C in 171 minutes; a linear interpolation puts 8°C (the CDC upper limit) at roughly 45-55 minutes (https://www.scientificlabs.com/handlers/libraryFiles.ashx?filename=Technical_Data_Sheets_T_TSX1205PV.pdf). **Therefore, an external UPS or generator at every site is a mandatory line item regardless of which refrigerator you select.** The "battery backup" specifications advertised by manufacturers power only the controller/alarms, not the compressor.

**3. Recommendation: Helmer Scientific GX Solutions as primary**, with Thermo Fisher TSX as a fully acceptable alternative if native cellular monitoring outweighs energy efficiency and service-cost predictability in your weighting. Rationale is developed criterion-by-criterion below.

---

## CANDIDATE PROFILES

### A. Helmer Scientific GX Solutions (i.Series / Horizon Series)
Representative clinic-size models: iPR105-GX undercounter (5.3 cu ft / 150 L, up to 4,000 doses), iPR113-GX (13.3 cu ft), iPR120-GX (20.2 cu ft), iPR125-GX (25.2 cu ft). All pharmacy ("PR") GX models are ETL-certified to NSF/ANSI 456, ENERGY STAR certified, R600a hydrocarbon refrigerant, variable-capacity compressor (OptiCool), +2°C to +10°C range, +5°C setpoint (https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-01/Vaccine-Storage-Solutions-380474-1.pdf; https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iPR113GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380443-1.pdf).

Documented performance (factory test data):
| Model | Uniformity | Stability | Recovery to 8°C after 3-min door opening | Pull-down | Energy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPR105-GX (5.3 cu ft) | ±1.0°C | 0.72°C | 11 min | 37 min (to 4°C) | 1.37 kWh/day |
| iPR120-GX (20 cu ft) | ±1.0°C | 0.41°C | 6 min | 49 min (to 5°C) | 3.01 kWh/day |
| iPR125-GX (25 cu ft) | ±1.0°C | — | — | — | — |
| iPR245-GX (45 cu ft) | ±1.0°C | 0.44°C | 10 min | 64 min | — |
(https://www.laboratory-equipment.com/ipr105-gx-iseries-ada-undercounter-pharmacy-refrigerator-solid-door-helmer-scientific-5115105-1.html; https://www.laboratory-equipment.com/media/asset-library/i/p/ipr120-gx-iseries-upright-pharmacy-refrigerator-glass-doors-data-sheet-helmer-scientific.pdf; https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2019-10/iPR245GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380422-1.pdf)

### B. Thermo Fisher Scientific TSX Series (Pharmacy models)
Representative models: TSX1205PA (11.5 cu ft, 115V NEMA 5-15), TSX2305PA (23 cu ft), TSX3005PA (29.2 cu ft), TSX5005PA (51.1 cu ft). NSF/ANSI 456 certified, ENERGY STAR, R290 refrigerant, V-drive variable-speed compressor, +2°C to +8°C range, +5°C setpoint (https://www.thermofisher.com/order/catalog/product/TSX3005PV; https://www.fishersci.com/shop/products/tsx-series-high-performance-pharmacy-refrigerators/TSX2305PA).

Documented factory test performance:
| Model | Uniformity | Stability | 1-min door recovery | Pull-down to 5°C | Warm-up 5→15°C (unloaded) | Energy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSX1205 (12 cu ft) | 0.9°C | 2.3°C | 3 min | 9 min | 171 min | 3.2 kWh/day |
| TSX3005 (30 cu ft) | 0.8°C | 2.3°C | 2 min | 10 min | 180 min | 4.0 kWh/day |
| TSX5005 (50 cu ft) | peak variation +1.6/-2.5°C | — | — | — | — | — |
(https://www.scientificlabs.com/handlers/libraryFiles.ashx?filename=Technical_Data_Sheets_T_TSX1205PV.pdf; https://www.scientificlabs.com/handlers/libraryFiles.ashx?filename=Technical_Data_Sheets_T_TSX3005PV.pdf; https://katalog.lhlab.dk/upload_dir/docs/datablade/TH-TSX5005PV-DATABLAD(4C).pdf)

### C. Panasonic/PHCbi MDF-DU702VH-PA (DISQUALIFIED for refrigerated vaccine storage)
-86°C-class ULT freezer; cascade dual 750W compressors; 7.30 kWh/day steady-state / 7.87 kWh/day with door openings (ENERGY STAR); 220V only; ~$24,319-$24,496; 5-year parts & labor warranty (https://markitbiomedical.com/knowledge-center/files/11559_3_PHCBI_MDF_DU702VH_technical_spec_vf.pdf; https://daiscientific.com/product/phcbi-mdf-du702vh-pa-vip-natural-refrigerants-series-ultra-low-temperature-freezers/). Not NSF/ANSI 456 certified; temperature range incompatible with 2-8°C vaccines. Retain only if your formulary requires -70°C/-80°C ultra-cold capacity at a hub site.

---

## CRITERION 1: BATTERY BACKUP DURING 6-12 HOUR OUTAGES

**What the units actually provide:**
- **Helmer GX (i.Series):** "Battery Back-up: Yes, 20 hr display & alarm back up for i.C3® touchscreen | Rechargeable 12V, lead acid" (https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iPR125GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380420-1.pdf; https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iPR256GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380424-1.pdf). This keeps temperature display, data logging, power-failure and high/low temperature alarms, and the remote alarm contacts alive for ~20 hours — fully covering a 12-hour outage **for monitoring and alerting only. It does not run the compressor.**
- **Thermo TSX:** Power-failure alarm (audible/visual); the separate Smart-Vue Pro monitoring loggers are battery-backed and buffer 4,000 readings per sensor (https://www.laboratory-equipment.com/media/asset-library/t/s/tsx-series-high-performance-undercounter-refrigerators-brochure-thermo-fisher-scientific.pdf; https://www.fishersci.com/shop/products/smart-vue-pro-remote-monitoring-cellular-data-plans-18/11731057). No compressor backup.
- **Panasonic ULT:** Power-failure alarm; no cooling backup in standard configuration.

**Cooling holdover reality check (quantitative):**
- TSX1205 factory warm-up: 5°C→15°C in 171 min unloaded. Rate ≈ 10°C/171 min = 0.0585°C/min. Estimated time from 5°C setpoint to the CDC 8°C ceiling: 3°C ÷ 0.0585 ≈ **51 minutes** (unloaded; a full vaccine load adds thermal mass but the order of magnitude holds). TSX3005: 180 min → ≈54 min (sources above).
- Independent peer-reviewed commentary confirms the class behavior: pharmaceutical refrigerators warm to 8°C in under one hour without power, and refrigerator selection in outage-prone grids must be paired with power backup planning (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4896515/).
- Helmer does not publish warm-up/holdover figures; construction class is comparable, so assume the same ~1-hour envelope absent test data. **This is an evidence gap — request holdover test data from Helmer before award.**
- Contrast with purpose-built outage-resilient designs (not on your shortlist): ice-lined/WHO-PQS units hold 2-8°C for 60+ hours to 6 days (e.g., Haier HBC series holdover 60 h 50 min to 8°C; TempArmour up to ~6 days) (https://pdf.medicalexpo.com/pdf/haier-biomedical/haier-ice-lined-refrigerator-hbc-80-150-260/299012-269212.html; https://www.onehealth.ca/Portals/1/TempArmour%20User%20Guide%20BFRV84%20-%20May%202020.pdf). If any of your 8 sites cannot support a UPS/generator, this product class — not any of the three shortlistees — is the technically correct answer.

**Required backup-power sizing per site (using average power from nameplate energy data):**
- Helmer iPR105-GX: 1.37 kWh/day ÷ 24 h ≈ 57 W average → 12-h outage ≈ 0.68 kWh. A 1.5 kVA double-conversion UPS (~1 kWh usable, sized for compressor start surge) covers 12 h.
- TSX1205PA: 3.2 kWh/day ≈ 133 W average → 12 h ≈ 1.6 kWh → 2 kWh-class UPS.
- Panasonic ULT: 7.87 kWh/day ≈ 328 W average, 220V, dual 750W compressors → 12 h ≈ 3.9 kWh and a 220V UPS/transfer switch — materially more expensive and a hard electrical retrofit in small clinics.
- Montana context: NorthWestern Energy's SAIDI (average interruption duration including major event days) is 233.4 minutes/year, i.e., outages of several hours are routine, and multi-hour tail events are exactly your planning case (https://powerbillfacts.com/utility/northwestern-energy-llc-mt-12825/).

**Verdict:** Helmer wins this criterion on (a) the only documented multi-hour *monitoring* autonomy (20 h) and (b) the smallest load, which halves the required UPS capacity and cost per site.

## CRITERION 2: TEMPERATURE RECOVERY AFTER POWER RESTORATION

- **Helmer GX:** Documented recovery to 8°C after a full 3-minute door opening: 6 min (20 cu ft) to 11 min (undercounter); pull-down from ambient to setpoint 37-49 min. Variable-capacity compressor runs 1300-4000 rpm to modulate recovery (sources above). Stability 0.41-0.72°C.
- **Thermo TSX:** Recovery to 5°C after a 1-minute door opening: 2-3 min; pull-down to 5°C: 9-10 min. V-drive detects usage patterns and raises compressor speed after door openings (https://www.fishersci.ca/shop/products/tsx-series-high-performance-pharmacy-refrigerators/tsx5005pd). Stability 2.3°C in factory cycle testing — notably wider than Helmer's published 0.41-0.72°C, though both sit well inside ±1.0-2.5°C uniformity envelopes required by NSF 456.
- After a full outage where the cabinet has drifted toward ambient, expect either brand to return to setpoint in well under one hour (pull-down data above); the controlling risk is the outage duration, not recovery speed.
- **Panasonic ULT:** pull-down/recovery curves published only for the -80°C regime; not applicable.

**Verdict:** Both refrigerator lines recover quickly; Helmer publishes tighter stability (0.41°C vs 2.3°C) and stronger door-opening recovery at comparable sizes. Slight edge Helmer.

## CRITERION 3: CDC VACCINE STORAGE AND HANDLING TOOLKIT COMPLIANCE

CDC requires: purpose-built/pharmaceutical-grade storage; a digital data logger (DDL) with detachable buffered probe; min/max display; uncertainty ±0.5°C; programmable logging interval of at least every 30 minutes; out-of-range alarm; low-battery indicator; and a current Certificate of Calibration (recalibrated every 2-3 years) (https://www.cdc.gov/pinkbook/hcp/table-of-contents/chapter-5-vaccine-storage-and-handling.html; https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/hcp/downloads/storage-handling-toolkit.pdf).

| Toolkit element | Helmer GX | Thermo TSX | Panasonic MDF-DU702VH-PA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose-built medical-grade | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ (medical device, wrong temperature class) |
| NSF/ANSI 456 certification | ✓ ETL certified | ✓ certified | ✗ |
| Buffered probe | ✓ 4 oz ballast bottle; NSF option includes Certificate of Calibration (https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iLR113GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380447-1.pdf) | Via Smart-Vue Pro calibrated loggers or third-party DDL | Air probe (Pt-1000); not designed for 2-8°C DDL practice |
| Min/max, event log, ≤30-min logging | ✓ i.C3 logs/graphs; USB/PDF/CSV export (https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2019-09/product-guide-ic3-pdf-reports-380458-1.pdf) | ✓ via monitoring system | LCD log, USB export |
| Alarms (power fail, high/low, door, low battery) | ✓ incl. low-battery alarm | ✓ | ✓ (power, high/low, sensor, door) |
| Calibration certificate/service | ✓ NIST/ISO 17025 via TrueBlue PM (https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2024-01/Technical-Service-Preventative-Maintenance-and-Calibration-Programs-S3R039.pdf) | ✓ via service/Smart-Vue calibrated loggers | ISO factory certs; no vaccine-program calibration pathway |

**Verdict:** Helmer and TSX both satisfy the Toolkit when paired with a calibrated DDL (budget a redundant independent DDL per site either way — standard VFC practice). Panasonic fails the temperature-class requirement outright.

## CRITERION 4: REMOTE MONITORING OVER CELLULAR WITH SPOTTY CONNECTIVITY

- **Thermo TSX + Smart-Vue Pro — strongest native answer.** LoRaWAN sensors (up to 9 km in-building/campus range) feed a gateway available in **Ethernet or 4G cellular**; cloud platform with SMS/email/phone/push alerts; 21 CFR Part 11 audit trail; each logger buffers 4,000 readings (store-and-forward through coverage gaps — the single most important feature for spotty rural LTE); cellular data plans sold per year covering "up to 10 devices," which neatly fits an 8-clinic network (https://www.laboratory-equipment.com/media/asset-library/s/m/smart-vue-pro-monitoring-system-brochure-thermo-fishser-scientific-2021.pdf; https://www.fishersci.com/shop/products/smart-vue-pro-remote-monitoring-cellular-data-plans-18/11731057; https://www.fishersci.com/shop/products/smart-vue-pro-laboratory-remote-monitoring-pro-kits-16/11731031). Note: with 8 geographically dispersed clinics you need one 4G gateway *per site* (the 9 km LoRa range does not bridge towns); the per-plan "10 devices" covers sensors, not gateways.
- **Helmer GX — capable but requires a bolt-on.** i.Series provides Ethernet/RJ45 with a documented REST API and Modbus TCP, remote alarm contacts, and USB (https://www.helmerinc.com/connectivity; https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2022-02/iPR245GX-Technical-Data-Sheet-380422-1.pdf). There is **no native cellular option**. Two workable architectures: (a) clinic LTE router/gateway feeding the Ethernet API to your monitoring platform; (b) remote alarm contacts wired to a third-party cellular DDL/alarm dialer — the common rural VFC pattern. Helmer's own remote alarm panel holds only ~2 hours of battery, so do not rely on it as the outage-notification path (https://www.helmerinc.com/sites/default/files/2020-06/Remote-Alarm-Operation-Service-Manual-360112-1.pdf). Local resilience is excellent: the i.C3 stores months of event data and ~20 h of battery-backed logging/alarming locally even if the network is down.
- **Panasonic ULT:** USB and remote alarm contacts only; fully dependent on third-party monitoring.

Field evidence that cellular remote temperature monitoring works in hard-to-serve areas: a Haiti study of 16 remote monitoring devices on 24 vaccine refrigerators across solar/propane/grid sites found RTMD use feasible, with measured costs of $686 start-up, $179/year maintenance, and $9/year electricity per refrigerator (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5805098/). Use these as grounded benchmarks for your third-party monitoring budget if you choose Helmer.

**Verdict:** TSX/Smart-Vue Pro wins natively (integrated 4G, buffering, Part 11 audit trail). Helmer reaches functional parity with ~$250-$700/site of third-party cellular hardware plus ~$150-$300/site/year subscription, per the Haiti cost benchmark.

## CRITERION 5 & 7: 10-YEAR TOTAL COST, INCLUDING MT/WY UTILITY RATES AND RURAL SERVICE

**Utility rate basis (commercial sector, EIA-derived):**
- Montana commercial: ≈11.0-13.5 ¢/kWh (EIA annual 11.87¢; Dec 2024 11.00¢; NorthWestern Energy bundled commercial 13.51¢) (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_02_10.html; https://powerbillfacts.com/state/montana/2024-12/; https://powerbillfacts.com/utility/northwestern-energy-llc-mt-12825/)
- Wyoming commercial: ≈9.3-10.0 ¢/kWh (EIA 9.27¢; EPM 9.79-10.01¢) (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_02_10.html; https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a)
- I use MT 11.9¢ and WY 9.3¢ as midpoints. These are small (<0.5 kW) loads — demand charges are immaterial.

**Energy cost math (8 units, 10 years):**
- Helmer iPR105-GX: 1.37 kWh/day × 365 × 8 = 4,001 kWh/yr → 40,010 kWh/10 yr → **$4,761 (MT) / $3,721 (WY)**. (If you deploy 20 cu ft uprights at 3.01 kWh/day, roughly double these figures.)
- TSX1205PA: 3.2 kWh/day × 365 × 8 = 9,344 kWh/yr → 93,440 kWh/10 yr → **$11,119 (MT) / $8,690 (WY)**.
- Panasonic ULT: 7.87 kWh/day × 365 × 8 = 22,980 kWh/yr → 229,800 kWh/10 yr → **$27,346 (MT) / $21,371 (WY)**.
- **Backup-power consumption cost is trivial:** a 12-h outage draws 0.68-1.6 kWh per refrigerator ≈ **$0.08-$0.19 per outage at MT/WY commercial rates**. Even 8 outages/year × 8 sites is under $150/year network-wide. Your backup investment is capital (UPS/generator), not energy — do not let utility tariffs drive backup sizing decisions.

# Research Report: Longwood Gardens' "Nature's Castles: The Treehouse Reimagined" (2008)

## Bottom Line

Longwood Gardens' 2008 installation "Nature's Castles: The Treehouse Reimagined" (Kennett Square, PA) featured three treehouses created by **two specialist treehouse design-build firms, working with a collaborating architect** — not a single designer:

- **Canopy Cathedral** and **The Birdhouse** were designed and constructed by **Peter ("Pete") Nelson and Jake Jacob of TreeHouse Workshop, Inc., Seattle, Washington** (the firm was founded by Nelson and Jacob in 1997).
- **Lookout Loft** was designed and built by **Forever Young Treehouses of Burlington, Vermont**, a nonprofit co-founded by **Bill Allen and Phil Trabulsy** specializing in universally accessible treehouses.
- **Matthew Millan Architects of Philadelphia** served as the collaborating architectural firm, working "with Longwood Gardens and the two premier treehouse companies in the U.S." on all three structures.

The strongest contemporaneous sources describing the design concept and construction process are two newspaper articles published **April 24, 2008** — the *Daily Local News* (West Chester, PA) and the *Delco Times* (Bette Alburger) — supplemented by the *Philadelphia Inquirer* (April 25 and May 16, 2008), the *Washington Post* (October 1–2, 2008), and *Main Line Today* (August 27, 2008). All are cited with URLs below.

---

## 1. Who Designed the Treehouses

### TreeHouse Workshop, Inc. (Seattle, WA) — Canopy Cathedral and The Birdhouse

The *Daily Local News*, April 24, 2008: "The largest is called Canopy Cathedral, a two-story ornate house inspired by a Norwegian Stave Church. **Designed by Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob of Treehouse Workshop Inc in Seattle, Wash.**, the 400-square foot house will have an intricate glass facade and hand carved fantastic creatures throughout." (https://www.dailylocal.com/2008/04/24/longwood-builds-natures-castles-in-the-gardens-trees/)

The *Delco Times*, April 24, 2008 (Bette Alburger): "...it was inspired by a Norwegian Stave Church, according to **designers Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob of TreeHouse Workshop Inc. in Seattle, Washington**... Nelson, author of the leading books on treehouses, also designed the third treehouse. Called the Birdhouse, it's the tallest of the three..." (https://www.delcotimes.com/2008/04/24/treehouses-are-looking-up-at-longwood-gardens/)

The *Washington Post*, October 1–2, 2008, "Artisan Treehouses Extend Their Lease at Longwood Gardens": "The other two treehouses at Longwood, called the Birdhouse and the Canopy Cathedral, were **designed and constructed by the Seattle-based TreeHouse Workshop, founded in 1997 by Pete Nelson and Jake Jacob**. They have built more than 100 in 32 states and nine countries..." (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/2008/10/02/artisan-treehouses-extend-their-lease-at-longwood-gardens/0872cd19-1d4a-445c-a2f0-d7206d80de84/)

Longwood Gardens' own website (retrospective confirmation): "Designed by **Peter Nelson of TreeHouse Workshop, Inc. in Seattle**, it boasts an intricate glass façade and hand-carved fantastical creatures throughout its 400 square-feet." (https://longwoodgardens.org/gardens/lakes-district/large-small-lake)

### Forever Young Treehouses (Burlington, VT) — Lookout Loft

*Daily Local News*, April 24, 2008: "Lookout Loft is a 720 square foot rustic Adirondack-style structure behind the Peirce House on Forest Walk. Designed to be handicapped accessible... **Designed by Forever Young Treehouses of Burlington, Vt.**..."

*Delco Times*, April 24, 2008: "...the largest of the treehouses, it was designed by **Forever Young Treehouses of Burlington, Vermont, co-founded by Bill Allen and Phil Trabulsy**. Measuring 720-square-feet... Forever Young Treehouses is known for creating and promoting construction of treehouses that can be enjoyed by individuals with disabilities and special needs. A large ramp leading up to Lookout Loft makes it accessible to all."

*Philadelphia Inquirer*, May 16, 2008 ("Builder makes trees accessible for all," Virginia A. Smith): "Bill Allen's Burlington, Vt., nonprofit is aptly named Forever Young Treehouses... For the last eight years, Forever Young has built universally accessible tree houses around the country, including at Paul Newman's Hole in the Wall Gang summer camp in Ashford, Conn.... **Forever Young recently created Lookout Loft, one of three tree houses in Longwood Gardens' 'Nature's Castles' exhibit**..." (https://www.inquirer.com/philly/columnists/virginia_smith/20080516_Builder_makes_trees_accessible_for_all.html)

### Matthew Millan Architects (Philadelphia, PA) — Collaborating Architect

The firm's own portfolio (retrospective, but the firm's direct claim): "**Matthew Millan Architects worked with Longwood Gardens and the two premier treehouse companies in the U.S. to create these unique arboreal structures**... we designed each treehouse to respond to their individual settings and offer different interpretive opportunities." (https://millanarchitects.com/portfolio/institutional/natures-castles-the-treehouses-at-longwood-gardens-the-canopy-cathedral/)

Contemporaneous corroboration of Millan's role exists in an archived event listing for an April 21, 2008 Longwood lecture, "Treehouses: the Nuts & Bolts & What Holds Them Up": "**Peter Nelson, Jake Jacobs and Matthew Millan** of the Treehouse Workshop discuss topics such as tree selection, construction specifics and the building process." (https://archive.upcoming.org/event/treehouses-the-nuts-bolts-what-holds-them-up-427292)

---

## 2. Contemporaneous Sources (2008 or Earlier) on Design Concept and Construction

### Primary recommendations

**A. Bette Alburger, "Treehouses are looking up at Longwood Gardens," *Delco Times*, April 24, 2008** (https://www.delcotimes.com/2008/04/24/treehouses-are-looking-up-at-longwood-gardens/) — the single richest contemporaneous account of both concept and construction:

- **Design concept**: The display "showcases the creative work of the nation's best treehouse designers"; for children "a chance to climb up into a treehouse and get a birds-eye view of the Gardens... while being reconnected with nature"; for adults it "rekindles memories of childhood." Longwood Director Paul Redman: "The 'Nature's Castles' display is designed to celebrate trees and engage our guests in an exciting and unique way about the beauty and importance of trees."
- **Construction process / sustainability**: "Sharon Loving, head of Longwood's horticulture department, stressed that the treehouses were designed and built with sensitivity to the environment... recycled or reclaimed lumber was used in construction and no root systems were disturbed... the houses themselves do not rely on the trees for structural support." Specifics: the Birdhouse's lumber "was recovered from an old dairy farm in Washington state. The floorboards came from a dismantled toothpaste factory in Toronto, Canada, and the 2-by-8-foot rafters were recovered from a dismantled warehouse in Vancouver, British Columbia... windows of tight-grained Douglas Fir came from trees felled in landslides or blown down in storms." Lookout Loft "is held up by more than 1,300 pounds of steel" [note: the *Daily Local* says 13,000 pounds — see discrepancies below].
- Details: Lookout Loft's handrail was "inspired by the Gothic Folly in Longwood's recently opened Indoor Children's Garden"; Canopy Cathedral "features an intricate glass facade and hand-carved fantastical creatures... A large deck allows visitors to enjoy a panoramic perch amid a grove of stately tulip poplars."

**B. "Longwood builds 'nature's castles' in the gardens' trees," *Daily Local News*, April 24, 2008** (https://www.dailylocal.com/2008/04/24/longwood-builds-natures-castles-in-the-gardens-trees/) — written from the press preview (attended by Pocopson Elementary third-graders), it documents:

- Lookout Loft's foundation engineering: "13,000 pounds of salvaged steel holding it up – very unobtrusively... **a special pin foundation has concrete footings with extended steel rods that go between the tree roots and cause no damage**"; railings of naturally contoured wood; finish "containing citrus oil and beeswax."
- The Birdhouse: "320 square feet, is made from salvaged wood from an old dairy barn. It rises 20 feet off the ground... carefully built over a large rotted out tree trunk, which has been kept so visitors will be able to peer deep inside the trunk."
- Canopy Cathedral: "Carefully placed so it would not injure nearby trees"; unfinished at opening (missing carvings and railings).

### Additional contemporaneous sources

- **Kristin Granero, "Open house – up in the Longwood trees," *Philadelphia Inquirer*, April 25, 2008** — opening-weekend coverage; notes visitors could "meet tree-house designers." (https://www.inquirer.com/philly/phillywomen/20080425_Open_house_-_up_in_the_Longwood_trees.html)
- **Virginia A. Smith, "Lofty ideas," *Philadelphia Inquirer*, May 16, 2008** — situates the exhibit in the 2008 wave of public-garden treehouse exhibits (Morris Arboretum, Tyler Arboretum, Kew Gardens); reports Nature's Castles "opened April 26" and "Cost: $1 million." (https://www.inquirer.com/philly/entertainment/20080516_Lofty_ideas.html)
- **Eileen Smith Dallabrida, "Lofty Digs," *Main Line Today*, August 27, 2008** — "The other two treehouses... are the work of Peter Nelson and Jake Jacobs of TreeHouse Workshop"; Canopy Cathedral "has a 589-square-foot interior"; "**The Longwood treehouses took about as long to build—four months—and cost as much as traditional homes, $1 million**." (https://mainlinetoday.com/life-style/lofty-digs/; verified via search excerpt; full page not directly retrievable)
- ***Washington Post*, October 1–2, 2008** (cited above) — documents that the exhibit was so successful "plans to close and dismantle it around Thanksgiving have been abandoned. The creations will remain at Longwood for possibly five years, said director Paul Redman."
- **Gretchen McKay, "At Longwood Gardens, fantastic treehouses grow," *Pittsburgh Post-Gazette*, July 5, 2008** (https://www.post-gazette.com/life/homes/2008/07/05/at-longwood-gardens-fantastic-treehouses-grow/stories/200807050158; existence confirmed, though the page body was not retrievable in this session)
- **NBC 10 Philadelphia coverage, April 17–18, 2008** (preserved via a contemporary blog): quotes designer Pete Nelson on the design concept — "**The trees dictate the design**... Nelson said he finds the trees first before coming up with a design." (http://www.pocketburgers.com/2008/04/luxurious-tree-houses-have-adults-never.html)
- **Contemporaneous visitor documentation**: a visiting blogger on April 26, 2008 recorded the interpretive signage: "These houses are all tree-friendly. They are not anchored to the trees themselves... **They are built using a pin system that stabilizes the treehouse without doing any damage**... the treehouses were all built of reclaimed wood from old mills, factories and barns"; Lookout Loft has "over 75 feet of ramps" and "a built-in skylight that a tree grows right through." (http://fromheretomaine.blogspot.com/2008/04/treehuggers-delight.html)
- **Longwood's own 2008 events announcement** (via Hotel Executive wire, 2008): "Nature's Castles (April 26–September 1) is a spectacular display of treehouses created around the Gardens." (https://www.hotelexecutive.com/newswire/6508/longwood-gardensandamp39-2008-calendar-of-events)

---

## 3. Key Facts and Figures (as reported in 2008)

| Item | Canopy Cathedral | The Birdhouse | Lookout Loft |
|---|---|---|---|
| Designer | Peter Nelson & Jake Jacob, TreeHouse Workshop Inc. (Seattle) | Peter Nelson / TreeHouse Workshop (Seattle) | Forever Young Treehouses (Burlington, VT) |
| Style | Two-story, Norwegian stave church-inspired | Cedar, built over a rotted trunk; bird's-eye view | Rustic Adirondack, ADA-accessible ramped platforms |
| Size | 400 sq ft (Longwood/Daily Local/Delco); 589 sq ft interior (Main Line Today) | 320 sq ft, ~20 ft up | 720 sq ft |
| Notable materials | Reclaimed Douglas fir, cedar, glass façade, hand-carved creatures | Dairy-barn wood (WA), toothpaste-factory floorboards (Toronto), warehouse rafters (Vancouver, BC) | ~13,000 lbs salvaged steel (Daily Local), natural-contour railings, citrus-oil/beeswax finish |

- **Cost**: ~$1 million for the project (*Philadelphia Inquirer*, May 16, 2008; *Main Line Today*, Aug 27, 2008).
- **Construction time**: about four months (*Main Line Today*, Aug 27, 2008; also cited by Penn State's PA Book project: "In 2008, after four months of construction, Longwood invited visitors to explore 'Nature's Castles: The Treehouse Reimagined'" — https://pabook.libraries.psu.edu/literary-cultural-heritage-map-pa/feature-articles/longwood-gardens-preservation-paradise).
- **Dates**: press preview in the week before opening (on or about April 17–24); public opening Arbor Day weekend, April 25–27, 2008 (the *Inquirer* and *Main Line Today* give April 26 as opening day); advertised to run through November 23, 2008.
- **Permanence**: though marketed as seasonal, the structures were pin-founded and durable; the *Daily Local* (April 24, 2008) quoted Redman that they "definitely would not be torn down in November," and the *Washington Post* (Oct 2008) reported the dismantling plan was abandoned. Longwood's current website confirms: the treehouses "were meant to live through Labor Day of the year they were constructed, but they proved so popular they remain here today." (https://longwoodgardens.org/gardens/lakes-district/large-small-lake)

---

## 4. Discrepancies and Uncertainty

- **Canopy Cathedral square footage**: 400 sq ft in most 2008 press accounts (and on Longwood's site today) vs. 589 sq ft in *Main Line Today* and a contemporary visitor blog — the larger figure likely includes the wrap-around balcony/deck.
- **Lookout Loft steel weight**: 13,000 lbs (*Daily Local*) vs. "more than 1,300 pounds" (*Delco Times*). The 13,000-lb figure is more plausible for 720 sq ft of structure on steel, but this cannot be resolved from the available sources.
- **Opening date**: sources variously say the exhibit opened April 24 (preview), April 25, or April 26, 2008; the weight of evidence points to a press preview April 24 and public opening over Arbor Day weekend, April 25–27, 2008.
- **Birdhouse size**: 320 sq ft per two contemporaneous sources; one secondary report cited 255 sq ft from a *Lancaster New Era* article (Jane Holahan, April 24, 2008) that I could not retrieve directly in this session, so that citation remains unverified.
- The *Washington Post* and *Pittsburgh Post-Gazette* article texts could not be fully retrieved in this session; their key passages were verified through search-result excerpts, and the Post-Gazette article is independently referenced by the Penn State PA Book project.

## Conclusion

The answer to the task: the three "Nature's Castles" treehouses were not the work of one architect but of **two treehouse design-build firms — TreeHouse Workshop, Inc. of Seattle (Peter Nelson and Jake Jacob), which created the Canopy Cathedral and the Birdhouse, and Forever Young Treehouses of Burlington, Vermont (Bill Allen and Phil Trabulsy), which created the accessible Lookout Loft — with Matthew Millan Architects of Philadelphia as the collaborating architectural firm**. The best contemporaneous documentation of the design concept and construction process is the pair of April 24, 2008 newspaper features in the *Delco Times* (Bette Alburger) and the *Daily Local News*, which describe the celebrate-trees concept, the reclaimed-lumber sourcing, the tree-friendly pin-foundation construction that avoided root damage, and the independent steel support systems — all corroborated by 2008 coverage in the *Philadelphia Inquirer*, *Washington Post*, and *Main Line Today*.
