Plus baseline fleet overhead if kept warm: to get 1–3 s pickup you keep ~a few idle agents during business hours — add maybe $5–10/day fleet idle cost → +$0.07–0.13/run. Total Buildkite ≈ **$200–600/1,000 runs** all-in (excluding platform fee). Show arithmetic.
- Note macOS/Windows multipliers change picture; polyglot JVM builds may need bigger runners — sensitivity: if builds need 4-core larger runners (GitHub $0.016/min), GitHub → $1,760/1k.

**Maintenance burden:**
- GitLab: 200 repos × `.gitlab-ci.yml` with `include:` from central templates project; `inputs` (GA 2024) enable parameterized templates; CI/CD Catalog for versioned components; compliance: pipeline execution policies (Ultimate) force stages/jobs across all projects — strong central control. Change management: semantic versions of components; downstream repos pin to major version. Residual per-service file: ~10–30 lines. Platform team maintains template repo(s) + runner fleet (if self-managed) — est. 1–2 FTE.
- GitHub: central `platform/.github` repo? No — reusable workflows live in any repo; org standard = `org/ci-templates` repo with versioned reusable workflows (tagged v1/v2), plus required workflows via org rulesets to enforce security scan workflows. Limits: reusable workflow called at job level (not step level), ≤4 nesting levels (I believe 4), ≤20 reusable workflows per workflow? — I recall "up to 20 unique called workflows"? The docs said: "a single workflow can call up to 20 reusable workflows" — hmm, I think the documented limit is 20 called workflows per workflow run, nested depth 4. Also can't use `github.event` contexts inside called workflow the same; outputs mapping clunky; matrix can't be defined in reusable workflow easily from caller? These frictions are real. Residual per-service caller workflow ~15–40 lines. No runtime generation — pipelines are static YAML resolved at queue time; matrix helps. Maintenance est. 1–2 FTE.
- Buildkite: one "pipeline generator" (code, e.g., Go CLI or Buildkite SDK) invoked by `buildkite-agent pipeline upload`; per-service repo holds only a tiny `pipeline.yml` (or even nothing — generated from service metadata catalog like Backstage). A single generator change rolls out instantly to all 200 services on next run — lowest marginal maintenance for fleet-wide change; but platform team owns agent fleet (AMI baking, autoscaling, Docker/build cache layers) — est. 2–3 FTE including infra, offset by dynamic gen savings. Buildkite Pipeline Templates (2024) offer UI-managed standardization alternative. Risk: generator becomes critical code — needs tests.

**Secrets rotation:**
- GitHub: org/repo/env secrets, manual or API-driven rotation (no native scheduled rotation); best practice: OIDC federation to cloud (no long-lived secrets at all) — `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` with role-to-assume; GitHub OIDC token claims customizable. Environments gate prod secrets. Rotation: push new value via API/Terraform; runners fetch at job start so rotation propagates immediately on next run.
- GitLab: CI/CD variables (masked/protected); external secrets: HashiCorp Vault (JWT auth), AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP (GA-ish 2024); `id_tokens` with aud claims. Rotation in Vault is transparent to pipelines (fetch at runtime). File-type variables for kubeconfig etc.
- Buildkite: no built-in project secrets store (by design — your threat model); agents fetch from AWS SSM/Secrets Manager/Vault via environment hooks or plugins (e.g., AWS SSM plugin); Buildkite OIDC tokens (2023+) allow agents/jobs to mint cloud creds; secrets never stored by Buildkite. Rotation = rotate in source store; zero pipeline changes. Strong fit for fintech because secret material stays in your boundary; audit via CloudTrail/Vault audit.
- For fintech: short-lived OIDC credentials are the modern answer; all three support OIDC now.

**Compliance audit trails:**
- GitLab Ultimate: streaming audit events, audit event API, compliance center, separation of duties (protected branches + protected environments + approval rules), pipeline execution policies, artifact evidence, retention. Strongest out-of-box SOC2/PCI mapping.
- GitHub Enterprise: audit log (API/streaming to SIEM), rulesets, environment required reviewers, deployment history + statuses API, artifact attestations (SLSA provenance), CODEOWNERS review enforcement. Solid but evidence assembly across repos is DIY.
- Buildkite: audit events (GraphQL/API, Enterprise), job logs stored in your S3 (you control retention/WORM), annotations/metadata for evidence; but compliance story largely constructed on your side (good: data never leaves your infra; bad: you build the reporting). Pair with Backstage/Scorecards.

**Rollback orchestration / progressive delivery:**
- GitLab: `environment` + `action: stop`, rollback = retry previous deployment job (docs: "Retrying and rolling back"); auto rollback via `on_failure` job that runs rollback script; canary: weighted deploys via Kubernetes incremental rollout (legacy) or Flagger/Argo Rollouts integrated via CI; `deployment_approvals` API (Ultimate).

(careful: pre-exit hooks). Mature pattern: attribute-driven dynamic rollback step injection.

I vaguely recall Equifax: "from 1 hour to minutes..." Not sure. I'll cite customers index + name Rabobank hedged. Also "Deutsche Börse"? no. "Tatra banka"? There IS a GitLab case study "Tatra banka"? unsure. Keep Rabobank + index.
- GitHub Actions at scale in finance: GitHub customer stories: "American Fidelity"? unsure. "DTCC"? GitHub customer story exists for "DTCC"? I don't recall. "Moody's" — I believe there IS a GitHub customer story for Moody's. Also "Nationwide" — I recall a Nationwide (UK building society) GitHub Enterprise story. And "Stripe"? no. "Wise"? no. Monzo deploys: I'm fairly confident Monzo has publicly stated deploying dozens-to-hundreds of times per day across ~thousands of services. Their blog: https://monzo.com/blog/technology. Hedge.

Score across: dev wait time (Buildkite best), maintenance burden for 200 services (Buildkite dynamic gen best; GitLab close second with includes+policies; GitHub third), compliance (GitLab Ultimate best; Buildkite good if DIY; GitHub Enterprise good), progressive delivery (Buildkite/GitLab tie, Buildkite more flexible), cost at this volume (Buildkite cheapest at scale if spot; GitHub competitive; GitLab SaaS costliest but bundles platform).

# Vertical Integration in the Global Cocoa Processing Oligopoly: Barry Callebaut, Cargill, and Olam/ofi (2018–2024)

## 1. Executive Summary

The three largest global cocoa processors pursued convergent but strategically distinct vertical integration strategies between 2018 and 2024. All three deepened upstream control in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana through direct sourcing from farmer cooperatives, proprietary sustainability programs (Forever Chocolate/Cocoa Horizons, Cargill Cocoa Promise, Cocoa Compass/AtSource), and farm-level digital mapping. The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) — applicable from 30 December 2024, later postponed to 30 December 2025 — transformed these programs from marketing assets into license-to-operate infrastructure, and all three now monetize traceability as a competitive differentiator in winning premium manufacturing contracts with Lindt, Ferrero, and Mondelēz. Key differentiators: Barry Callebaut leads on certification-linked customer programs and public EUDR advocacy; Cargill made the largest disclosed origin-processing capex ($113M in 2019–2021); Olam/ofi achieved 100% direct-supply-chain traceability earliest (2020) and has the deepest farm-gate origination network, but publishes the least granular capex and income-change data. On farmer incomes, independently verified data shows all three remain far from living-income goals: a Wageningen (WUR) analysis of 90,000+ households in Cargill's Ivorian supply chain found only 9% earn a living income and nearly half sit below the $2.15/day extreme poverty line (https://www.living-income.com/fileadmin/living_income/Publications/Other_Relevant_Publications/WAR_Unlocking_targeted_approaches_to_improve_household_resilience_of_cocoa_farmers_2024.pdf).

---

## 2. Company Strategies and Upstream Integration

### 2.1 Barry Callebaut — "Direct sourcing plus customer-funded impact programs"

Barry Callebaut is "fully vertically integrated along the entire value chain," sourcing cocoa directly from smallholder farmers in Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Cameroon, Indonesia, Brazil, Ecuador and Nigeria, supplemented by third-party suppliers (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Report%20on%20non-financial%20matters%20according%20to%20Swiss%20Co.%202023_24_1628.pdf). Its integration model rests on three pillars:

- **Direct farmer-group sourcing at scale.** In Côte d'Ivoire alone it purchases ~210,000 tonnes of beans from ~250,000 farmers against a local grinding capacity of ~230,000 tonnes (https://www.incotedivoire.net/economic/new/Barry%20Callebaut%20plans%20to%20triple%20chocolate%20production%20capacity%20in%20C%C3%B4te%20d%E2%80%99Ivoire). Its strategy explicitly favors direct purchasing "rather than over the commodity exchanges" — a policy dating to 2007–2008 that deepened through 2018–2024 (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/about-us/media/news-stories/barry-callebaut-making-difference-africa).
- **Sustainability certification infrastructure.** The Cocoa Horizons Foundation (est. 2015) is its preferred vehicle, operating in seven countries and collaborating with traders Touton, Sucden and ETG in Côte d'Ivoire; it is funded by customer premiums plus a CHF 4M Barry Callebaut donation in 2023/24 (https://www.cocoahorizons.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/The%20Cocoa%20Snapshot%20Full%20Year%2023-24_1.pdf). Share of cocoa and chocolate products sold containing certified or verified cocoa rose from 37.0% (2019/20) to 42.6%, 49.4%, 51.5%, 55.5% (2023/24) and 55.8% (2024/25) (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2025-11/ESG%20Datasheet%202024_25_0.pdf).
- **A data-driven pivot from training to services.** Based on a six-year Agri-Logic/IDH/Rainforest Alliance study (Farmer Field Book methodology), it shifted investment from farmer training to paid "labor groups," planting material and soil management. The paid labor group program scaled from 19,326 ha in 2022/23 (+138.3%) to ~44,000 ha in 2023/24 (+125.8%); farm services reached 169,981 farmers (2022/23) and 197,763 (2023/24); ~3.2M cocoa seedlings were distributed in 2023/24 (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2023-05/Barry%20Callebaut%20Agrilogic%20White%20Paper%202023_1.pdf; https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en-ZA/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202324).

### 2.2 Cargill — "Origin grinding plus a directly sourced, assured Promise supply chain"

Cargill is the second-largest global cocoa and chocolate producer. It directly sources from six countries (Brazil, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Ecuador, Ghana, Indonesia) and indirectly from 19 more origins; it operates 24 processing facilities, two in West Africa — Yopougon (Côte d'Ivoire) and Tema (Ghana) (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf).

- **Direct sourcing share.** The Cargill Cocoa Promise (CCP) — its direct, sustainability-managed supply chain — "accounts for about one third of the cocoa we source" and is KPMG-assured (limited assurance) (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf). Within key origins the direct share is much higher: historically 96% of Ivorian cocoa was sourced directly through farmer organizations (2015), and 85% of its *sustainable* cocoa was sourced directly via farmer organizations and cooperatives (2016/17) (https://www.cargill.com/doc/1432076281572/ccp-full-report.pdf; https://www.3blmedia.com/news/cargill-cocoa-promise-report-charts-clear-path-toward-cocoa-sustainability). The CCP network comprised 178 farmer organizations in 2024 (147 Côte d'Ivoire, 14 Ghana, 13 Cameroon) (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf).
- **Cooperative professionalization.** CCP invests in cooperative capacity (Coop Academy — leaders from 80 cooperatives trained), VSLAs with CARE (236,589 people reached in Côte d'Ivoire/Ghana since 2008), and professional farm-service groups, including eight pruning groups in Côte d'Ivoire serving 285 farmers specifically for customer Ferrero, and the CANOHYE input-finance program in Ghana (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf; https://www.cargill.com/doc/1432227748042/a-decade-of-impact-in-cocoa-communities.pdf).
- **Certification:** CCP volumes carry Rainforest Alliance or Fairtrade certification layered with Cargill's own program.

### 2.3 Olam/ofi — "Deepest farm-gate origination; traceability-first platform"

Olam's cocoa business (rebranded ofi — Olam Food Ingredients — within Olam Group) is a top-three global grinder and one of the largest bean buyers. Its model is built on direct origination: in Ghana it is among the biggest Licensed Buying Companies, sourcing ~140,000 MT of beans via 6,000 commission agents across ~13,000 communities (2019) (https://thecocoapost.com/amp/olam-cocoa-ghana-celebrates-20-years-of-growth/).

- **Definitions disclosed.** ofi formally defines direct sourcing as volumes procured "directly from farmers, farming cooperatives, farmer groups, or local buying agents/aggregators restricted to a specific group of farmers," including owned estates; indirect includes exchange-traded volumes, government entities, national aggregators and unrestricted intermediaries (https://assets.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/701vWnha1u6CIE8r8kHL6b/a27daac5d82c54c512dcea36ef70d960/ofi_Cocoa_Compass_Report_FINAL_09_Dec_2025.pdf).
- **Program coverage.** Over 90% of the direct supply chain is under managed (AtSource) programs as of December 2024 — split AtSource Fairtrade 6%, Rainforest Alliance 51%, AtSource Plus 19%, customer-specific programs 24%, organic 1% (https://www.kakaoforum.de/wp-content/uploads/Roadmap_Olam_Food_Ingredients.pdf). ofi supports 330,000+ farmers across nine countries (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/3kP6GKwcCJ0fgI7l4KyQzt/1e9e08c83c41c07f66885ef329a30872/cocoa-compass-impact-report_2022.pdf).
- **Landscape investment.** From 2018–2024 it distributed 9.8 million trees for agroforestry and maintained six landscape partnerships (https://assets.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/701vWnha1u6CIE8r8kHL6b/a27daac5d82c54c512dcea36ef70d960/ofi_Cocoa_Compass_Report_FINAL_09_Dec_2025.pdf).

---

## 3. Direct-Sourced vs. Broker/Indirect Cocoa — Comparative Figures

| Company | Direct share disclosed | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Barry Callebaut** | Not published as a single %; direct supply chain explicitly covers farmer groups in Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Cameroon, Nigeria, Brazil, Ecuador, Indonesia; remainder via third-party suppliers (e.g., Touton, Sucden, ETG inside Cocoa Horizons) | 85.6% of *direct* supply chain plots mapped (2024/25) implies direct is the dominant but unquantified share (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2025-11/ESG%20Datasheet%202024_25_0.pdf) |
| **Cargill** | ~33% of total global cocoa via the direct, assured CCP supply chain; up to 96% of Ivorian volumes direct via farmer organizations; 85% of *sustainable* cocoa direct | https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf; https://www.cargill.com/doc/1432076281572/ccp-full-report.pdf |

## 5. Documented Farmer Income Changes

All three companies report activity-level income metrics; independent household-level outcomes remain sobering.

**Barry Callebaut.** Claims 475,752 (2023/24) and 557,739 (2024/25) farmers "in our supply chain lifted out of poverty" against a 500,000-by-2025 Forever Chocolate target (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en-ZA/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202324; https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202425). Its own Agri-Logic white paper documents the baseline problem: Ivorian farms average 5.12 ha (3.61 ha under cocoa), yields ~341 kg/ha, with cocoa supplying 70–85% of household income in Côte d'Ivoire and ~two-thirds in Ghana (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2023-05/Barry%20Callebaut%20Agrilogic%20White%20Paper%202023_1.pdf). Note the 2024/25 figure *exceeds* the 2025 target but the methodology counts cumulative farmers supported, not verified net-income transitions — a material caveat. Independent modeling (Frontiers, 2021) shows that even doubling farm-gate price leaves 53–65% of households below the living-income benchmark; yield growth is the dominant lever (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sustainable-food-systems/articles/10.3389/fsufs.2021.732831/full).

**Cargill.** The richest micro-level income evidence: (i) one-to-one GAP coaching in Côte d'Ivoire produced +49% average yields (2016/17); (ii) crop-protection adoption delivered +23% average yield, +US$194 net income and 430% ROI; (iii) demonstration plots achieved +40% yield = +US$380/ha/yr ≈ US$1,139 extra annual income on a typical 3-ha farm; (iv) earlier program data showed long-term CCP participants earning 53% more than new entrants, with gross household income ~US$3,500 vs ~US$2,000 national per-capita income (https://www.3blmedia.com/news/cargill-cocoa-promise-report-charts-clear-path-toward-cocoa-sustainability; https://www.cargill.com/doc/1432076281572/ccp-full-report.pdf; https://doczz.net/doc/4545423/the-2014-global-cargill-cocoa-promise-report). However, the 2024 WUR/Cargill segmentation study of >90,000 Ivorian households found **only 9% achieve a living income and ~50% earn below the $2.15 extreme-poverty line**, driving Cargill's shift to three-segment targeted interventions (https://www.living-income.com/fileadmin/living_income/Publications/Other_Relevant_Publications/WAR_Unlocking_targeted_approaches_to_improve_household_resilience_of_cocoa_farmers_2024.pdf).

**Olam/ofi.** 44,000 farmers supported to earn a living income in 2023 against a 2030 goal of 150,000 (living income benchmark ~US$7,300/yr vs extreme poverty ~US$2,300/yr for an average Ivorian cocoa family); seedling distribution lifted program-farmer yields +13% vs 2021; its Farmer Income Tool tracks living-income gaps across nine countries via OFIS, with Ghana's median farmer closing more of the gap over three years while Indonesia/Nigeria regressed (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/37uF0nYZ3aF62YUDaFrJ6K/c8fae0d5027bc1b798b453094d89c47c/cocoa-compass-impact-report-2023.pdf; https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/cocoa-compass-olam-cocoa-commits-to-living-incomes-for-farmers.html). ofi also implements Nestlé's Income Accelerator for 4,000+ farmers in 220+ Ivorian communities, where KIT's midline evaluation found average cumulative cash transfers of only US$70 (year 1) and US$141 (year 2) versus the intended €500/yr — illustrating the execution gap (https://www.kit.nl/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Nestle-Income-Accelerator-Program_Midline-report-of-the-pilot-phase.pdf).

**Cross-cutting context.** The Côte d'Ivoire–Ghana Living Income Differential (LID, $400/t from 2020/21) likely delivered larger income effects than any corporate program, with modeled impacts "ranging from zero to sizeable" depending on market pass-through (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306919222001580). A Ghana-focused review of ten companies found programs reaching 60–90% certified/program sourcing but only one company with a concrete living-income commitment (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vx8k7qlsy12).

---

## 6. EUDR Compliance Responses (Regulation in force June 2023; application 30 Dec 2024, postponed to 30 Dec 2025)

### Traceability systems implemented
- **Barry Callebaut:** Commissioned Cognizant to build a near-real-time, plot-level traceability and EUDR-compliance platform covering direct *and* indirect suppliers, delivered in 12 months with automated validation embedded in SAP procurement workflows; publicly lobbied *against* the 12-month EUDR delay and against diluting amendments, positioning compliance as a differentiator; committed to cover all technical compliance costs for farmers and farmer groups (https://www.cognizant.com/us/en/case-studies/barry-callebaut-leads-the-way-in-cocoa-sustainability-and-compliance; https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/about-us/media/news-stories/statement-eudr; https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Forever%20Chocolate%20Progress%20Report_1.pdf). Its investor webinar anticipated Côte d'Ivoire/Ghana being rated high-risk, requiring full due diligence and batch-level Due Diligence Statements (a 5,000 t bulk shipment can aggregate ~80,000 farms) (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-09/EUDR%20Investor%20Webinar%20-%20Barry%20Callebaut.PDF; https://www.callebaut.com/sites/default/files/2025-01/EUDR%20Introduction%20for%20Distributors%20and%20Artisans%20-%20Callebaut.pdf).
- **Cargill:** Two-phase program launched early 2023 (readiness/gap assessment, then management-system implementation) across five workstreams: due-diligence management system, geolocation precision, inbound + EU-domestic traceability, DDS preparation/submission (per batch, with reference numbers transmitted to customers), and ongoing monitoring/verification (https://www.cargill.com/food-beverage/emea/news/almost-ready-for-eudr-inside-our-compliance-preparations; https://www.cargill.com/food-beverage/emea/news/preparing-for-eudr-you-and-your-customers-need-to-know).
- **Olam/ofi:** Leverages its pre-existing Track & Trace digital solution and OFIS/AtSource stack (farm GPS, purchasing, transport, facility data), plus an AI Carbon Stock Monitoring tool built with NGIS; reports being "well-prepared," with third-party reviews independently evaluating EUDR readiness; both Olam Agri and ofi told Mongabay (Dec 2024) they expected to be ready ahead of the deadline (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/59dP6xwmGeJLdC7ziQ3ImL/677b6dd2042d6301873f9e59a3ed614e/Cocoa_Compass_Impact_Report_2023_FINAL.pdf; https://news.mongabay.com/2024/12/agribusiness-giant-olam-gets-head-start-on-eudr-its-suppliers-not-so-much/).

### Supply-chain mapping completion rates (direct supply chains)
- **Barry Callebaut:** plots mapped within the direct cocoa supply chain: 66.0% → 72.3% → 79.7% (2021/22, 399,413 plots) → 78.9% (2022/23) → 83.0% (2023/24; 669,174 plots, +22.2%) → 85.6% (2024/25); by 2024/25 it reported **full farm-level traceability for all directly sourced cocoa for the European market**, 100% deforestation-free sourcing for volumes feeding its Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire facilities (within EUDR scope), and >1.5 million cocoa farms mapped cumulatively (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2025-11/ESG%20Datasheet%202024_25_0.pdf; https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202425).
- **Cargill:** within the CCP/Promise chain, polygon mapping reached 92.2% of farmers globally (257,856 farms), ~96% in Côte d'Ivoire (81,406) and 65.1% in Ghana (32,097), with first-mile digital traceability deliveries at 76.6% globally (100% in the lead origin; lower in Ghana) (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf). CFI 2023/24 disclosures: 103,407 farms mapped and 98,619 t traceable farm-to-first-purchase-point in Côte d'Ivoire; 20,025 farms and 6,079 t in Ghana (https://www.cargill.com/doc/1432279866465/cargill-cocoa-and-forests-initiative-2024-progress-report.pdf). Cargill also completed a supply-chain mapping exercise for *all* relevant EUDR products (https://www.cargill.com/food-beverage/emea/news/preparing-for-eudr-you-and-your-customers-need-to-know).
- **Olam/ofi:** 100% traceability in the direct supply chain achieved in 2020 (≈12% of world cocoa; 325,000+ farmers on OFIS) — earliest of the three; 79% of farms in sustainability programs polygon mapped (April 2024); 83% of direct-supply-chain farms in Ghana + Côte d'Ivoire polygon mapped (CFI 2023); >85% of the direct chain traceable to farm (December 2024 update), with the indirect chain flagged as the biggest compliance concern (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-cocoa-hits-100-percent-traceability-target-across-its-direct-global-supply-chain.html; https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/ofi-cocoa-shares-how-transparency-and-traceability-are-driving-sustainability-impact-for-food-and-beverage-sector; https://assets.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/MNOTvCMNXGFU04UJ3bBru/d3bcff898d772300dc8bd5786a21204f/CFI-2023-report-latest.pdf; https://www.kakaoforum.de/wp-content/uploads/Roadmap_Olam_Food_Ingredients.pdf).

### Non-compliant volume exclusions
- **Cargill** is the only one of the three to disclose an explicit exclusion mechanism: in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire it "activated additional measures… to exclude, as much as possible, farmers not having all their cocoa plots polygon mapped or showing signs of deforestation since December [2020] from our sourcing activities" (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf).
- **ofi** states it ceases work with any supplier breaching its supplier code unless remediated, and its segregation of compliant vs non-compliant volumes follows the EUDR no-mixing rule; no volume figures disclosed (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/3kP6GKwcCJ0fgI7l4KyQzt/1e9e08c83c41c07f66885ef329a30872/cocoa-compass-impact-report_2022.pdf).
- **Barry Callebaut** disclosed no excluded volumes but stated it would immobilize/withdraw products upon suspected non-compliance and achieved 100% deforestation-free status for EUDR-scope volumes into its West African plants (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202425).
- Industry-wide context: CFI signatories reported 85% of direct-supply-chain cocoa traceable in 2022; national systems were still catching up — Côte d'Ivoire's CCC had mapped ~91% of farmers (>1M farmers, 3.2M ha) and Ghana's COCOBOD had registered 792,954 farmers/1,239,169 farms (1.37M ha) under its new Cocoa Management System — but ~300,000 Ivorian farms still needed mapping by the 2024/25 season (https://www.foodnavigator.com/Article/2024/09/09/Cocoa-traceability-and-the-EUDR/; https://zerodeforestationhub.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/EUDR-preparedness-check-CIV_EN.pdf; https://zerodeforestationhub.eu/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/20250312-EUDR-Preparedness-check-of-Ghana.pdf). External observers warn that EUDR pressure is causing large traders to drop unready smallholder suppliers — the principal unquantified exclusion risk (https://news.mongabay.com/2024/12/agribusiness-giant-olam-gets-head-start-on-eudr-its-suppliers-not-so-much/).

---

## 7. Competitive Positioning for Premium Chocolate Contracts (Lindt, Ferrero, Mondelēz)

**Ferrero** publishes its tier-1 cocoa supplier list, which includes **all three processors — Barry Callebaut, Cargill, and ofi** (alongside Ecom, Sucden, Touton, ETG/Beyond Beans, Blommer, Mars, etc.) (https://www.ferrero.com/int/sites/ferrero_int/files/2026-07/ferrero_cocoa-supply-chain_tier-1-suppliers-and-farmer-groups_24-25.pdf). Ferrero sources 99% of its cocoa through Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade, and **Barry Callebaut's Cocoa Horizons** standard, and requires farm-level physical traceability — meaning Barry Callebaut's proprietary scheme is directly embedded in Ferrero's compliance architecture, a structural commercial advantage. Cargill differentiates through bespoke co-investment (eight pruning groups in Côte d'Ivoire serving 285 farmers, built "for our customer Ferrero") (https://www.ferrero.com/int/en/people-planet/source-our-ingredients-sustainably/cocoa; https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf).

**Mondelēz** runs its own Cocoa Life program and multi-sources: Barry Callebaut is its largest industrial chocolate partner (the 2010 Kraft outsourcing deal was Barry Callebaut's biggest ever, exceeding an 80,000 t/yr Hershey contract) and co-developed Barry Callebaut's paid-labor-team strategy; Cargill and ofi are Cocoa Life implementation suppliers (Cargill in Côte d'Ivoire; ofi in Indonesia, where the pair announced the world's largest sustainable commercial cocoa farm, 2,000 ha, in 2021) (https://www.confectionerynews.com/Article/2015/11/03/Mondelez-and-Barry-Callebaut-team-on-cocoa-sustainability/; https://ir.mondelezinternational.com/news-releases/news-release-details/mondelez-international-and-olam-food-ingredients-announce; https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2023-11/Barry_Callebaut_Annual_Report_2022-23_Sustainability_0.pdf). A 2025 compliance case study confirms all three remain tier-1 suppliers to Mondelēz, and flags a residual EUDR risk: Mondelēz's indirect exposure via traders to cooperatives with post-2020 deforestation (e.g., SOCOCCI, sourced by Barry Callebaut 2019–2023 per Trase) could jeopardize "negligible risk" due-diligence ratings (https://compliance-checker.org/static/documents/case_studies/cocoa_sococci_2025_12.pdf).

**Lindt & Sprüngli** is structurally different: a bean-to-bar maker with its own Farming Program (100% traceable, externally verified beans since the 2020 harvest; 100% Rainforest Alliance certified cocoa announced 2026), it buys beans directly rather than relying on processor certification schemes (https://www.lindt-spruengli.com/media/press-releases-news/manually-entered-articles/lindt-spruengli-achieves-sustainability-milestone-100-traceable-and-verified-cocoa-beans/; https://www.foodnavigator.com/Article/2026/06/18/lindt-hits-100-cocoa-milestone-amid-big-confectionery-sustainability-drive/). For Lindt, the processors compete mainly on semi-finished liquor/butter supply where origin grinding capacity (Cargill's Yopougon, Barry Callebaut's Abidjan/San Pedro, ofi's San Pedro/Kumasi) and segregated traceability lines determine contract eligibility.

**Adjacent premium evidence:** Barry Callebaut extended its Unilever strategic supply agreement (June 2023, innovation + sustainability), is a key Nestlé Income Accelerator partner, and enabled the Ben & Jerry's–Tony's Chocolonely "Love A-fair" collaboration; Nestlé's Income Accelerator in Côte d'Ivoire also runs through ofi (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2023-06/PRR%20Unilever%20strategic%20supply%20agreement%20EN.pdf; https://www.nestle.com/sites/default/files/2023-07/income-accelerator-program-progress-report-july-2023.pdf).

**Net positioning assessment:** (1) **Barry Callebaut** converts sustainability infrastructure most directly into premium contract wins — its certification brand (Cocoa Horizons), customer co-designed programs, public anti-delay EUDR stance, and Europe-ready traceability make it the default partner for brands selling sustainability narratives. (2) **Cargill** leverages scale and the largest origin-grinding asset base plus the only disclosed exclusion mechanism — attractive for volume premium contracts needing segregated dark-powder and EUDR-clean supply. (3) **ofi** monetizes the deepest origination data (AtSource insights sold as a customer-facing platform; 24% of its direct chain already on bespoke customer programs), positioning it strongly for bespoke single-origin and segregated-ingredient contracts, though its smaller recent origin capex and Olam Group's portfolio restructuring create more uncertainty about long-term processing ambition.

---

## 8. Limitations and Uncertainties

1. **Direct-vs-broker percentages** are not published on a like-for-like basis by any company; Cargill's ~one-third global direct share is the only audited figure. Barry Callebaut and ofi report KPIs relative to their (undefined-in-volume) direct chains.
2. **Farmer income data** mix self-reported program metrics (yields, +$194–$1,139 income increments) with rare independent household studies (WUR: 9% at living income in Cargill's Ivorian chain). Barry Callebaut's "lifted out of poverty" counts are cumulative program-reach figures, not verified income transitions.
3. **Capex figures** are company-announced project values, not audited capex line items; ofi disclosed no new origin grinding capex in-window, and its January 2026 $200M announcement falls outside 2018–2024.
4. **EUDR baselines moved:** application was postponed from 30 Dec 2024 to 30 Dec 2025, and country risk classifications (which Barry Callebaut expects to be "high" for Côte d'Ivoire/Ghana) were pending finalization at the time of the underlying disclosures. No company has disclosed quantified non-compliant volume exclusions in tonnes; Cargill's exclusion policy is the most specific public statement.
5. Some 2024/25 and late-2025 sources were used to establish end-of-period status; metrics are labeled by fiscal year throughout.

# Edge Computing and the Transformation of Industrial IoT Architectures (2024): Three Use Cases

## Executive Summary

As of 2024, edge computing has shifted industrial IoT from a "sense-and-ship-to-cloud" model to a hierarchical "decide-at-the-edge, learn-in-the-cloud" model. Across manufacturing predictive maintenance, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and energy distribution, the pattern is consistent: time-critical inference and control move to on-premises gateways, edge servers, or telecom-embedded MEC (multi-access edge computing), while the cloud retains fleet-scale training, orchestration, and long-term analytics. Quantified impacts found in the evidence base: inference/control latency drops from 200–800 ms cloud round-trips to <50 ms (and down to ~1 ms for 5G URLLC robot control); bandwidth consumption falls by 90–99.9%+ through edge filtering and event-based reporting; and availability metrics improve markedly (70–78% reductions in unplanned downtime in manufacturing; 45–94% reductions in customer outage impact in distribution grids). The trade-offs are real: higher distributed hardware capex and fleet-management opex, a widened physical attack surface, and new lifecycle-management burdens (OTA model updates, device patching), partially offset by consolidation (e.g., Audi's virtualized PLCs) and by cheaper, "brainless" robots (NAVER, Toshiba).

---

## Use Case 1: Manufacturing Predictive Maintenance (PdM)

### (a) Architecture: Before vs. After

**Before (cloud-centric):** Vibration, temperature, and current sensors stream raw data through a plant gateway over WAN/Internet to a cloud IoT platform, where ML models run and alerts are generated and sent back to the plant. Two structural flaws are documented in practice: (i) round-trip latency of 200–800 ms meant "anomalies were detected too late to prevent failure," and (ii) intermittent factory connectivity caused data gaps (Amtarc case study: https://www.amtarc.com/resources/case-studies/iot-predictive-maintenance). Raw high-frequency vibration data is also economically unstreamable: a single machine sampled at 10 kHz produces ~800 MB/hour (https://ifactory.jrsinnovation.com/predictive-maintenance/edge-computing-predictive-maintenance-processing-data-machine), and Siemens' own edge analytics documentation shows vibration channels sampled at 46.875 kHz per channel (https://docs.industrial-operations-x.siemens.cloud/r/en-us/insights-hub-edge-analytics/limits/limits/use-case-vibration-spectra-calculation).

**After (edge-distributed):** A three-tier architecture: (1) sensors/PLCs; (2) on-device or near-device inference on industrial gateways (Raspberry Pi 4, NVIDIA Jetson Nano, STM32MP1, or Siemens Industrial Edge), using quantized models — e.g., INT8-quantized LSTMs compressed from 45 MB to 2.3 MB with <3% accuracy loss — with a local MQTT broker and store-and-forward queuing for connectivity loss; (3) the cloud relegated to fleet model training, OTA model distribution (blue/green deployment with automatic rollback if confidence drops), and fleet observability (Amtarc, ibid.). This is the same pattern industrialized by Siemens Industrial Edge + AWS IoT SiteWise Edge, which buffers data locally during outages and forwards "only harmonized, compressed data" (https://www.siemens.com/en-gb/content/architecture-hub/aws-ot-it-integration/; https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/guidance/integrating-an-industrial-data-fabric-with-siemens-industrial-edge-on-aws/), and by Holcim deploying C3 AI Reliability on edge devices to monitor thousands of sensors on critical assets such as vertical roller mills (https://c3.ai/blog/how-the-c3-ai-platform-helps-holcim-overcome-limitations-of-edge-devices-to-deliver-real-time-ai-powered-predictive-maintenance).

### (b) Quantified Impacts

**Latency:**
- Edge inference <50 ms vs. 200–800 ms cloud round-trip — a 4–16× improvement (75–94% latency reduction) (Amtarc: https://www.amtarc.com/resources/case-studies/iot-predictive-maintenance).
- Real-time edge inference at the machine is characterized as ~10 ms, enabling autonomous machine protection even offline (https://ifactory.jrsinnovation.com/predictive-maintenance/edge-computing-predictive-maintenance-processing-data-machine).
- At the control tier, Audi's "Edge Cloud for Production" runs virtualized PLCs that must execute in 5–10 microseconds within a 250 µs total performance budget; non-real-time edge workloads target 25 ms from an edge cloud 200 m–10 km away (https://www.edgeir.com/audi-using-vmware-edge-compute-stack-at-the-industrial-edge-20241010).

**Bandwidth:**
- Worked calculation (from the iFactory data): one machine at 10 kHz vibration = 800 MB/hour = 19,200 MB/day raw. Edge filtering transmits <80 MB/day of health scores, alerts, and compressed trends. Reduction = (19,200 − 80) / 19,200 = 99.6%. The source characterizes production platforms as filtering 90–99% of raw data at the edge and cutting cloud storage costs 10–50× (https://ifactory.jrsinnovation.com/predictive-maintenance/edge-computing-predictive-maintenance-processing-data-machine).

**Availability / SLA:**
- 70% downtime reduction, 91% prediction accuracy across 140+ edge devices; 11 significant equipment issues caught in the first quarter that the prior cloud system missed; measurable ROI within 60 days (Amtarc, ibid.).
- 78% reduction in unplanned downtime (from a baseline of 45 hours/month) in an Indian steel plant using STM32MP1 edge gateways with on-device inference and local buffering (https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/industrial-iot-predictive-maintenance).
- Siemens' Drivetrain Analyzer Edge claims up to 45% downtime reduction via on-premises AI analytics with no additional sensors (https://www.siemens.com/dta-edge).
- Analyst benchmarks consistent with these figures: PdM increases productivity ~25%, reduces breakdowns ~70%, lowers maintenance costs ~25% (Deloitte position paper: https://www.beekeeper.io/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Deloitte_Predictive-Maintenance_PositionPaper.pdf); increases equipment uptime/availability 10–20% and cuts maintenance planning time 20–50% (Deloitte Insights: https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/manufacturing-industrial-products/industry-4-0/using-predictive-technologies-for-asset-maintenance.html); McKinsey observes +5–15% asset availability and −18–25% maintenance costs (https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/operations/our-insights/digitally-enabled-reliability-beyond-predictive-maintenance). Context: unplanned downtime costs industrial manufacturers an estimated $50B/year (Deloitte, ibid.).

### (c) Trade-offs

**Cost.** Edge hardware is cheap per node (Raspberry Pi 4 / Jetson Nano class) but multiplies across hundreds of devices; the offsetting saving is network and cloud egress/storage (10–50× lower storage cost) and avoided downtime (~$3M/year loss at the Amtarc client). At the plant IT layer, Audi's consolidation play is instructive: a typical factory runs 10,000+ industrial PCs and 4,000 HMI systems; virtualizing IPCs/PLCs on VMware Edge Compute Stack lowered capital and operating costs (energy, troubleshooting, maintenance), with one vPLC controlling a robot cell of eight robots (EdgeIR, ibid.). NIST's survey notes PdM maintenance-cost reductions ranging widely (15–98%) with documented ROIs of 3.5:1 to 10:1, underscoring outcome variability (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ams/NIST.AMS.100-18.pdf).

**Security.** Distributing compute enlarges the attack surface: IIoT devices have limited resources for encryption, may carry un-patchable zero-days, and connectivity "significantly increases the attack surface" of industrial systems (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11820253/). Audi explicitly cited the patching complexity of heterogeneous IPCs as a security risk that consolidation mitigates (EdgeIR, ibid.). Countervailing benefits: edge processing keeps sensitive OT data on premises, and current guidance recommends ISA/IEC 62443 zones-and-conduits plus zero-trust principles adapted to OT's safety-availability-integrity-confidentiality priority inversion (https://www.isagca.org/hubfs/2023%20ISA%20Website%20Redesigns/ISAGCA/PDFs/ISAGCA%20Zero%20Trust.pdf). Notably, ISA's IIoT certification work concludes that implementing essential control functions in the cloud does not meet IEC 62443 requirements — an architectural argument for keeping control at the edge (https://isagca.org/hubfs/2022%20ISA%20Website%20Redesigns/ISASecure/PDFs/IIoT%20System%20Certification%2062443%20Paper_ISASecure_ISAGCA.pdf).

**Maintainability.** Edge nodes run where there are "few or no onsite personnel," must operate disconnected, and number in the thousands — the core design constraints VMware cites for its Edge Compute Stack pull-based orchestration and zero-touch provisioning (EdgeIR, ibid.). Model lifecycle management becomes the dominant burden: Amtarc pushes retrained weights every 30 days via OTA with blue/green deployment and automatic rollback, plus per-device accuracy-drift detection (Amtarc, ibid.). Siemens Industrial Edge Management partially mitigates this by not requiring uninterrupted internet and by centralizing application deployment across plants (AWS/Siemens guidance, ibid.).

---

## Use Case 2: Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs)

### (a) Architecture: Before vs. After

**Before:** Two legacy patterns dominated. (1) On-robot autonomy over Wi-Fi: each robot carries a full compute stack and navigates independently; Wi-Fi roaming causes seconds-long handover gaps — Makino "frequently experienced instability" because "the delay in the Wi-Fi handover process" broke HTTPS/WebRTC sessions with the control server (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/makino-improves-performance-of-autonomous-mobile-robots-with-aws-wavelength-and-5g-network/). Milvus Robotics cited Wi-Fi "breakdowns, low speeds, narrowness of the broadcast area of access points, [and] delays in data transfer" as the main problems in multi-robot warehouses (https://www.robotics247.com/article/milvus_turkcell_ericsson_demonstrate_5g_mobile_robot_safe_crossing_turkish_warehouse). (2) Uncoordinated fleets: at Bosch's Reutlingen fab, legacy AGVs "are not aware of each other," causing coordination stalls and suboptimal routing (https://5gsmart.eu/wp-content/uploads/5G-SMART-D4.4-v1.0.pdf).

**After:** 5G (private or public) plus edge cloud, with robot "brains" centralized at the edge. Makino moved its AMR control servers to AWS Wavelength embedded in KDDI's public 5G network, avoiding internet traversal and getting a flat intranet between robots and servers, launched in under 5 months (AWS, ibid.; https://atmarkit.itmedia.co.jp/ait/articles/2107/27/news025.html). NAVER's 1784 building runs "Rookie" delivery robots with the cloud (NAVER ARC brain) as a shared brain over Samsung private 5G "as a neural network," enabling robots without on-board chipsets — 40 robots on 3 floors initially, scaling to hundreds across 36 floors (https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-collaborates-with-naver-cloud-to-launch-koreas-first-private-5g-network; https://www.koreaherald.com/article/2880324; https://medium.com/naver-cloud/find-the-hidden-naver-cloud-technologies-in-navers-second-office-building-1784-6e9f11cadd7e). At Bosch Reutlingen, AGV intelligence was "completely removed and reimplemented in a cloud native manner in the edge cloud," validated in a live semiconductor fab (https://standards-tracker.5g-ppp.eu/5g-smart-5g-semiconductor-factory; https://exa.ai/library/publication/5kywwkd6462). Safety-critical reflexes (emergency stop, obstacle avoidance) remain on-robot; fleet coordination, SLAM map fusion, and task allocation move to the edge. A complementary edge-native pattern keeps navigation fully on-device (on-SoC NPU, on-device SLAM) with peer-to-peer mesh coordination, eliminating cloud dependency entirely (https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/edge-ai-warehouse-robotics).

### (b) Quantified Impacts

**Latency:**
- AWS Wavelength targets single-digit millisecond latencies at the 5G edge (https://press.aboutamazon.com/2019/12/aws-announces-aws-wavelength); KDDI measured 40–50% RTT reduction vs. 4G in Wavelength trials (https://news.kddi.com/kddi/corporate/english/newsrelease/2020/12/16/4980.html).
- Research testbeds show the achievable floor: a 5G URLLC + TSN prototype on an industrial shopfloor held latency to 1 ms for 99.9% of 100,000 packets (spread ~0.5–1.2 ms, rare outliers to ~2 ms) (https://publications.rwth-aachen.de/record/848246/files/848246.pdf).
- Engineering reality check from Makino's deployment: an AGV moving 0.6–0.8 m/s travels only 6–8 cm in 100 ms and 3–4 cm in 50 ms, so "tens of milliseconds" of latency suffice — ultra-low single-ms latency is unnecessary for AMR control; stability matters more (@IT, ibid.). The 5G-SMART consortium validated high-level motion control of mobile robots from a close-proximity edge cloud over production 5G (https://5gsmart.eu/wp-content/uploads/5G-SMART-D2.3-v1.0.pdf).

**Bandwidth:** Centralizing brains requires uplink-heavy sensor streaming, which edge placement makes feasible: Samsung's private 5G radios "nearly double the upload capabilities of conventional commercial 5G radios" (Korea Herald, ibid.). Edge preprocessing on the robot side cuts backhaul where applied — the same 90%+ filtering logic as PdM applies to LiDAR/camera streams, though published fleet-level bandwidth figures remain proprietary (Rapid Circuitry notes client throughput results are unpublished).

**Availability / SLA:**
- Makino: 5G eliminated Wi-Fi handover instability, delivering "real-time stable operability" with seamless base-station handover while moving (AWS, ibid.).
- Toshiba: server-centralized swarm control over Local 5G with radio-map routing improved robot operation rates by ~16%, cut per-robot power consumption ~14% (smaller batteries, no heavy compute), and reduced automated-transport installation cost ~10% (https://www.global.toshiba/ww/technology/corporate/rdc/rd/topics/23/2311-01.html).
- Turkcell/Ericsson/Milvus: private 5G AMRs operated "safely, efficiently and smoothly" in a live warehouse, overcoming Wi-Fi disconnections and delays, including scanner-supervised blind-spot crossings (Robotics 24/7, ibid.).

### (c) Trade-offs

**Cost.** Private 5G is expensive — "tens of millions of yen," plus spectrum licensing and specialized skills, is the chief barrier in Japan (@IT, ibid.). Makino's countermove — public 5G + Wavelength — "achieved both cost reductions and real-time stable operability" versus building private 5G (AWS, ibid.). Edge centralization also cheapens the robots themselves: removing on-robot brains reduces per-robot cost, size, and battery (NAVER ARC brain; Toshiba ~14% power reduction; 5G-SMART notes robot hardware "can be simplified, become cheaper and occupy less space"). But the cost shifts to the network and edge infrastructure, and to per-site engineering.

**Security.** Private 5G gives dedicated spectrum, SIM-based device identity, and on-premises data paths — NAVER chose it explicitly for "data privacy and high performance" (Samsung blog: https://www.samsung.com/global/business/networks/insights/blog/0629-samsungs-private-5g-network-5g-autonomous-mobile-robots-in-korea/). The flip side: centralizing control in an edge cloud concentrates risk — the edge server and the wireless link become single points whose compromise affects the whole fleet, and centralized data aggregation is itself "an attractive target" (NIST CSWP 33: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/CSWP/NIST.CSWP.33.ipd.pdf). Mesh/peer-to-peer AMR architectures reduce central risk but distribute the attack surface across every robot.

**Maintainability.** Cloud-brain fleets are updated once at the edge rather than robot-by-robot — "quickly improve service quality without having to upgrade individual robots one by one" (Samsung, ibid.). Makino gained remote monitoring and a serverless AMR control stack, reducing on-site server maintenance (AWS News Feed summary: https://aws-news.com/article/2023-09-11-makino-improves-performance-of-autonomous-mobile-robots-with-aws-wavelength-and-5g-network). The new burden is wireless lifecycle engineering: Toshiba's system depends on continuously updated radio maps of the robot swarm, and Makino's project required joint design across robot, cloud, and network engineers — skills most factories lack in-house (@IT, ibid.).

---

## Use Case 3: Energy Distribution

### (a) Architecture: Before vs. After

**Before (centralized SCADA/DMS):** Field devices (reclosers, feeder terminal units, PMUs) stream measurements over LTE or dedicated links to a control center where fault detection, location, and service restoration decisions are made — often with manual control-room analysis and truck rolls. Restoration of a permanent fault could take tens of minutes to hours. Distribution networks typically lack the fiber connectivity that transmission-level WAMS/WAMPAC schemes assume (https://exa.ai/library/publication/mx39lttjtl7).

**After (edge-distributed):** Intelligence migrates to substations and feeders: recloser controllers and edge gateways detect and locate faults locally, execute FLISR (fault location, isolation, service restoration) autonomously in seconds, buffer data against packet loss, and upload only events rather than continuous streams (Sodin et al., Applied Sciences: https://exa.ai/library/publication/mx39lttjtl7; SEL: https://selinc.com/solutions/software/flisr/). Iberdrola's i-DE built "SmartPoint" on AWS IoT Core/Greengrass with video AI inference at the edge (NVIDIA edge tools; models trained in SageMaker) across substations, poles, transformation centers, and lines in Spain and Portugal (https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/innovators/iberdrola/; https://aws-news.com/article/2024-08-02-iberdrola-reduces-incidents-at-power-distribution-facilities-using-aws-iot-and-edge-services). The cloud retains the digital twin, fleet analytics, and model updates — e.g., a confidence-aware split where routine faults are decided on the edge fast path and hard DER/topology cases escalate to the cloud (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vf860xyfqmq).

### (b) Quantified Impacts

**Latency:**
- Edge-based distribution fault detection with S-transform feature extraction: response time ≤0.005 s (5 ms) with up to 100% detection accuracy (https://exa.ai/library/publication/plpj0qnlg85).
- Edge-deployed GRU-Attention model: 113 ms system response vs. slower cloud-based solutions, 96.1% fault-identification accuracy, 289 s average early-warning lead time (https://exa.ai/library/publication/xhv31f52r4z).
- Cloud-edge split GNN fault location: 118 ms median decision latency, 98.4% section-level accuracy, 0.21 km mean distance error, only 31.5 kB uplink per event — no continuous raw-waveform upload (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vf860xyfqmq).
- Operational FLISR: National Grid resolves faults remotely "usually within around a minute" (https://www.nationalgrid.com/about-us/innovation/flisr); SEL systems isolate and restore "in a matter of seconds" (SEL, ibid.) — versus manual restoration measured in tens of minutes to hours.

**Bandwidth:**
- Worked calculation from GridAI: replacing continuous 105-byte measurements (151 KB/day) with 15-byte heartbeats plus on-demand 40-byte fault reports (~40 bytes/day) yields a reduction of (154,624 − 40) / 154,624 ≈ 99.97% — "more than three orders of magnitude," with ~99% detection accuracy retained on Raspberry Pi-class hardware (https://exa.ai/library/publication/4w3v1t08k4p).
- The PMU edge-cloud framework similarly reports "significant" steady-state traffic reduction because detection is local, with edge buffering eliminating packet-loss exposure over LTE (Sodin et al., ibid.).

**Availability / SLA:**
- U.S. DOE smart-grid evaluation: FLISR reduced customers interrupted (CI) by up to 45% and customer-minutes interrupted (CMI) by up to 51% per outage event (https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2016/10/f33/Fault_Location_Impact_Duration_Dec_2014.pdf).
- Orlando Utilities Commission (Rosemont pilot): 94% reduction in customers affected (13,542 → 829 — verified: (13,542−829)/13,542 = 93.9%), 92% reduction in CMI, 73% fewer momentary interruptions (https://oucblog.com/self-healing-grid-system-is-a-game-changer/).
- National Grid: 10–11% fewer customers experiencing outages during storms across Massachusetts and New York (National Grid, ibid.).
- Iberdrola i-DE SmartPoint: 40% reduction in reported incidents and 50% fewer trips to facilities, across millions of heterogeneous assets (https://aws.amazon.com/solutions/case-studies/innovators/iberdrola/).

### (c) Trade-offs

**Cost.** Edge FLISR reuses existing switching devices ("improve coordination of switching devices already present... and extend their utility" — SEL, ibid.), avoiding fiber build-out by tolerating LTE QoS through edge autonomy and buffering (Sodin et al., ibid.). Raspberry Pi-class edge nodes (GridAI) make per-transformer monitoring economically feasible. The avoided-cost side is large: Iberdrola's 50% truck-roll reduction and regulators' CML/CI penalty regimes (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10445810/). Costs shift to device fleets across millions of assets, communications plans, and the software platform itself (i-DE built an in-house platform on AWS rather than buying vendor silos — explicitly to avoid per-manufacturer information silos: https://www.iberdrola.com/innovation/international-startup-program-perseo/substation-control-room-automation).

**Security.** Distribution grids are critical infrastructure under active policy scrutiny (e.g., U.S. NSM-22), and IIoT-style edge expansion increases the attack surface while constraining on-device cryptography (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11820253/; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/MSEC.2024.3432208). Mitigations align with zero-trust + shared-responsibility hybrids for IIoT (IEEE Security & Privacy, ibid.) and IEC 62443 zoning extended to cloud-connected edge (ISAGCA, ibid.). Edge autonomy also has a resilience-security benefit: reclosers "operate as their own autonomous islands with no requirement for intervention from the central control room," so a WAN outage or compromised center cannot disable protection (PMC10445810, ibid.).

**Maintainability.** Heterogeneity is the core burden — i-DE manages "millions of operational assets with a very heterogenous nature," which drove an abstraction platform to unify sensor vendors (AWS, ibid.). Cellular-connected fleets need remote access for settings and event collection (Westar's DA system used cellular modems plus secure Ethernet gateways for remote engineering: https://selinc.com/api/download/107722/). Cloud-edge split inference adds model-governance overhead — the cloud must "distribute calibrated model updates to field gateways" and verify low-confidence edge decisions (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vf860xyfqmq).

---

## Cross-Cutting Synthesis and Caveats

**Common 2024 architecture.** All three use cases converged on the same three-tier pattern: (1) sense/actuate at the device; (2) decide at the edge (gateway, on-prem edge cluster, or telco MEC like AWS Wavelength); (3) learn and govern in the cloud (fleet training, OTA updates, digital twins). The edge tier exists for three quantified reasons: latency (cloud RTTs of 200–800 ms vs. <50 ms edge inference; ~1 ms URLLC for robot control), bandwidth (90–99.97% reduction via filtering/event-based reporting), and autonomy (operations continue through WAN outages — a recurring design requirement in every cited deployment).

**Summary table of headline metrics:**

| Use case | Latency (before → after) | Bandwidth reduction | Availability/SLA impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| PdM | 200–800 ms cloud RTT → <50 ms edge inference (Amtarc); ~10 ms machine-level | 90–99.6% (800 MB/hr → <80 MB/day) | Downtime −70% (Amtarc), −78% (steel plant), −45% (Siemens drivetrain); uptime +10–20% (Deloitte) |
| AMRs | Wi-Fi handover stalls → ~1 ms @ 99.9% (URLLC testbed); single-digit ms (Wavelength); "tens of ms sufficient" (Makino) | Upload-heavy streams enabled by edge placement; on-robot filtering where applied | Operation rate +16%, power −14% (Toshiba); stable mobility (Makino); 40→hundreds of robots (NAVER) |
| Energy | Minutes–hours manual restoration → ≤5 ms detection, ~118 ms edge decision, seconds-scale FLISR | 99.97% (151 KB/day → 40 B/day, GridAI); 31.5 kB/event vs. continuous waveforms | CI −45%, CMI −51% (DOE); −94% customers affected (OUC); incidents −40%, trips −50% (Iberdrola) |

**Trade-off trilemma.** Cost moves from cloud egress and downtime toward distributed hardware and private-5G/edge infrastructure (private 5G: tens of millions of yen per site); security posture improves on data locality and WAN-outage resilience but worsens on physical attack surface and device-patchability, pushing practitioners to IEC 62443 zones/conduits and OT-adapted zero trust; maintainability improves via centralized orchestration and OTA (blue/green model rollout, zero-touch provisioning) but demands new disciplines — per-device model-drift monitoring, radio-map upkeep, and multi-vendor abstraction layers.

**Evidence limitations.** Many quantified results are vendor- or integrator-reported (AWS, Siemens, Samsung, C3 AI, Amtarc, Rapid Circuitry) and not independently audited; several foundational figures (DOE FLISR 2014; KDDI Wavelength 2020; NAVER 1784 and 5G-SMART trials 2021–2023) predate 2024 but remain the operative published benchmarks and underpin the 2024 production deployments cited (Iberdrola August 2024; Audi October 2024; Holcim July 2024). Where academic testbed numbers (1 ms URLLC; 5 ms fault detection) exceed what production systems achieve, I have flagged them as testbed results rather than field SLAs.
