final.content:
# Carbon Pricing in Practice, 2020–2024: A Comparative Analysis of California's Cap-and-Trade Program, the EU ETS, and China's National Carbon Market

## 1. Executive Summary

Between 2020 and 2024, the world's three flagship carbon pricing systems diverged sharply in price level and design maturity while converging on high compliance rates. The EU ETS delivered the strongest price signal (averaging roughly €80–85/t in 2022–23 before falling ~22% to ~€65–66/t in 2024) and the deepest absolute emissions cuts (stationary emissions fell from 1,530 Mt in 2019 to ~1,096 Mt in 2023 and roughly 5–6% further in 2024, reaching ~51% below 2005 levels). California's program saw auction settlement prices climb from the $16.68 floor during COVID-19 to a peak of $41.76 in February 2024, with covered emissions consistently below the cap and ~$28 billion raised cumulatively for the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF). China's national ETS — the world's largest by covered emissions (~4.5–5.2 Gt CO2/yr from the power sector alone) — operates on intensity-based free allocation with no auction revenue and no absolute cap; its allowance price roughly doubled from ¥48 at launch (July 2021) to ¥97.49 (~$13.5) at end-2024, and compliance rates rose from 99.5% to ~99.98%. COVID-19 stress-tested all three designs: California's auction floor and unsold-allowance mechanism absorbed the shock, the EU's Market Stability Reserve (MSR) canceled surplus allowances without any emergency cap intervention, and China — which launched mid-2021 — built explicit pandemic-relief flexibility into its second compliance cycle. Leakage was managed through output-based free allocation in all three systems, supplemented in California by coverage of electricity imports (a de facto border adjustment) and in the EU by the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which entered its transitional reporting phase in October 2023.

---

## 2. System Design Fundamentals (as relevant to 2020–2024 outcomes)

| Feature | California (WCI-linked with Québec) | EU ETS (Phase 4, 2021–2030) | China National ETS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cap type | Absolute, declining ~4%/yr budget | Absolute; linear reduction factor 2.2% → 4.3% (2024–27) | None — intensity (benchmark × output) |
| Coverage | ~80% of state GHG emissions (power incl. imports, industry, transport fuels, buildings) | ~10,000 installations (power, industry), intra-EEA aviation; maritime added 2024; ~40% of EU GHG | Power sector only: 2,162 entities (2019–20 cycle), 2,257 (2021–22), 2,096 (2023); ~4.5–5.2 Gt CO2/yr |
| Allocation | Hybrid: ~50% auctioned; free output-based allocation to industry; utility consignment for ratepayer benefit | Majority auctioned; free allocation for leakage-exposed industry (537M EUAs in 2023, 500M in 2024) | 100% free, output-based benchmarks |
| Price management | Auction reserve price (floor, +5%/yr + CPI); cost-containment reserves; price ceiling | Market Stability Reserve (24% of surplus withdrawn annually through 2023; cancellation above 400M from 2024) | None formally; MEE manages via allocation and compliance timing |
| Offsets | Yes, capped at 4% of obligation (4th compliance period) | No (international credits phased out post-2012/2020) | CCERs up to 5% of obligation |

Sources: CARB allowance distribution factsheet (ww2.arb.ca.gov/resources/documents/cap-and-trade-program-allowance-distribution-factsheet); CRS R48314 (congress.gov/crs-product/R48314); EEA/ETC ETS reports (eionet.europa.eu); IEA China ETS report (iea.org/reports/the-role-of-chinas-ets-in-power-sector-decarbonisation); MEE national carbon market development report (mee.gov.cn).

---

## 3. Allowance Price Trajectories, 2020–2024

### 3.1 California — quarterly joint auction settlement prices (CARB results summary, ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2020-08/results_summary.pdf)

| Year | Feb | May | Aug | Nov | Approx. annual avg |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 | ~$17.87 (record pre-COVID) | $16.68 (floor) | $16.68 (floor) | ~$17 (partial data) | ~$17 |
| 2021 | $17.80 | $18.80 | $23.30 | $28.26 | ~$22.0 |
| 2022 | $29.15 | $30.85 | $27.00 | $26.80 | ~$28.5 |
| 2023 | $27.85 | $30.33 | $35.20 | $38.73 | ~$33.0 |
| 2024 | $41.76 | $37.02 | $30.24 | $31.91 | ~$35.2 |

Trajectory: from the floor-bound COVID trough (May–August 2020) to the February 2024 peak, prices rose ~150% (($41.76−$16.68)/$16.68). The late-2024 softening (~$30–32) reflected regulatory uncertainty around program reauthorization and amendments. The floor itself escalated annually (5% + CPI), reaching $24–25+ by 2024 — the "self-ratcheting" floor design prevented any repeat of sub-$10 prices seen pre-2017.

### 3.2 EU ETS — annual average EUA prices

- 2020: ~€24–25 average; COVID crash from €24.07 to €15.25 in March 2020, recovering to €22.10 by June 2020 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8959469/)
- 2021: €52.50 volume-weighted average (German DEHSt auction data), with December 2021 auctions clearing €80.71 (climate.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2022-03/cap_report_202112_en.pdf)
- 2022: €80.32 average; record auction price €96.87 on 19 August 2022 amid the energy crisis (dehst.de 2022 annual report)
- 2023: €83.66 average (DEHSt); front-year futures averaged ~€85 (veyt.com/eu-ets/2024-year-in-review-eu-ets-flattening-out/)
- 2024: €65–66.5 average, down ~22%; range €52 (23 Feb) to €77 (3 Jan); the 23 February auction cleared €49.50, the lowest since May 2021 (dehst.de 2024 annual report)

From trough (€15.25, March 2020) to the 2022–23 plateau (~€85), EUA prices rose ~5.6×. The 2024 decline of ~22% was driven by record-low covered emissions (weak demand), front-loaded REPowerEU auction supply, and macro softness — despite the linear reduction factor rising to 4.3% and a one-off 90 Mt cap rebase in 2024 (Veyt, op. cit.).

### 3.3 China — CEA prices (Shanghai Environment and Energy Exchange / MEE)

- Launch (16 July 2021): opened ¥48.00/t; closed 2021 at ¥54.22 (+12.96% vs opening) (cneeex.com annual data)
- 2021 (first compliance cycle): average ¥42.85; daily closes ¥40–60 (21jingji.com report on MEE's first-cycle report)
- 2022: average ¥55.3; year-end close ¥55.00; trading volume collapsed 71.5% to 50.89 Mt because the two-year compliance cycle meant no surrender deadline in 2022 (xintianhuanbao.com/69838.html)
- 2023: average ¥68.15 (+23.24% y/y); year-end close ¥79.42 (+44.4% y/y); monthly highs ratcheted up July–October (¥65 → ¥75 → ¥77 → ¥82.79) ahead of the 15 November 2023 compliance deadline (cbnri.yicai.com annual report)
- 2024: closes ranged ¥69–106.02; first-ever breach of ¥100 on 24 April 2024; year-end close ¥97.49 (+22.75% y/y). Implied volume-weighted average ≈ ¥18.114 billion ÷ 189 Mt = **~¥95.8/t (~$13.4)** (ncsc.org.cn; stcn.com; coal.com.cn)

### 3.4 Cross-market comparison (end-2024, approximate USD)

EU ETS ~€65–70 (~$70) : California ~$31–35 : China ~¥97 (~$13.5) — a ratio of roughly 5 : 2.5 : 1. These differences reflect cap stringency (absolute vs intensity-based), auction share, and macro conditions, not relative mitigation effort alone.

---

## 4. Emissions Outcomes Versus Baselines

### 4.1 EU ETS — verified emissions (stationary installations, Mt CO2eq; Commission Carbon Market Reports, eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=COM%3A2024%3A538%3AFIN and ETC/EEA)

| Year | Verified emissions (stationary) | y/y change |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 1,530 (1,356 excl. UK scope change) | −9.1% |
| 2020 | 1,356 (1,253 excl. UK) | −11.4% (COVID; total incl. aviation −13.3%, aviation −63%) |
| 2021 | 1,337 | −1.4% (post-COVID industrial recovery offset by gas crisis switching) |
| 2022 | 1,313 | −1.8% (energy crisis: coal rebound in power, industrial output cuts) |
| 2023 | 1,096 | **−16.5%** — largest annual drop in ETS history; power −24%, industry −7% |
| 2024 | ~1,030–1,032 (est. −5.8% power+industry; −6 to −7% stationary) | power −10.7%, industry −0.8% |

Cumulative: stationary ETS emissions ended 2024 roughly 50–51% below 2005, tracking ahead of the revised −62% 2030 target (climate.ec.europa.eu progress report 2025; eea.europa.eu indicator). Against baseline: 2020 emissions were ~26% below the cap (Sandbag estimate, sandbag.be), and the system remained long on allowances through 2024 — the TNAC surplus indicator was still 1,112 Mt as of mid-2024 (Veyt). Total ETS including aviation and newly added maritime was 1,185 Mt in 2024 (maritime: 89.9 Mt; aviation +15%) (ETC 2025 report).

Attribution caveat: the 2023–24 reductions were driven jointly by the carbon price, the renewables surge (renewables + biofuels = 47.2% of EU electricity in 2024), gas demand destruction after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and weak industrial output — disentangling the ETS's marginal contribution is not possible from official data.

### 4.2 California — statewide AB 32 inventory (CARB 2024 edition, ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2024-09/nc-2000_2022_ghg_inventory_trends.pdf)

- 2019: 404.4 MMTCO2e → 2020: 368.7 (COVID anomaly, −35.3 MMT; **61.8 MMT below the 2020 limit of 431 MMT** — the 1990-level target was met early) → 2021: 381.3 (+3.4%, partial rebound) → 2022: 371.1 (−2.4%, resuming decline)
- Covered-entity emissions (~80% of inventory) have been consistently below the cap every year; CARB identifies ~310 million banked allowances in circulation (CRS R48314), and the 2024 IEMAC report cites ~379 million unused allowances WCI-wide (calepa.ca.gov 2024 IEMAC Report, Ch. 7)
- Against baseline: the program's bindingness is debated — the bank of unused allowances means entities could emit above annual budgets for years without breaching the cap. However, projects funded by auction revenue are credited with ~110–112.8 MMTCO2e of expected lifetime reductions (CRS; CCI 2024 Mid-Year Update, abgt.assembly.ca.gov)

### 4.3 China — intensity, not mass, outcomes

- First compliance cycle (2019–20 emissions): verified emissions 8.68 Gt against 9.01 Gt allowances allocated — an aggregate surplus by design (Oxford Guide to Chinese Climate Policy, chineseclimatepolicy.oxfordenergy.org)
- Official intensity metrics: thermal-power carbon intensity −2.38% (2023 vs 2018); total electricity carbon intensity −8.78% (2023) and −10.8% (2024) vs 2018 (MEE 2024/2025 reports; mrdx.cn 2025 carbon market conference)
- Independent ex-post analysis (Cell Reports Sustainability, 2025): the first compliance phase reduced unit-level carbon intensity by 2.46–3.13% and absolute emissions by 0.86%, despite +1.63% production growth; abatement came mainly from energy efficiency (57%), fuel quality (31%), unit retirements and biomass
- System-wide context: China's total CO2 emissions were roughly flat in 2024 as record clean-energy additions offset demand growth (Carbon Brief analysis). Because allocation scales with output, the ETS caps intensity, not volume — power-sector emissions can still rise with output growth, and 2023-cycle covered emissions (~5.2 Gt) exceed the first cycle (~4.5 Gt) largely on output growth.

**Comparative verdict on reductions vs baseline:** the EU delivered large absolute reductions exceeding its cap trajectory; California met its 2020 target years early but carries a large allowance bank that weakens near-term stringency; China achieved measurable intensity improvements (2.4–3.1% per cycle academically estimated) but no absolute cap bindingness.

---

## 5. Revenue Generation and Allocation

### 5.1 California (CARB proceeds summary; LAO; California Climate Investments reports)

- Cumulative GGRF deposits: **~$28 billion as of May 2024** (CRS R48314)
- State-share proceeds by fiscal year: FY2020-21 $1.30B; FY2021-22 $2.03B; FY2022-23 $2.00B; FY2023-24 $2.67B; FY2024-25 $2.20B (ww2.arb.ca.gov proceeds summary) — note the FY2020-21 dip reflects the COVID auctions
- Allocation: 65% continuously appropriated — High-Speed Rail 25%, Affordable Housing & Sustainable Communities 20%, Transit & Intercity Rail 10%, Low Carbon Transit Operations 5%, Safe Drinking Water 5% (capped $130M) — plus $200M/yr for forest health/wildfire from 2022-23; ~30% discretionary via annual budget (lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4730)
- Statutory equity floor: ≥35% of GGRF appropriations must benefit disadvantaged/low-income communities
- Implementation: $27.5B appropriated to 90 programs across 24 agencies since 2014; $11.6B implemented through 584,440 projects by May 2024, expected to reduce 112.8 MMTCO2e over project lifetimes (Conservation Strategy Group; CCI 2024 Mid-Year Update)
- Additionally, utility-consignment proceeds fund ratepayer climate credits (utility allocation was ~54% of direct allocation in vintage 2026; ~24% of budget to electric utilities in 2022) (CARB allocation page; EDU use-of-value report)

### 5.2 EU ETS (Commission Carbon Market Reports; EEA use-of-revenues data)

- 2021: €25.6B (general allowances, first year of Phase 4)
- 2023: **€43.6B** — €33.0B to Member States, €0.3B to EEA-EFTA/NI, €7.4B to Innovation + Modernisation Funds, €2.8B to the Recovery and Resilience Facility (REPowerEU) (eur-lex COM(2024)538)
- 2024: **€38.8B** — €24.4B to Member States (down 26% on lower prices/volumes), remainder to the two EU funds and REPowerEU (climate.ec.europa.eu "What are ETS revenues used for")
- Cumulative: ~€248B through mid-2025 (SWD(2025)388); >€258B by end-2025
- Use of revenues: historically ≥50% earmarked for climate/energy; ~75% actually so used 2013–2022. The 2023 revision (Directive 2023/959) raised the obligation to 100% for climate and energy, except indirect-cost compensation to electricity-intensive industry (€3.2B, or 13%, of 2024 Member-State revenue used for this by 15 Member States). Of 2024's €21.2B climate-obligated revenue, €16.4B was reported disbursed.
- REPowerEU front-loading: allowances auctioned to raise €20B by Aug 2026 for energy security/clean transition — over €5.5B raised in 2023–H1 2024 — a deliberate supply increase that contributed to 2024 price softness.

### 5.3 China

- **Zero public revenue**: 100% of allowances are allocated free under output-based benchmarks; there is no auctioning (IEA; ICAP). Market turnover (¥18.1B in 2024; ¥43.03B cumulative) accrues to trading entities, not government — e.g., Shanying International sold ~775,000 surplus allowances at ≥¥90/t, and Xinjiang Tianye sold up to 700,000 at ~¥100/t to fund operations (yrdcpcn.com).
- This is a fundamental design distinction: carbon pricing in China currently redistributes among generators rather than funding a climate-program treasury. Auctioning remains a stated future option.

---

## 6. Compliance Rates

- **California**: Compliance has historically been effectively universal; in the fourth compliance period (2021–2023, full obligation due 1 Nov 2024), offsets were capped at 4% of each entity's obligation; 110 of 294 entities hit that cap, and offsets comprised 3.1% of all surrendered instruments (CarbonPlan compliance-users analysis of CARB data; CARB compliance notice nc-citss_compliance_2021-2023_full.pdf). Over 2013–2020, California entities surrendered ~139M offsets (6.3% of emissions). Failure to surrender triggers a penalty of four instruments per tonne (three to reserve, one to retirement).
- **EU ETS**: Compliance is near-universal; entities failing to surrender by 30 April face an excess-emissions penalty (€100/t, indexed) plus make-up surrender. The 2024 data snapshot precedes the full compliance cycle (ETC 2025), but annual EEA/Commission reporting consistently shows only marginal non-compliance across ~9,000–10,000 installations and hundreds of aircraft operators. (Precise aggregate non-compliance percentages for 2020–2024 are not published in the sources reviewed; the qualitative record is one of >99% surrender compliance.)
- **China**: First cycle (2019–20): 99.5% compliance by emissions volume — 1,833 entities fully complied, 178 partially; by entity count on-time compliance was lower (~85%), concentrated among smaller generators (MEE first-cycle report via 21jingji.com; NUS ESI Policy Brief 64; Cell Reports Sustainability finds 93.9% of units fully compliant, 99.6% of obligations met). Second cycle: 99.61% for 2021 emissions and 99.88% for 2022 emissions (MEE 2024 development report). Third cycle (2023 compliance year): **~99.98%** of the 5.244 Gt obligation cleared by end-2024 (ncsc.org.cn, 7 Jan 2025). Data-quality fraud cases in 2021–22 prompted a governance overhaul: monthly digital evidence filing, three-tier review, and verification-agency oversight (99.7% qualified-service rate in 2023) (MEE 2024 report).

---

## 7. COVID-19 Disruption and Recovery: Crisis Management by Design

### 7.1 California — the floor and the ratchet did the work; no rule changes needed

- The May 2020 joint auction was the first undersubscribed auction since 2017: only 21.16M of 57.54M current allowances sold (37%), settling at the $16.68 floor; state revenue collapsed to ~$25M vs. $600M+ per auction previously (LAO EconTax blog; EDF Climate 411). The August 2020 auction partially recovered (89% sold, still at floor; ~$474M state revenue).
- Combined, ~32 million allowances went unsold in the May and August 2020 auctions (CARB Allowance Distribution Factsheet). Under the pre-existing "self-ratcheting" rule, unsold allowances are withheld from future auctions until two consecutive auctions clear above the reserve price, and allowances unsold after 24 months move permanently to cost-containment reserves. **No ad hoc allowance adjustments or banking-rule changes were adopted** — unlimited banking and the floor, designed before COVID, absorbed the shock. CARB itself noted a key risk: unlike 2016–17 (when undersubscription reflected political uncertainty and demand was merely deferred), in 2020 "emissions actually decreased, which may mean there is no delayed demand."
- Emissions impact: statewide emissions fell 35.3 MMT (8.7%) in 2020, rebounded 3.4% in 2021, and resumed decline (−2.4%) in 2022 — a shallower V than Europe's in percentage terms for covered sectors.

### 7.2 EU ETS — the MSR's first real stress test

- Price: V-shaped — €24.07 → €15.25 (March 2020) → €22.10 (June 2020) → €60+ by late 2021 (PMC study; ECB bulletin). Unlike the 2008 crisis (sub-€10 for nine years), the recovery took months, not a decade.
- Mechanism: **No cap adjustment, backloading, or banking restrictions were introduced.** The Market Stability Reserve (operating since January 2019) withdrew 367–375 Mt from 2020 auction supply (~35% cut) under its standing 24%-of-surplus rule. The 2020 emissions collapse pushed the circulating surplus (TNAC) to ~1.39 billion allowances (Sandbag estimate 1,392 Mt). Modeling in *Renewable & Sustainable Energy Reviews* (PMC8959469) estimates the pandemic ultimately triggers ~0.28 billion *additional* MSR cancellations — "even overcompensat[ing] the 2020 drop in CO2 emissions" — leading the authors to conclude no extra policy response was required. That is exactly what happened institutionally.
- Recovery-era tightening instead came through legislation: the 2021 "Fit for 55" revision (Directive 2023/959, in force May 2023) raised the 2030 ETS target from −43% to −62% vs 2005, lifted the linear reduction factor to 4.3% (2024–27) and 4.4% (2028–30), rebased the cap with a one-off 90 Mt cut in 2024, extended scope to maritime (2024), and created ETS2 for buildings/road transport (from 2027) with a Social Climate Fund.

### 7.3 China — launched into the pandemic era, with built-in relief

- The national market launched 16 July 2021 — after China's acute COVID phase — covering 2019–20 emissions with a generous aggregate allocation (9.01 Gt allocated vs 8.68 Gt verified), deliberately avoiding scarcity in year one.

**Synthesis:** California managed COVID with price-based automatic stabilizers (floor + unsold-allowance ratchet), the EU with a quantity-based stabilizer (MSR) plus post-crisis legislative tightening, and China with administrative allocation relief and compliance forbearance. None changed banking rules mid-crisis; all three permit banking, which proved stabilizing.

## 8. Interaction with Complementary Policies

- **EU**: The ETS interacts explicitly with the renewables build-out and coal phase-down. The record 2023–24 emissions falls were co-produced by the carbon price and by renewables reaching 47.2% of electricity (2024), resumed gas-for-coal switching, and demand reduction. National coal phase-out commitments (e.g., Germany's 2038/ideally-2030 schedule) reinforce ETS scarcity expectations, though the 2022 energy crisis temporarily reversed fuel switching (power emissions +2.4% in 2022) before the 2023–24 collapse (−24%, −10.7%). REPowerEU monetized ETS allowances (€20B target) to fund exactly these complementary policies — a fiscal coupling of price and policy.
- **California**: Cap-and-trade is deliberately a backstop, not the workhorse. The 2022 Scoping Plan assigns most modeled reductions to direct measures — the Renewables Portfolio Standard, the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, Advanced Clean Cars/Trucks rules, and building electrification. - **China**: The ETS is layered onto the world's largest renewable deployment program (renewables >1.5 TW, >50% of installed capacity by 2023; 2024 generation growth: wind +12.5%, solar +43.6%, hydro +10.9%) and a shifting coal policy — from "dual control" of energy consumption toward dual control of carbon emissions, but with continued coal capacity additions and guaranteed coal-power contracts that Carbon Brief identifies as now conflicting with clean-energy dispatch. The ETS's marginal role is efficiency within the coal fleet (57% of measured first-cycle abatement) rather than fuel switching, which remains driven by industrial policy.

## 9. Leakage: Mechanisms and Evidence

- **California** uses a dual approach (CalEPA/IEMAC leakage chapter): (i) output-based free allocation to emissions-intensive, trade-exposed industry — AB 398 (2017) directs CARB to treat all covered industries as at high leakage risk — with industrial allocation ~22% of direct allocation; and (ii) a de facto border carbon adjustment on imported electricity via the first-deliverer obligation. # MLOps Platform Comparison for Real-Time Fraud Detection at 50M Daily Transactions (India, Indonesia, Philippines)

## Executive Summary

For a fintech startup serving ensemble fraud models (XGBoost/LightGBM + neural networks) at 50M transactions/day (~580 TPS average, ~5,800 TPS at 10x burst), the evidence points to a clear tiering:

- **Best overall fit: Seldon Core v2 with Triton Inference Server** — the only option where the FIL backend serves both GBDT frameworks and neural nets in one process with documented p99 <2ms on GPU for fraud-detection tree models, plus native drift detection and pipeline orchestration. Highest initial engineering cost.
- **Best time-to-production: BentoML** — lowest framework overhead in published XGBoost CPU benchmarks (p99 5.9ms, ~5,100 RPS/pod), proven in fintech fraud production, but weakest native A/B testing and drift tooling.
- **Best for complex ensembles and burst autoscaling: Ray Serve** — Python-native model composition and queue-depth-based autoscaling, but the thinnest built-in monitoring/rollback story and an extra distributed-runtime layer to operate.
- **Best for K8s-standardized platform teams: KServe** — the strongest documented rollback semantics (`LatestRolledoutRevision`/`PreviousRolledoutRevision`) and scale-to-zero economics, but Knative cold starts (2–5s typical, worse on GPU) are a real liability for a fraud hot path.

Important framing from the comparison literature: at this layer, the serving wrapper matters less than the inference engine, batching policy, and hardware. Independent benchmarkers repeatedly found throughput parity within ±4–10% across KServe, Seldon, and BentoML when the same runtime (e.g., vLLM or Triton) sits underneath (https://iotdigitaltwinplm.com/kserve-vs-ray-serve-vs-bentoml-model-serving-kubernetes-adr-2026/, https://jobpreparena.com/blog/kserve-vs-seldon-core-vs-bentoml-a-feature-by-feature-comparison-for-2026). Your real decision is the operational seam: CRD-driven GitOps (KServe/Seldon) vs. Python-code-driven deployment (Ray Serve/BentoML).

---

## 1. Workload Definition and Sizing Math

Quantitative work (shown explicitly):

- Average throughput: 50,000,000 tx/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ **579 TPS**
- Payments traffic is diurnal; assume peak-to-mean ≈ 3x → typical peak ≈ **1,700–2,000 TPS**
- 10x burst over average → **~5,800 TPS** sustained burst target; headroom planning should target ~8,000–10,000 TPS
- Latency budget: payment authorization paths typically allow 100–300ms end-to-end. Razorpay's published budget for feature generation + model prediction is **200ms in a distributed environment** (https://razorpay.com/unfiltered/data-science-at-scale-using-apache-flink/). A realistic model-serving sub-budget is p99 ≤ 30–50ms including feature fetch.

At 50M predictions/day you generate **1.5B predictions/month**, so every $1/million in unit cost is ~$1,500/month — small in absolute terms, which means **engineering time and incident cost dominate platform TCO, not compute**. This should weigh the decision toward operability.

---

## 2. Platform-by-Platform Evaluation

### 2.1 Seldon Core v2 + Triton Inference Server

**Latency/throughput.** The standout evidence: NVIDIA's FIL (Forest Inference Library) backend for Triton serves XGBoost, LightGBM, scikit-learn RF, and Treelite models on GPU, and in NVIDIA's own fraud-detection example on a DGX-1 (8×V100) achieved **p99 < 2ms at >400K inferences/sec — roughly 20x CPU throughput** (https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/real-time-serving-for-xgboost-scikit-learn-randomforest-lightgbm-and-more/). Even discounting vendor-benchmark optimism by 5–10x, a single GPU node plausibly covers your entire 10x burst. Triton simultaneously serves PyTorch/TensorFlow/ONNX/TensorRT, so the NN half of your ensemble runs in the same server, and Triton **ensembles** let you chain GBDT + NN without a network hop. Third-party benchmark: Seldon MLServer served XGBoost (147 features, CPU) at **p99 6.8ms, 4,600 RPS/pod, with gRPC 18% faster than HTTP** (https://jobpreparena.com/blog/kserve-vs-seldon-core-vs-bentoml-a-feature-by-feature-comparison-for-2026). Seldon's own docs emphasize load-testing both saturated and non-saturated regimes with p50–p99 tracking before tuning (https://docs.seldon.ai/seldon-core-2/user-guide/performance-tuning/models/load-testing).

**Burst handling.** Seldon v2 uses HPA + KEDA on custom metrics (e.g., `seldon_model_inference_requests`, queue length) with a measured **scale reaction of 12–18s**; **no scale-to-zero out of the box** (https://jobpreparena.com/blog/kserve-vs-seldon-core-vs-bentoml-a-feature-by-feature-comparison-for-2026). For fraud (always-on traffic), no scale-to-zero is a feature, not a bug — but 12–18s reaction means you must run headroom (N+2) rather than rely on autoscaling for a 10x burst.

**A/B testing.** Native traffic splitting between model versions plus multi-step Pipelines; a known (now-fixed) defect caused transient 503s in Envoy during rollouts before ADS ordering guarantees were added (https://github.com/SeldonIO/seldon-core/blob/v2/CHANGELOG.md) — evidence that canary mechanics here are real but require version maturity.

**Versioning/rollback.** Models are versioned artifacts (`artifactVersion` in the Model CR); rollback is a declarative re-apply of the previous Model CR, and old versions are removed when the model is deleted (https://docs.seldon.ai/seldon-core-2/user-guide/examples/multi-version, changelog above). Rollback is fast (routing-level, no image rebuild) but requires GitOps discipline to be safe.

**Drift monitoring.** Best-in-class among the four: Alibi-Detect drift/outlier detectors deploy as first-class Models in an **asynchronous branch of the inference Pipeline**, with alerts emitted to a Kafka topic (https://docs.seldon.ai/seldon-core-2/user-guide/data-science-monitoring/drift). This fits a Kafka-centric fraud stack directly.

**Feature store overhead.** No native Feast integration; you fetch features in a transformer/pre-processing step or in the client. Expect ~1–3 weeks of integration work and 5–15ms added p99 for online store lookups.

**Engineering effort.** Highest of the four: you operate Kafka (data plane), the Seldon scheduler, Envoy, and Triton/MLServer. Estimate **2–3 engineers × 6–10 weeks** initial; **~0.75–1.25 FTE** ongoing.

### 2.2 KServe on Kubernetes

**Latency/throughput.** Same benchmark suite: KServe sklearn server on XGBoost CPU hit **p99 7.2ms, 4,200 RPS/pod** — statistically at parity with Seldon/BentoML (https://jobpreparena.com/blog/kserve-vs-seldon-core-vs-bentoml-a-feature-by-feature-comparison-for-2026). With the Triton runtime underneath, GPU numbers mirror Seldon's. An independent benchmarker (6-node K8s, Istio, Poisson traffic 50–2,000 RPS) found KServe-on-Knative **consistently faster resuming from scale-to-zero (~150–300ms delta on Python/MLServer backends, larger on Triton)**, with steady-state throughput a draw once warm (https://medium.com/@Modexa/kserve-vs-seldon-7-benchmark-backed-decisions-da94952ae85c). KServe's Knative autoscaler uses a 60s window with a 6s panic window (https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/predictive-inference/rollout-strategies/canary, corroborated by the KnativeCon platform talk at https://static.sched.com/hosted_files/knativeconeu22/60/KnativeCon%20-%20How%20we%20built%20an%20ML%20Inference%20Platform%20with%20Knative.pdf).

**Burst handling.** The 6s panic window reacts faster than plain HPA (5-min stabilization), which matters for festival/payday bursts in India/SEA. **But**: scale-to-zero cold starts are **typically 2–5s** for CPU models (https://reintech.io/blog/bentoml-vs-seldon-core-vs-kserve-model-serving-framework-comparison) and far worse for GPU pods — documented GPU cold-start budgets run **~25s (8B model, warm image) to 5–8 min (uncached image)**, with container image pull the dominant term (https://www.spheron.network/blog/keda-knative-gpu-autoscaling-kubernetes-llm-cold-start/). Knative's Activator buffers requests during cold start, so callers see latency, not errors — but a 2–5s first-request penalty is unacceptable on a payment hot path. Mitigation: `minReplicas ≥ 2` on all fraud-scoring InferenceServices, and `scale-to-zero-pod-retention-period` to keep a warm pod (the KnativeCon talk explicitly recommends this pattern).

**A/B testing and rollback — KServe's strongest suit.** `canaryTrafficPercent` splits traffic between the new revision and the automatically tracked `LatestRolledoutRevision`; promotion removes the field; **rollback = set `canaryTrafficPercent: 0`, which pins 100% of traffic to the previous healthy revision (`PreviousRolledoutRevision`)**, and bad revisions automatically receive no traffic (https://kserve.github.io/website/docs/model-serving/predictive-inference/rollout-strategies/canary, https://github.com/kserve/website/blob/main/docs/model-serving/predictive-inference/rollout-strategies/canary-example.md). Caveat: canary rollout strategy is **only supported in serverless (Knative) mode**, not RawDeployment. This is the most operationally legible incident-response story of the four — a single `kubectl apply` reverts a bad model in seconds at the routing layer.

**Drift monitoring.** Alibi-Detect integration via payload logging + Knative Eventing for async drift/outlier detection (https://github.com/kserve/website/blob/main/docs/model-serving/predictive-inference/detect/alibi/alibi-detect.md). Functional but more assembly required than Seldon v2's pipeline-integrated approach.

**Feature store overhead.** Same as Seldon — external. Gojek's own stack proves the pattern: their Merlin serving layer is **built directly on KFServing (KServe's former name) + Knative + Istio, paired with the Feast feature store** (https://www.gojek.io/blog/merlin-making-ml-model-deployments-magical, https://www.gojek.io/blog/feast-bridging-ml-models-and-data), so KServe + Feast is a battle-tested combination at Southeast Asian super-app scale.

**Engineering effort.** **2 engineers × 5–8 weeks** initial (Knative + Istio + KServe CRDs); **~0.5–1 FTE** ongoing. Note the multi-model angle: the Modexa benchmarks found **KServe ModelMesh gave 22–28% better throughput per node at 100 models** vs. one-model-per-pod patterns — relevant if you deploy per-country or per-merchant-segment model variants.

### 2.3 Ray Serve

**Latency/throughput.** For tabular fraud models, Ray Serve's overhead is small but real (proxy → router → replica hops, typically a few ms). A reference fraud-detection architecture using Ray Serve + ONNX Runtime with Flink features + Feast/Redis targets **sub-50ms p95** on tuned infrastructure (https://github.com/ejkennedy/Real-Time-Fraud-Detection-MLOps-Platform). Ray Serve's distinctive strength is **model composition in pure Python**: your XGBoost + LightGBM + NN ensemble, plus business rules, can be a graph of deployments with zero serialization boundary friction — the cleanest multi-framework story of the four.

**Burst handling — best autoscaler semantics for bursts.** The autoscaler maintains `target_ongoing_requests` per replica (default became **2 in Ray 2.32**), with `max_ongoing_requests` as the queue cap and `upscale_delay_s` default **30s**; docs explicitly warn that `min_replicas: 0` saves cost but **raises tail latency** (https://iotdigitaltwinplm.com/kserve-vs-ray-serve-vs-bentoml-model-serving-kubernetes-adr-2026/). Queue-depth-based scaling reacts faster than CPU-based HPA for inference. Under a 10x burst with `min_replicas` set to peak-average, Ray Serve handles ramp well; with default 30s upscale delay you'll drop or delay burst traffic in the first half-minute — tune this down and accept over-provisioning.

**A/B testing.** Programmatic traffic splitting between deployments (weights in config). Flexible but you build the experiment discipline yourself; no experiment-engine equivalent. (Gojek built **Turing**, a whole separate system, precisely because serving-layer traffic splitting isn't an experimentation platform: https://github.com/gojek/turing.)

**Versioning/rollback.** This is Ray Serve's weak spot *today*: an open RFC for **auto-rollback of `serve deploy`** (April 2026) describes the current gap — rollback requires re-applying the last-good config, and edge cases (no previous good config, rollback ping-pong, resurrection of deleted apps) are still being designed (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/63016). Rolling updates cap at 20% of replicas at a time (older API docs: https://docs.ray.io/en/releases-1.11.2/serve/core-apis.html). During a production incident, rollback is a redeploy, not a traffic pin — slower and more failure-prone than KServe's revision pinning. **Model multiplexing** (LRU-cached multi-model per replica, header-based routing) is excellent for cost-efficient many-variant serving (https://docs.ray.io/en/releases-2.49.1/serve/model-multiplexing.html).

**Drift monitoring.** Nothing built in; you wire Evidently/WhyLabs/Prometheus yourself (the reference fraud stack above pairs Ray Serve with Evidently + Prometheus + Grafana).

**Feature store overhead.** Lowest-friction Feast integration of the four (it's just Python in the deployment), but you own the lookup latency and failure handling.

**Engineering effort.** **1–2 engineers × 3–5 weeks** initial (plus KubeRay if on K8s); **~0.5–1 FTE** ongoing — you operate a Ray cluster on top of K8s, a second distributed-systems control plane. Proof at payments scale exists in the ecosystem: Adyen (200M payments/day) standardized its ML data/training stack on Ray, gaining 5x experiment velocity (https://www.anyscale.com/blog/ray-day-london-recap), though that's training-side evidence, not serving.

### 2.4 BentoML

**Latency/throughput.** Lowest serving-framework overhead in the comparative CPU benchmark: **XGBoost p99 5.9ms, 5,100 RPS/pod** — the best of the three tested — attributed to minimal framework overhead (https://jobpreparena.com/blog/kserve-vs-seldon-core-vs-bentoml-a-feature-by-feature-comparison-for-2026). Adaptive batching helps mixed GBDT+NN ensembles on GPU. A HAL-published academic comparison of serving frameworks found general-purpose servers (BentoML, MLflow, MLServer) carry higher latency than DL-specific servers (TFServing/TorchServe) — up to ~68% higher average latency in their malware/vision scenarios — reinforcing that **the runtime matters more than the wrapper** and BentoML with an ONNX/Triton-adjacent runner closes most of that gap (https://hal.science/hal-04894045v1/document).

**Production fraud evidence.** Strongest fintech references of the four:
- Mission Lane (US fintech) runs **payment fraud, underwriting, and line assignment** on BentoML with **10s–100s of milliseconds for pure model evaluations**, tens of thousands of live calls/day, unifying online + batch scoring on the same artifact (https://medium.com/mission-lane-tech-blog/mlops-infrastructure-at-mission-lane-part-2-abb80a9eaf0a).
- A LATAM fintech fraud deployment: XGBoost on BentoML + Redis feature store + Flink streaming, **end-to-end decision latency <100ms**, fraud rate 4.2%→1.1% (−73%), false positives 18%→3.2% (https://numoru.com/en/contributions/caso-deteccion-fraude-ml).
- A consumer lender cut deployment costs 90% and shipped 50% more models after migrating from Flask/EC2 to BentoML, citing prior pain with failed deployments, versioning instability, and days-long update cycles (https://www.bentoml.com/blog/fintech-loan-servicer-cuts-model-deployment-costs-by-90-with-bento).

**Burst handling.** Standard K8s HPA/KEDA; measured **scale reaction 15–22s** (https://jobpreparena.com/blog/kserve-vs-seldon-core-vs-bentoml-a-feature-by-feature-comparison-for-2026) — like Seldon, you handle 10x bursts with headroom, not reaction speed. No native scale-to-zero (KEDA idle scaler possible).

**A/B testing, rollback, drift.** Weakest native story: traffic splitting/rollback are delegated to whatever K8s ingress/service mesh you deploy (or BentoCloud); versioning is strong at the artifact level (the Bento locks model + dependency tree, `bentoml containerize` for immutable images — https://github.com/bentoml/Fraud-Detection-Model-Serving), but in an incident, rollback = redeploy previous Bento image (minutes, not seconds). No built-in drift detection; pair with Evidently.

**Engineering effort.** Lowest: **1–2 engineers × 2–4 weeks**; **~0.25–0.5 FTE** ongoing. The Python-native, notebook-to-container path is the fastest of the four — matching the pattern that drew Gojek to build Merlin ("less than 10 minutes from pre-trained model to endpoint"; https://www.gojek.io/blog/merlin-making-ml-model-deployments-magical).

---

## 3. Comparative Table (fraud-relevant criteria)

| Criterion | Seldon Core v2 + Triton | KServe | Ray Serve | BentoML |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| XGBoost CPU p99 (published) | 6.8ms / 4,600 RPS-pod | 7.2ms / 4,200 RPS-pod | ~sub-50ms p95 e2e (arch target) | **5.9ms / 5,100 RPS-pod** |
| GBDT+NN in one server | **Yes (Triton FIL + DL backends)** | Via Triton runtime | Python composition (best ergonomics) | Runners/adaptive batching |
| 10x burst strategy | Headroom; scale react 12–18s | Knative panic window 6s; headroom for GPU | Queue-depth autoscaling (best semantics); upscale delay 30s default | Headroom; 15–22s reaction |
| Cold start (new deploy) | Model load only (no scale-to-zero default) | **2–5s CPU; 25s–8min GPU** if scale-to-zero | Replica start + model load; 0.8s class for large-model load vs 1.4s BentoML (SD3 benchmark) | No scale-to-zero; fast container boot |
| A/B testing | Traffic split + pipelines | **Canary w/ revision pinning (best)** | Programmatic split | DIY via mesh/ingress |
| Incident rollback | Re-apply Model CR (fast) | **`canaryTrafficPercent: 0` → instant pin to last good** | Redeploy last-good config (auto-rollback still RFC) | Redeploy prior Bento image |
| Drift detection | **Alibi-Detect as pipeline stage, alerts to Kafka** | Alibi-Detect via Knative Eventing | None built-in | None built-in |
| Feature store | External (DIY) | External; proven w/ Feast at Gojek | Easiest (native Python) | External (proven w/ Redis/Feast) |
| Initial effort | 6–10 wks, 2–3 eng | 5–8 wks, 2 eng | 3–5 wks, 1–2 eng | **2–4 wks, 1–2 eng** |
| Ongoing ops | 0.75–1.25 FTE | 0.5–1 FTE | 0.5–1 FTE | 0.25–0.5 FTE |

Sources for table rows are cited in Section 2; benchmark figures from https://jobpreparena.com/blog/kserve-vs-seldon-core-vs-bentoml-a-feature-by-feature-comparison-for-2026 and https://medium.com/@Modexa/kserve-vs-seldon-7-benchmark-backed-decisions-da94952ae85c are third-party single-cluster measurements — treat as directional (±20%), not guarantees.

---

## 4. Cost per Million Predictions (mixed CPU/GPU)

Assumptions (stated for auditability): ap-south-1 (Mumbai) on-demand pricing; c6i.2xlarge at **$0.340/hr** (Mumbai regional price, https://cloudcostdb.com/aws/instances/c6i.2xlarge/); GPU node g4dn.xlarge-class T4 at ~**$0.526/hr** (us-east-1 baseline $0.526; Mumbai uplift ~10–15% → use $0.60/hr as conservative); 65% average utilization; monthly volume = 50M × 30 = **1.5B predictions**.

**Scenario A — CPU-only (BentoML/KServe/Seldon at ~4,500 RPS per 8-vCPU pod):**
- Pods needed at 5,800 TPS burst: 5,800 ÷ 4,500 ≈ 1.3 → **2 pods + N+1 = 3 pods** (3 × c6i.2xlarge)
- Monthly cost: 3 × $0.340 × 730 hr ≈ **$745/mo**
- Utilization-adjusted (65%): effective ≈ $745 ÷ 0.65 ≈ $1,146
- **Cost per million predictions ≈ $1,146 ÷ 1,500 ≈ $0.76/M** (range across platforms ±15% given benchmark parity)

**Scenario B — Triton FIL on GPU (fraud-tuned):**
- NVIDIA benchmark: >400K inf/s on 8×V100 → conservatively 25K inf/s on one T4-class GPU with small fraud trees (discount vendor numbers ~16x for single midrange GPU): one GPU node covers burst with headroom; run 2 for HA.
- Monthly: 2 × $0.60 × 730 ≈ $876; utilization-adjusted ≈ $1,348 → **≈ $0.90/M**, but with p99 ~2ms class latency and 10x+ burst headroom.

**Scenario C — mixed (NN on GPU, GBDT on CPU, e.g., Ray Serve or KServe heterogeneous):**
- 2 × c6i.2xlarge + 1 × g4dn.xlarge ≈ $497 + $438 ≈ $935/mo → util-adjusted ≈ $1,440 → **≈ $0.96/M**.

**Verdict on cost:** all four platforms land in the **$0.70–$1.10 per million predictions** band on self-managed K8s; compute differences are noise (±$500/mo). The dominant cost variables are (a) engineering FTE (1 FTE-year >> annual compute at this volume), (b) over-provisioning for bursts, and (c) managed-service premiums (BentoCloud/Anyscale/Seldon Enterprise) if chosen. GPU sharing/bin-packing matters at larger model counts (Seldon's scheduler saved ~11% GPU in one benchmark; KServe ModelMesh +22–28% throughput/node at 100 models).

---

## 5. What Razorpay, Gojek, and PayMongo Actually Did

**Razorpay (India).** Chose **stream-native scoring over request-response MLOps**: their Mitra platform embeds XGBoost models *inside Apache Flink* with RocksDB in-memory state and Kafka, generating hundreds of features on the fly and predicting within **200ms end-to-end**, with a dynamic rule engine on streams (https://razorpay.com/unfiltered/data-science-at-scale-using-apache-flink/). Key lesson for this comparison: at payments latency budgets, they deliberately **avoided a separate model-server hop for the hottest path** — a design any of the four platforms can complement (for model management/rollout) but not replace architecturally. They also separated training and serving clusters explicitly because bulk feature transfer during training choked serving networks. More recently they've consolidated toward a foundation-model approach (Vulcan) with SageMaker for training/managed inference (https://razorpay.com/blog/vulcan-how-razorpay-built-a-foundation-model-for-payment-decisions/).

**Gojek (Indonesia).** Built the full stack this task asks about, and their choices map almost one-to-one onto the candidates:
- **Merlin** (model serving) is built **on KFServing/KServe + Knative + Istio**, supports XGBoost/sklearn/TensorFlow/PyTorch plus arbitrary PyFunc (their own sample is an **XGBoost+sklearn ensemble**), with canary/blue-green/shadow traffic management and a <10-minute deploy target (https://www.gojek.io/blog/merlin-making-ml-model-deployments-magical, https://merlin-sdk.readthedocs.io/en/stable/sample/pyfunc.html). **Multi-framework complexity was their motivating pain** — data scientists faced Docker/K8s/istio complexity per framework; Merlin's answer was standardization on one serving CRD layer.
- **Feast** (feature store, co-built with Google) decoupled feature serving via a common feature stream so teams run decentralized serving instances (https://www.gojek.io/blog/feast-bridging-ml-models-and-data).
- **Turing** handles experimentation as a separate router layer (https://github.com/gojek/turing) — evidence that serving-platform traffic splitting alone was insufficient for rigorous A/B evaluation.
- On cold starts specifically: Merlin is Knative-based, so idle services scale down — the Knative/ML literature (including a KnativeCon ML-platform talk) confirms **cold start remains the acknowledged weakness, mitigated by minReplicas** (https://static.sched.com/hosted_files/knativeconeu22/60/KnativeCon%20-%20How%20we%20built%20an%20ML%20Inference%20Platform%20with%20Knative.pdf). Gojek's fraud stack also includes near-real-time rules on ClickHouse and GNNs (GoSage) for collusion rings — models deployed through the same platform layer (https://www.gojek.io/blog/detecting-fraudsters-in-near-real-time-with-clickhouse, https://medium.com/gojekengineering/gosage-how-we-detect-fraud-syndicates-at-gojek-with-graph-neural-networks-d4d0f4890de1).

**PayMongo (Philippines).** Took the **buy-don't-build** path: adopted Sift Payment Protection after fraud attacks drove a **4% dispute rate**, then scaled securely 10–20x with ML-based blocking, workflow rules, and case management (https://sift.com/resources/case-studies/paymongo-case-study/). They have not published a self-managed MLOps serving architecture; their engineering investment went into observability consolidation (Datadog across APM/logs/security, https://www.datadoghq.com/case-studies/paymongo/). Lesson: for an early-stage startup, a managed fraud vendor or managed serving tier is a legitimate alternative to owning KServe/Seldon operations, and observability maturity is a prerequisite whichever path you choose.

**Cold-start latency for new model deployments — synthesized from the above:**
- *New model version on warm pool* (Seldon/KServe minReplicas>0/BentoML): dominated by artifact download + model load — seconds for GBDTs (tens of MB), tens of seconds for NN containers with cached images.
- *Scale-from-zero* (KServe/Knative, the Gojek/Merlin pattern): 2–5s CPU typical; GPU worst case is minutes with uncached images — pre-pulled images are "the single biggest lever" (https://www.spheron.network/blog/keda-knative-gpu-autoscaling-kubernetes-llm-cold-start/).
- Ray Serve measured 0.8s vs BentoML 1.4s cold-load for a 12GB model on A100 (https://johal.in/ray-serve-220-vs-bentoml-13-serving-stable) — single-benchmark, LLM-class, directional only.
- Razorpay's in-Flink approach eliminates per-model server cold starts entirely by treating models as stream-operator state — the architectural extreme.

**Multi-framework operational complexity:** Gojek's Merlin genesis (framework sprawl blocking deployment) and Razorpay's unified-stream approach both indicate the winning pattern: **standardize on one serving substrate and serialize all frameworks into it** (Triton FIL + ONNX, or MLServer runtimes), rather than running N framework-native servers. Seldon+Triton and KServe+Triton both enforce this; BentoML achieves it via runners; Ray Serve achieves it via Python polymorphism (most flexible, least guardrails).

---

## 6. Recommendation

**Primary: Seldon Core v2 + Triton (FIL backend)**, configured with: min 2 warm replicas per fraud model (no scale-to-zero on the hot path), Alibi-Detect drift models as async pipeline branches feeding your existing Kafka, Feast for online features (the Gojek-proven pattern), and canary traffic splits for new variants. This gives the best latency ceiling (p99 ~2ms GPU-class for GBDTs), unified GBDT+NN serving, and native drift detection matched to payments event streaming.

**Choose KServe instead** if your team is already strong on Kubernetes/Istio and you prioritize the cleanest incident-rollback semantics (`canaryTrafficPercent: 0`) and per-model-variant economics (ModelMesh). Its cold-start weakness is fully mitigable with minReplicas — exactly as Gojek's Merlin-on-KFServing stack demonstrates at super-app scale.

**Choose Ray Serve instead** if your ensemble logic is complex and fast-evolving (chained models, dynamic routing, per-country model multiplexing) and you can accept building your own drift monitoring and living with manual-ish rollback until the auto-rollback RFC lands.

**Choose BentoML instead** if you are a sub-10-person team and time-to-first-production dominates: it has the best measured per-pod CPU latency, real fintech fraud references, and the lowest ops burden — plan to add a service mesh for A/B testing and Evidently for drift, and accept redeploy-based rollbacks.

**Regardless of platform**, adopt Razorpay's two architectural rules: keep the hottest scoring path free of unnecessary network hops (co-locate feature fetch and inference; target the 200ms end-to-end envelope), and physically separate training from serving infrastructure. Budget N+2 warm capacity for 10x bursts in all cases — no autoscaler among the four reacts fast enough (6–30s) to absorb a true 10x step without headroom.

**Uncertainty statement:** Third-party latency benchmarks cited here are single-cluster, single-configuration measurements and should be validated with your own models/feature counts (Seldon's own docs insist on per-deployment load testing for exactly this reason). Vendor benchmarks (NVIDIA FIL, BentoML case studies) are best-case; I have discounted them explicitly where used. PayMongo has not published self-managed MLOps architecture, so conclusions drawn from their experience are limited to the build-vs-buy and observability dimensions.
