### 4.2 Converting to fuel per acre at 12–15 mph

Honest caveat: **12–15 mph is not heavy-tillage or seeding speed.** Heavy tillage runs 4.5–8 mph; air seeding 5–7 mph. 12–15 mph is high-speed compact-disc/vertical-tillage or fast transport-adjacent work. NTTL drawbar tests top out at ~10 mph, so I extrapolate moderately loaded conditions. Both tractors gear to these speeds easily (Deere 15th–18th gear of 18; Case 13th–16th of 16; both ~40 km/h top).

Field capacity: ac/hr = speed (mph) × width (ft) ÷ 8.25 × field efficiency (0.85)

At 12 mph with a 40-ft high-speed tool: 12 × 40 / 8.25 × 0.85 = **49.5 ac/hr (20.0 ha/hr)**
At 15 mph with a 40-ft tool: **61.8 ac/hr (25.0 ha/hr)**

Required drawbar power for high-speed tillage at 12+ mph on clay-loam ≈ 9–11 drawbar hp/ft → 40 ft ≈ 360–440 drawbar hp, i.e., near both tractors' tested max (~409–440 drawbar hp). Fuel burn:

- **9RX 540:** 400 hp ÷ 15.90 hp·hr/gal = 25.2 gal/hr = 95.2 L/hr → 95.2 ÷ 20.0 ha/hr = **≈ 4.8 L/ha (0.51 US gal/ac)**
- **Steiger 540 QT:** 400 hp ÷ ~15.8 = 25.3 gal/hr = 95.8 L/hr → **≈ 4.8 L/ha (0.51 US gal/ac)**

**Difference: ~0.05 L/ha (~C$0.05/ha at C$1.05/L dyed diesel) — economically negligible.** At your intensity (~20 ha/hr × 1,800 hr ≈ 36,000 ha/yr across all passes... realistically 25,000–36,000 ha/yr of cumulative passes), a 1% fuel difference is worth roughly C$1,700–2,500/yr. Real-world fuel use will be dominated by draft control, ballast, and slip management (keep slip 2–4% on tracks) far more than by brand.

### 4.3 DEF — a real differentiator

NTTL-measured DEF dosing rates:
- 9RX 540: **0.020–0.025 lb/hp·hr** drawbar (Tests 2252/2310)
- Steiger 540 QT: **0.047 lb/hp·hr** at 75% pull (Test 2188); PTO DEF at max power 2.86 gal/hr vs Deere's ~0.86 gal/hr

At 400 drawbar hp sustained:
- Deere: 0.0225 × 400 = 9.0 lb/hr ÷ 9.071 lb/gal = **0.99 gal/hr (3.75 L/hr)** → at C$0.55/L DEF = **C$2.06/hr**
- Case: 0.047 × 400 = 18.8 lb/hr ÷ 9.071 = **2.07 gal/hr (7.85 L/hr)** = **C$4.32/hr**

**Δ ≈ C$2.25/hr → ~C$4,000–5,000/yr at 1,800–2,200 hr → C$40,000–50,000 over 10 years in Deere's favor** (~C$0.11–0.15/ha). Case's SCR-only design trades DEF for the absence of a DPF; the Deere JD14 also has no DPF yet doses roughly half the DEF.

## 5. TRACK DURABILITY ON CLAY-LOAM AT 180+ DAYS/YEAR

Design differences (documented):
- The 9RX undercarriage (Camso-built) uses a **20% longer belt**, a larger 39.5-in drive sprocket, more drive-lug engagement, higher belt tension, and 8RT-derived midrollers; Deere claims 20% less belt travel per unit distance → ~20% longer belt life. 30"/36" Camso Duradrive 3500/6500 belts (https://www.farmprogress.com/farm-business/john-deere-officially-launches-9rx-four-track-tractor ; https://www.dtnpf.com/agriculture/web/ag/blogs/machinerylink/blog-post/john-deere-goes-four-track/2015-08-26 ; Camso brochure: https://camso.co/content/files/products/AG/2401_AG_TrackBrochure2019_JD_8.5x8.5_EN_V4_Web.pdf).
- The Quadtrac undercarriage is Case's in-house design (since 1996) with belts from Camso or ContiTech (https://www.thecombineforum.com/threads/deere-rx9620-vs-caseih-quadtrac-620.269386/).

Field-reported belt life (anecdotal, forums — treat with caution):
- Quadtrac: ~3,000 hr typical before lug cracking/carcass separation; up to 6,000 hr on 36" belts with religious alignment and roading ≤13 mph (https://combineforum.freeforums.net/thread/250/track-longevity ; https://www.thecombineforum.com/threads/hours-expected-out-of-tracks-before-needing-replacement-on-a-600-hp-tractor.355474/).
- 9RX: one Manitoba report of wires showing at ~3,000 hr; others expecting more; Deere-side forum claims a 2,000-hr track warranty via John Deere; Camso warranty is prorated by time/usage for both brands (https://www.thecombineforum.com/threads/deere-rx-camso-tracks.352513/).

**Implications for your conditions:**
- Clay-loam is moderately abrasive and high-draft; when wet it packs and increases carcass strain — but the dominant, controllable wear factors are **alignment, roading speed, and slip**, not soil brand-to-brand. Saskatchewan operators confirm: "Track width, alignment, and average road speed/distance seem more important to track life than anything" (Combine Forum, above).
- At 1,800–2,200 hr/yr you will consume a set of belts every **1.5–2.5 years regardless of brand**. Budget 5–6 belt sets over 10 years. If Deere's +20% claim holds (unproven independently), that is roughly one fewer belt set per decade: ~C$40,000–60,000 saved (belts ~C$12–15k each × 4).
- Deere's midrollers are shared with the proven 8RT line and easier to service; Quadtrac rollers historically need daily oil checks on older designs (newer sealed units have improved). Slight maintenance-time edge to Deere, offset by Case's longer engine service interval (Section 8).

**Track durability verdict: modest Deere edge on design and claimed life; real-world outcome will be decided by your alignment discipline and roading speed cap (≤20–21 km/h). Insist on 36" belts for flotation on clay-loam and to run cooler.**

I didn't get to search for CCA specifically. I know from general knowledge: In Canada, self-propelled tractors are Class 10 (30% declining balance) — historically Class 8? Farm tractors: Class 8 (20%) or Class 10 (30%)? CRA: Class 10 (30%) includes tractors... The user references "Saskatchewan's accelerated capital cost allowance" — I did not gather sources on this. I'll compute a generic CCA schedule on, say, C$650,000 purchase price for both, showing the 10-year tax shield, noting rates need accountant verification. I don't have a sourced new price for 9RX 540. Used 2023 Steiger 540 with 762 hrs listed (no price shown). I'll present estimates with uncertainty: new 9RX 540 ~US$650-750k; Steiger 540 Quadtrac ~US$600-700k; Deere typically commands 5-10% premium. Let me structure quantitative work:

Field capacity: ac/hr = speed(mph) × width(ft) ÷ 8.25 × 0.85 efficiency.

Case at ~15.8 → 25.3 gal/hr → same 0.51 gal/ac.
Difference: <1%, i.e., ~C$0.02/ac. Over 200 acres — trivial; over 20,000 acres ~C$400/yr.

I'll state this correction politely with uncertainty (no sources gathered on tax; flag for accountant).

5. 10-year TCO at 1,800 h/yr (18,000 h total):
- Purchase (est): Deere C$950k?? Let me use USD conversions... Used 2022 Case CVX US$489,900 with 950 h. New: estimate Deere 9RX 540 ~C$850k, Case Steiger 540 QT ~C$800k (unverified, flag). Actually Canadian list prices for 9RX 540 ~C$750-900k depending on options. I'll present as assumption.

- DEF: Deere 3.3 L/h → 59,400 L × 0.55 = C$32.7k; Case 7.9 L/h → 141,300 L × 0.55 = C$77.7k → Case +C$45k.
- Tracks: Deere 5 sets? At 3,600 h → 18,000/3,600 = 5 sets × 55k = 275k; Case 6 sets × 55k = 330k. Plus midrollers/idlers ~C$15k per cycle.

- Residual after 10 yr / 18,000 h: low, maybe 15-20% — both.

Total rough 10-yr: Deere ≈ C$2.75M vs Case ≈ C$2.80M — within noise; uptime/service network and telematics fit decide.

Per hectare: hectares worked over 10 years: 18,000 h × 20 ha/h = 360,000 ha → TCO/ha ≈ C$7.6-7.8/ha excluding labor. Fuel alone ~C$3.4/ha.

Also address 200-acre reality check: at 200 acres (81 ha), even at 5 passes/yr = 400 ha/yr = ~20-30 h/yr; a 540-hp tractor is wildly oversized; 180 operational days implies ~20,000+ acres. Flag inconsistency; proceed with stated intensity.

Actually let me reconsider the "12-15 mph" claim — heavy tillage at 12-15 mph is not typical; seeding at 12-15 mph no. I'll note that at those speeds both are in upper gears (Deere 15th-18th; Case 14th-16th), loads are moderate, and per-acre fuel converges; heavy draft work (where these machines differ more) happens at 4.5-8 mph where Nebraska data applies.

# Trust-Building Mechanisms for Gig Platforms in Argentina, Colombia, and Brazil: A Comparative Research Report

Prepared for: UX Director, gig economy platform expansion
Scope: Rating systems, identity verification, payment/escrow, dispute resolution — and how users' prior trust-system experience shapes adoption

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Argentina, Colombia, and Brazil share three structural conditions that should drive your trust UX: (1) informality employs roughly half the workforce, so most of your supply side has never had an institutional guarantor of their work relationships; (2) interpersonal and institutional trust are among the lowest in the world — which paradoxically *increases* demand for platform-mediated trust substitutes (ratings, escrow, verified identity); and (3) each market has already been "trained" on a dominant trust infrastructure — Mercado Libre/Mercado Pago and interoperable QR in Argentina, Nequi/Daviplata wallets in Colombia, and Pix plus Reclame Aqui in Brazil. Platforms that map onto these learned mental models convert faster; platforms that ignore local due-process expectations (especially Brazil's courts and Colombia's SIC) accumulate legal and reputational risk.

Key numeric anchors: informal employment is ~49% (Argentina, 2019, ILO/World Bank) and ~57% (Colombia, 2019); interpersonal trust ("most people can be trusted") runs 24% in Argentina, 20% in Colombia, and only ~5–10% in Brazil; Pix processed 63.8 billion transactions in 2024 and is used by ~83% of Brazilians; 74% of Argentine digital-wallet users are on Mercado Pago; Nequi reaches ~37% of Colombians. Sources and caveats below.

---

## 2. Market Context: Informality and Trust Baselines

### 2.1 Informal economy participation

| Market | Informal employment (% of non-agricultural employment) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Argentina | 49.4% (2019); recent ILO-cited figures ~52.8% (2025) | CEIC/World Bank–ILOSTAT: https://www.ceicdata.com/en/argentina/employment-and-unemployment/ar-informal-employment--of-total-nonagricultural-employment ; https://emprego.com/guides/compare/argentina-vs-colombia |
| Colombia | 57.3% (2019); ~56% (2025) | https://www.ceicdata.com/en/colombia/employment-and-unemployment/co-informal-employment--of-total-nonagricultural-employment |
| Brazil | Not directly captured in this research pass; shadow economy ≈ 29.8% of GDP (World Economics estimate); LAC regional informal employment average is 51.7% (ILO) | https://www.worldeconomics.com/Informal-Economy/Argentina.aspx ; https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2025-01/Americas_Informality%20Regional%20statistical%20profile.pdf |

**Uncertainty note:** I did not obtain a clean, primary-sourced informal *employment* rate for Brazil in this pass; commonly cited IBGE/ILO figures place it near 40%, but treat that number as unverified here. The directional conclusion (informality between 40–60% across all three markets) is robust.

Structural detail that matters for UX: in LAC, ~1/3 of workers are self-employed and ~38% of informality occurs *in compliance with the law* — i.e., many informal workers are not evading anything; they sit outside systems designed for salaried employees (World Bank: https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/639b98001f52d3b10e2d05efd14cc626-0370012023/original/Melendez-Labor-informality-in-LAC.pdf). Gig work is therefore not a marginal hustle but a primary income infrastructure: the IDB/Uber–Ipsos survey of 13,722 drivers across eight countries (Aug–Sep 2024) found 75% live with debt, 88% report lacking financial security, only 30% contribute to a pension, and drivers average 19.3 hours/week (https://publications.iadb.org/publications/english/document/Driving-through-the-Gig-Economy-in-Latin-America--Uber-Drivers-Views-on-Needs-Risks-and-Opportunities.pdf ; https://efe.com/economia/2026-02-26/latinoamerica-uber-conductores-problemas-economicos/).

### 2.2 Trust baselines — the design-critical difference between the three markets

Interpersonal trust ("most people can be trusted"):

- **Brazil: 5%** (Latinobarómetro 2024, via BTI: https://bti-project.org/en/reports/country-report/BRA); 10.2% in 2022 cross-survey data (Our World in Data: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/interpersonal-trust-measured-in-different-surveys?tab=table). Brazil's 20-year Latinobarómetro average is ~7% — the **lowest in the region** (SciELO: https://www.scielo.br/j/sant/a/nCFdzrHg5sVqpxcQM76p84m/?lang=en).
- **Argentina: ~24–25%** (24.1% in 2022; 25% long-run average).
- **Colombia: ~20–21%** (20.5% in 2022; 21% long-run average).

Institutional trust is similarly weak: fewer than 4 in 10 Latin Americans trust their government, and institutional trust fell toward ~20% by 2018 (IDB: https://publications.iadb.org/publications/english/document/The-Elusive-Quest-for-Growth-in-Latin-American-and-the-Caribbean-The-Role-of-Trust.pdf ; UNDP: https://www.undp.org/latin-america/blog/whom-do-we-trust-less-institutions-and-more-communities-lac).

**Design implication:** In low-trust societies, users do not extend "benefit of the doubt" to strangers *or* to institutions — but they do adopt platform trust substitutes eagerly when those substitutes are concrete and verifiable (escrowed money, government-checked identity, transaction-linked ratings). The extreme Brazilian distrust (5%) means trust signals must be strongest and most explicit there; Argentina's comparatively higher interpersonal trust (24%) means peer/social proof carries relatively more weight. Across all three, the Latinobarómetro finding that personal experience ("si el servicio responde a mi necesidad") matters far more than third-party claims (40% vs 11–12% for media/friends) tells you onboarding must deliver a *successful first transaction* fast — trust is built experientially, not by marketing (https://www.latinobarometro.org/documents/LAT-2017/informe-latinobarometro-2017.pdf).

---

## 3. Mechanism 1: Rating Systems

### What each market has learned

**Regional reference model — Mercado Libre's reputation thermometer.** The dominant e-commerce platform in all three countries uses a color-coded reputation system: new sellers start gray; reputation turns green only with a complaint rate ≤2%, plus shipping-time and cancellation metrics, computed over a rolling ~3-month window; tiers (Mercado Líder Silver/Gold/Platinum) layer on top; reputation is computed **per country** (https://global-selling.mercadolibre.com/learning-center/news/seller-reputation-learn-how-it-works ; https://developers.mercadolibre.com.bo/en_us/news/sellers-reputation). Tens of millions of buyers and sellers across your three markets have internalized this model — colors, complaint-driven scores, and the idea that reputation is earned through completed, claim-free transactions.

**Evidence on how ratings drive trust and adoption (Colombia):** A 2024 peer-reviewed PLS-SEM study of 326 recent Mercado Libre Colombia buyers (Peña-García et al., Frontiers in Communication) found: (a) perceived *fake reviews significantly reduce trust in the rating system*; (b) high-quality reviews increase trust in reviews, in the marketplace, and in the rating system simultaneously; (c) trust in the rating system **mediates** the effect of review perceptions on customer experience — i.e., if users stop believing the rating system itself, the whole experience degrades (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1460321/full). The same paper, citing the institutional-based trust literature (Pavlou & Gefen), confirms that in emerging markets with low shopping experience, ratings act as a *trust-transfer mechanism*: trust flows from the platform's institutional guarantees to the individual stranger you transact with.

**The worker side is the weak link.** Ratings on gig platforms in the region are largely one-directional (customer rates worker) and function as algorithmic discipline. Fairwork Brazil 2025 (10 platforms incl. Uber, 99, iFood, Rappi, GetNinjas) found rating systems used as control mechanisms that "accelerate and increase work-related risks," with **no platform** demonstrating fair management practices such as a meaningful appeal path (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2025/09/Fairwork-Brazil-Report-2025-ENG_FINAL.pdf). Fairwork Argentina 2022 scored six platforms (Uber, Cabify, Rappi, PedidosYa, Beat, DiDi); only DiDi scored any points at all (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/en/fw/blog/fairwork-argentina-scores-2022-new-report-about-gig-economies-in-latin-america/). Brazilian court records show the concrete failure mode: an iFood courier with a **98.9 score and 770+ deliveries** was deactivated on an unproven fraud suspicion, and courts ordered reinstatement (https://www.migalhas.com.br/arquivos/2024/6/6B95C6A1FC6FA0_iFooddevereintegrareindenizare.pdf).

**Home-services precedent (Brazil):** GetNinjas — 2M+ registered professionals, 500+ categories, 3,000+ cities — relies on review volume plus a "verified profile" badge, and explicitly coaches customers to read prior-client evaluations before choosing (https://www.getninjas.com.br/ ; https://blog.getninjas.com.br/como-contratar-um-profissional-com-seguranca/).

### Rating-system recommendations

1. **Adopt the visual grammar users already know**: color/thermometer-style reputation states (gray→green logic) rather than raw stars alone; show complaint-free streaks and completed-job counts, which map to Mercado Libre's learned model.
2. **Transaction-verified reviews only**, and say so on the badge ("verificada"). Verified-purchase signals are specifically shown to increase trust in ratings (Frontiers study and Filieri, cited therein).
3. **Two-sided but retaliation-safe ratings**: workers must be able to rate customers/requesters; consider delayed or blind mutual rating to prevent score extortion — the one-sided model is a documented source of worker distrust and legal exposure in Brazil.
4. **Publish the algorithm's logic in plain language** (what moves your score, over what window). Transparency about rating calculation measurably increases trust (Luca & Zervas, cited in the Frontiers study), and algorithm-transparency language is appearing in regional regulation (Uruguay's Law 20,396 guarantees "intangibility of digital reputation and data portability"; Brazil's pending PLP 12/2024 would mandate monthly reports on scoring, blocking, and exclusion criteria — see §6).
5. **Decouple a single bad rating from livelihood**: never let ratings alone trigger deactivation without human review — this is the single most-litigated trust failure in Brazil (§5).

---

## 4. Mechanism 2: Identity Verification

### Available rails and norms per market

**Brazil** — the deepest verification infrastructure. SERPRO's **Datavalid** offers real-time API validation of CPF status and biographical data against Receita Federal, facial match against the CNH portrait held at Senatran, QR-code decoding of physical/digital driver's licenses (issued since May 2017), and liveness/PAD anti-spoofing (https://apicenter.estaleiro.serpro.gov.br/documentacao/datavalid/en/ ; https://docs.didit.me/api-reference/database-validation/brazil/cnh-facial-qrcode). KYC is legally mandatory for financial relationships (Law 9,613/1998; BCB Circular 3,978/2020), so Brazilian users *expect* document + selfie flows from any platform touching money (https://www.guep.com.br/en/solucoes/kyc/). Market rate for a full CNH+CPF+face-match check: ~US$0.50 per query.

**Colombia** — cédula cross-checks against the Registraduría with biometric face-match are commoditized (~US$0.33 for full KYC; https://didit.me/solutions/countries/colombia/). Compliance frame: SARLAFT 4.0 (AML), Ley 1581/2012 (data protection), Ley 2294/2023 (fintech). Critically, vendors in this market explicitly support the **PPT (Permiso por Protección Temporal)** — the document held by a large share of the ~2.8M Venezuelan migrants in Colombia, who are heavily represented in gig work. The IDB/Uber study found international migrants are up to 28% of drivers in some markets (Chile); Colombia's gig supply is similarly migrant-heavy (https://www.iadb.org/en/blog/labor-markets/drivers-seat-real-face-driving-uber-region).

**Argentina** — **RENAPER** holds 45M+ records and supports real-time DNI validation plus biometric selfie match with liveness (https://docs.bynn.com/docs/government-registry-verification-argentina ; https://documentation.jumio.ai/docs/references/riskSignals/govDatabaseCheck/Argentina/biometricArgentina). Argentina also has a distinctive formalization link: Uber requires drivers to self-register as formal independent workers (monotributo), and an AFD study of Uber, Zolvers (domestic work), and Home Solution found platforms can act as a *bridge to formality* — Zolvers workers showed significantly higher registration rates than off-platform domestic workers (https://www.afd.fr/sites/default/files/2022-03-07-39-12/Labour-transitions-that-lead-to-platform-work-Argentina.pdf ; https://www.afd.fr/sites/default/files/2022-03-07-59-20/Precarisation-or-Protection-Argentina.pdf). Identity verification in Argentina is thus not just fraud control; it is perceived by some workers as a route to formal status and protection.

**Verification depth precedent:** GetNinjas' "perfil verificado" = government document photo + specialist human review; the platform publicly instructs customers to ask to see the professional's ID documents at the door (https://www.getninjas.com.br/central-de-ajuda/cliente/pedidos-sou-cliente/o-que-e-profissional-com-perfil-verificado). Note the regional regulatory direction: Paraguay's draft platform law (summarized in Fairwork's comparative table) makes identity verification of *all* platform-ecosystem participants mandatory — expect similar requirements to spread (Fairwork Brazil 2025 report, Table 1).

### Identity verification recommendations

1. **Use the government rails, not document-photo review alone**: CPF/CNH+face match (Brazil), Registraduría+face match (Colombia), RENAPER+face match (Argentina). At US$0.33–0.50 per check, full e-KYC is affordable even for gig onboarding funnels.
2. **Tier the friction**: low-friction signup → verified badge after e-KYC → enhanced verification (liveness, background) for in-home services. Display the badge prominently; in a 5%-interpersonal-trust market (Brazil), the verified badge is doing the work that social trust does elsewhere.
3. **Accept the PPT in Colombia** (and equivalent migrant documents elsewhere) — excluding it excludes a large, experienced slice of the gig labor supply.
4. **Frame verification as worker benefit in Argentina** ("tu perfil verificado / tu trabajo registrado"), tapping the documented formalization effect.
5. **Verify both sides** and show it: customers inviting workers into homes want to see the worker is verified; workers want to see the *customer* is verified too — Fairwork Brazil documents severe harassment and violence against workers, especially women, with platforms unresponsive ("I report it and then the platform simply says it will notify the user"). Two-sided verification plus visible consequences is a safety mechanism, not just fraud control.

---

## 5. Mechanism 3: Payments and Escrow

### The payment rails your users already trust

**Brazil — Pix is the trust anchor.** Launched November 2020 by the Central Bank, Pix hit 63.8 billion transactions in 2024 — 25.6% more than credit, debit, prepaid, boleto, TED, and checks *combined* (Febraban via Extra Globo: https://extra.globo.com/economia/noticia/2025/05/com-638-bilhoes-de-transacoes-pix-foi-o-meio-de-pagamento-mais-usado-por-brasileiros-em-2024.ghtml). 83% of Brazilians use it; cash use fell from 76.6% to 40.5% of payments between 2019–2023; 97% of merchants accept it; 87% cite security/ease/acceptance as reasons for choosing it (BCB: https://www.bcb.gov.br/content/estabilidadefinanceira/Publicacoes_SPB/Relatorio_Decem_2023.pdf). 63% of the population used Pix at least monthly in 2024, averaging 32 transactions/month (FGV via Agência Brasil: https://www.capitalnews.com.br/nacional/em-2024-63-dos-brasileiros-usaram-o-pix-ao-menos-uma-vez-por-mes/418320). Two design-critical properties: (a) Pix settles in real time and is **final and irrevocable** (BCB SPI report: https://www.bcb.gov.br/content/financialstability/spi_annual_reports/SPI_2024.pdf) — so the platform, not the rail, must provide reversibility; (b) Pix fraud is common enough that the BCB built a dedicated refund mechanism (MED — Mecanismo Especial de Devolução: https://dadosabertos.bcb.gov.br/tl/dataset/pix). A BCB working paper also shows Pix is used for informal insurance/remittance networks after shocks — it is deeply embedded in exactly the informal-economy mutual-aid behaviors your workers rely on (https://bcb.gov.br/content/publicacoes/WorkingPaperSeries/WP600.pdf).

**Argentina — wallet + QR culture, Mercado Pago-led.** 96% of adults have at least one digital wallet; Mercado Pago is used by 74% of wallet users (Taquion consultancy, via El Observador — treat exact share as directional: https://www.elobservador.com.uy/argentina/economia-y-negocios/el-auge-las-billeteras-virtuales-argentina-crecimiento-preferencias-y-la-necesidad-cobrar-los-sueldos-n5973105). Interoperable QR payments grew 278% year-over-year (35.7M payments in a single month of 2024; BCRA via Ámbito: https://www.ambito.com/finanzas/cuenta-dni-tiene-total-liderazgo-qr-interoperables-los-motivos-y-como-quedan-mercado-pago-y-modo-n6007488). Crucially for your segment: **53% of QR payment users are in low-income strata (D1/D2/E) and ~30% are self-employed** (Coelsa via Infobae: https://www.infobae.com/economia/2024/09/24/mas-de-la-mitad-de-los-usuarios-de-pagos-qr-son-de-nivel-socioeconomico-bajo/). The state wallet Cuenta DNI (9M+ users) grew by paying emergency transfers (IFE) — evidence that government disbursements are a proven onboarding ramp to digital payments for informal workers. Yet >35% of transactions still occur outside the banking system (https://puntoconvergente.uca.edu.ar/codigo-qr-en-argentina-moda-pasajera-o-fin-de-la-economia-informal/), and 70% of Argentines say they want to receive their *salary* in a wallet — a direct opening for gig payout positioning.

**Colombia — Nequi/Daviplata as de facto bank accounts.** Nequi reached ~37.2% market reach in 2023, Daviplata ~17.6% (university thesis data — directional: http://repositorio.uts.edu.co:8080/xmlui/handle/123456789/18873). Both open with just a phone number + cédula, no minimum balance — making them the default account for unbanked and informal workers, and the standard disbursement rail for fintech microloans and, historically, government CCTs (DaviPlata paid 937,000 Familias en Acción beneficiaries from 2012: https://www.cgap.org/sites/default/files/Working-Paper-Going-Mobile-with-CCTs-Jun-2015.pdf ; https://creditolab.com/en/guides/nequi-and-daviplata-how-digital-wallets-power-colombian-microloans). Two trust frictions are documented: (a) **fake-receipt fraud** — edited screenshots and cloned apps ("Nequi DZ", "DaviTrampa") mean sellers/workers are trained to verify funds *in their own app* or via the official QR verification tool before handing over goods/services (https://colombiamove.com/blog/en/comprobantes-falsos-nequi-daviplata-verificar-pago-entrega/); (b) **outage fragility** — the October 2025 AWS outage froze Nequi and Daviplata, and commentators noted that for many users these wallets are their *only* account, so hours of downtime means missing rent or groceries; trust "erodes with each fall" (https://zonacaptiva.com/opinion/nequi-y-daviplata-el-futuro-de-la-banca-o-el-eterno-dolor-de-cabeza/).

### The escrow norm

The region's escrow reference is **Mercado Libre's Compra Protegida**: the platform holds the buyer's money; coverage runs 28 days for non-delivery and up to 30 days for product problems; platform staff intervene and refund to the Mercado Pago account instantly (Argentina: https://www.mercadolibre.com.ar/compra-protegida). Mercado Libre explicitly warns that paying outside the platform or via WhatsApp contact voids protection — training users that *staying inside the platform = safety* (https://www.mercadolibre.cl/l/compra-seguro). In Brazilian home services, GetNinjas' "Preço Fechado" replicates this for labor: "Seu pagamento fica retido até o serviço ser concluído. Se não sair como combinado, o GetNinjas resolve" — payment held until the job is confirmed complete (https://www.getninjas.com.br/precofechado). This is the single most directly transferable escrow pattern for a gig platform in the region.

### Payment/escrow recommendations

1. **Hold funds platform-side; never rely on the rail for reversibility.** In Brazil this is forced by Pix's irrevocability; everywhere it matches the learned Compra Protegida model. Release on customer confirmation or auto-release after a short, visible timer (the 21–30 day windows above set user expectations for dispute windows).
2. **Pay out to the rails workers already hold**: Pix keys/wallets (BR), interoperable CVU wallets incl. Mercado Pago/Cuenta DNI (AR), Nequi/Daviplata (CO). In Argentina, positioning payouts as "cobrá tu plata en tu billetera" aligns with the documented 70% desire to receive income in wallets.
3. **Design explicitly for Colombia's fake-receipt threat model**: workers must see funds *settled in their own in-app balance* (not a payer's screenshot) before a job is marked paid; provide an in-app verification affordance mirroring the wallets' QR-verification tools. This single pattern, if absent, will be exploited immediately.
4. **Keep cash on-ramps**: informality means a meaningful tail of customers (especially in Colombia and poorer Argentine segments) transact in cash; >35% of Argentine transactions remain unbanked. Cash payment with in-app confirmation, or cash-in via wallet agents, widens the top of funnel without abandoning escrow logic (hold worker payout until cash handoff is mutually confirmed).
5. **Show the escrow state machine visually** ("Dinero retenido → Servicio confirmado → Liberado"). GetNinjas proves users accept held payment when the guarantee is stated in one sentence.

---

## 6. Mechanism 4: Dispute Resolution Interfaces

### What users expect — and what the law now demands

**Brazil — the most formalized dispute expectations.** Two external interfaces dominate: **Reclame Aqui**, the public complaint site where consumers and even workers seek redress (an iFood worker's first recourse after an unexplained ban was a Reclame Aqui complaint: https://www.migalhas.com.br/arquivos/2024/5/05B76100C0240D_tjpr.pdf), and the **courts**, which repeatedly reinstate workers deactivated without evidence or due process, applying constitutional due-process rights (ampla defesa, contraditório) *horizontally* against platforms — e.g., a 99 driver excluded by an AI flag with no demonstrable violation was ordered reinstated (https://www3.tjrj.jus.br/gedcacheweb/default.aspx?GEDID=000418BC37831925ECAEC444BD1B6F16BA15C5162B0F4E29&USER=&UZIP=1 ; additional iFood rulings: https://www.conjur.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/doc_183654557.pdf). Pending **PLP 12/2024** would codify this: exclusion only for fraud/abuse/misuse "garantido o direito de defesa" (Art. 6) and a monthly transparency report covering criteria for job offers, scoring, blocking, suspension, and exclusion (Art. 8) (https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/projetos/ato_2023_2026/2024/plp/plp-012.htm ; https://www.camara.leg.br/proposicoesWeb/fichadetramitacao?idProposicao=2419243). Meanwhile Fairwork Brazil 2025 documents the current baseline: support channels exist but are **chatbot-dominated**, and workers whose accounts are blocked find themselves unable to reach support at all — the worst possible UX failure mode (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2025/09/Fairwork-Brazil-Report-2025-ENG_FINAL.pdf).

**Colombia — institutionalized conciliation culture.** The Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC) runs **SICFacilita**, a free, real-time online conciliation chat between consumer and provider covering warranties, distance selling, and identity theft (http://sicfacilita.sic.gov.co/SICFacilita/), plus formal PQRFS channels and "Demande aquí" online consumer-protection filings under Ley 1480 de 2011 (https://www.sic.gov.co/tema/asuntos-jurisdiccionales/como-hacer-una-demanda). Colombians are accustomed to a *structured complaint → facilitated chat → formal claim* ladder. On the labor side, **Law 2466 of 2025** gives delivery-platform workers rights to information, advance notice of contract changes, and complaint-filing, with worker registration at the Ministry of Labour (Fairwork Brazil 2025, Table 1). 

**Argentina — claim-driven reputation.** Mercado Libre's *reclamo* (claim) flow is the mental model: open a claim on a transaction, the platform's Compra Protegida team intervenes, refund lands in Mercado Pago; unresolved claims damage the counterparty's visible reputation (complaint rate feeds the thermometer) (https://www.mercadolibre.com.ar/compra-protegida ; https://global-selling.mercadolibre.com/learning-center/news/seller-reputation-learn-how-it-works). Fairwork Argentina 2022 shows gig platforms lag badly on fair management/grievance mechanisms (only DiDi scored any points), indicating a wide-open differentiation opportunity (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/en/fw/blog/fairwork-argentina-scores-2022-new-report-about-gig-economies-in-latin-america/).

### Dispute-resolution recommendations

1. **Mirror the claim ladder users know**: (a) in-transaction "Necesito ayuda / Preciso de ajuda" button → (b) structured claim with evidence upload → (c) facilitated in-app mediation chat (Colombia's SICFacilita pattern) → (d) platform adjudication with a stated deadline → (e) human appeal. Auto-refund to wallet on resolution, as Compra Protegida does.
2. **Never let a blocked account lose access to support.** Provide a dedicated appeal channel that works *from the block screen itself*. This is both the top Fairwork-documented failure and the fact pattern in the Brazilian court losses — cheap to fix, expensive to ignore.
3. **Deactivation due process as a designed flow**: notice with specific reason → evidence shown → response window → human review → written outcome. Brazil's PLP 12/2024 direction (and existing court doctrine) makes this a compliance feature, not a nicety; build it once, deploy in all three markets.
4. **Meet users on the external stages they trust**: maintain a staffed, responsive Reclame Aqui profile in Brazil; support SICFacilita conciliation in Colombia rather than forcing users into it as an adversary.
5. **Publish a monthly transparency summary** (blocks, suspensions, appeal outcomes, scoring criteria) — anticipating PLP 12/2024 Art. 8-type requirements and Uruguay-style reputation-portability norms spreading across the region.

---

## 7. How Prior Trust-System Experience Affects Adoption

The evidence supports four concrete transfer mechanisms:

**1. Institutional trust transfer is the adoption engine.** In low-trust markets, users do not trust the stranger; they trust the *platform's guarantees*, and that trust transfers to the counterparty (Pavlou & Gefen's institutional-based trust model, empirically confirmed for Colombia in the Frontiers/Mercado Libre study: reviews and the rating system mediate marketplace trust and experience — https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1460321/full). Practical consequence: your *institutional* signals (escrow badge, verified-ID badge, claim SLA) must be visible at the moment of first transaction — they are the product.

**2. Learned mental models lower activation energy — or raise switching costs.** Users arrive pre-trained: thermometer reputation and Compra Protegida escrow (Mercado Libre, all three markets); QR scan-to-pay (Argentina's 278%-growth interoperable QR; Brazil's Pix QR — 59% key-based, 37% QR/copy-paste: https://www.bcb.gov.br/content/estabilidadefinanceira/Publicacoes_SPB/Relatorio_Decem_2023.pdf); wallet balance as proof of payment (Colombia). Mapping your flows onto these models (hold-and-release escrow, QR payment, color reputation) requires no user education. Deviating from them (e.g., asking Colombians to trust a payer's screenshot) triggers fraud-hardened skepticism.

**3. Negative prior experiences create specific, predictable defenses.** Colombian users verify transfers in-app because fake receipts are endemic (https://colombiamove.com/blog/en/comprobantes-falsos-nequi-daviplata-verificar-pago-entrega/); Brazilians have absorbed Pix social-engineering fraud (hence the BCB's MED mechanism); Argentine users distrust anything that traps value outside instantly-accessible wallets (a plausible reading of the 70% who want salary paid to wallets — stated as inference, not direct evidence). Fraud-savvy users reward platforms that make verification *intrinsic* to the flow (settled-balance display, in-app confirmation, official-channel warnings like Mercado Libre's "never pay outside the platform": https://www.mercadolibre.cl/l/compra-seguro).

**4. State and marketplace incumbents seeded the first-account/first-transaction moment — ride on it.** 43% of adults in LMICs opened their first account to receive a wage or government payment (Global Findex 2025: https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/a4aaae5a017a5bea7922686af0ed3636-0050022025/original/PolicyResearchTalk-GlobalFindex-September2025.pdf). This is exactly how DaviPlata (CCT transfers from 2012) and Cuenta DNI (IFE emergency payments from 2020) acquired informal-economy users, and how Pix drove Brazilian account ownership from 76%→87.6% (https://www.bcb.gov.br/content/estabilidadefinanceira/Publicacoes_SPB/Relatorio_Decem_2023.pdf). For a gig platform, the analog is: the *first payout* is your trust-establishing event — make it instant, free, and into the wallet they already use. Note also that first-payout reliability matters more than feature richness: the documented Nequi/Daviplata outage backlash shows reliability failures destroy accumulated trust fastest among users for whom the wallet is their only account.

**5. Supply-side trust is earned through fairness mechanics, not just pay.** The IDB/Uber–Ipsos study shows workers join for income (76%) but only 52% say income expectations were met, and most carry debt with no social protection (https://efe.com/economia/2026-02-26/latinoamerica-uber-conductores-problemas-economicos/). Fairwork documents that workers "multi-app" precisely to hedge platform risk — low switching loyalty is a *learned response* to arbitrary deactivation and opaque algorithms (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2025/09/Fairwork-Brazil-Report-2025-ENG_FINAL.pdf). Conversely, Argentina's Zolvers case shows platforms that visibly *increase* formality/protection earn durable worker preference (https://www.afd.fr/sites/default/files/2022-03-07-59-20/Precarisation-or-Protection-Argentina.pdf). Workers' prior platform experience has taught them to expect opacity; transparent scoring, appealable decisions, and portable reputation (per Uruguay's Law 20,396 direction) are differentiators, not costs.

---

## 8. Cross-Market Design Summary

| Mechanism | Argentina | Colombia | Brazil |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ratings** | Mercado Libre thermometer is the mental model; claims visible in reputation | Same + fake-review sensitivity empirically documented; verified-transaction badges essential | Same + worker-side due process legally salient; retaliation-safe two-sided ratings |
| **Identity** | RENAPER DNI + face match; frame verification as formalization benefit | Registraduría + biometrics; **must accept PPT** for migrant workers | CPF/CNH + face match via Datavalid-class rails (~$0.50/check); KYC expected by users |
| **Escrow/payments** | Hold-and-release (Compra Protegida model); payout to interoperable wallets (Mercado Pago 74% share); QR native; keep cash on-ramp (>35% unbanked txns) | Hold-and-release; payout to Nequi/Daviplata; **in-app settled-balance proof** to defeat fake receipts | Escrow mandatory (Pix is irrevocable); Pix QR + key payouts; GetNinjas Preço Fechado proves acceptance for services |
| **Disputes** | Reclamo flow with deadlines; instant wallet refunds | Structured claim → facilitated chat (SICFacilita pattern) → adjudication; Law 2466/2025 complaint rights | Appeal-from-block-screen, human review, reasoned deactivation notices (court doctrine; PLP 12/2024); staffed Reclame Aqui presence |
| **Trust baseline** | Moderate-low (24% interpersonal) — peer proof works | Low (20%) — institutional signals + verification dominate | Lowest (5%) — maximal explicit trust signaling; reliability is a trust feature |

---

## 9. Uncertainties and Gaps (stated plainly)

- **Brazil's informal employment rate** was not primary-sourced in this pass; the ~40% figure is widely cited but unverified here. All directional conclusions hold regardless.
- Several usage statistics come from secondary or gray sources (Taquion wallet-share survey via El Observador; Nequi/Daviplata reach from a university repository thesis; Coelsa data via Infobae). Treat point estimates as directional (±several points).
- The Frontiers Colombia study uses a convenience sample (n=326, Mercado Libre buyers) — robust for mechanism direction, not for population-level effect sizes.
- Regulatory items (Brazil PLP 12/2024; PLP 152/2025; Argentina's draft platform statute) were pending at source dates; verify current status before committing compliance timelines.
- No direct experimental evidence was found comparing *gig-platform-specific* rating/escrow designs across these three countries; recommendations for gig contexts are extrapolated from adjacent evidence (e-commerce reputation, wallet behavior, labor-platform litigation) and should be validated with in-market A/B tests, especially first-payout timing and badge placement.

- Implication: low-trust environments → platform-mediated trust substitutes (ratings, escrow, verification) carry more weight; also users default to personal networks/WhatsApp.

**Payments:**
- Brazil: Pix dominant — 63.8B transactions in 2024, 25.6% more than all other methods combined (Febraban via Extra Globo). 83% of Brazilians use Pix (BCB 2023 survey); 87.6% account ownership; cash use fell from 76.6% to 40.5% (2019→2023). 63% used Pix monthly in 2024 (FGV). Pix is instant and irrevocable (SPI RTGS); MED fraud mechanism exists. Trust: 87% cite security/ease/acceptance. Pix fraud (social engineering, "sequestro relâmpago") is a known issue — I have MED mention from BCB dataset.
- Argentina: Mercado Pago dominant (74% of digital wallet users; 96% of adults have at least one wallet — Taquion via El Observador). Cuenta DNI leads interoperable QR (9M+ users). QR payments grew 278% YoY; 53% of QR users are low-income (D1/D2/E), 30% self-employed (Coelsa via Infobae). Compra Protegida (Mercado Libre's escrow/buyer protection): 28 days non-delivery, 30 days for problems; money held; refunds instant to Mercado Pago.
- Colombia: Nequi (37.2% market reach 2023) and Daviplata (17.6%) — wallets openable with just phone + cédula; used for CCT payments since 2012 (DaviPlata). Fraud: fake receipts/screenshots — users told to verify in own app or scan QR verification. October 2025 AWS outage took down Nequi/Daviplata — trust erosion from outages; proposed 1.5% withholding tax controversy. Escrow norm from Mercado Libre; GetNinjas-equivalent? In Colombia, Mercado Libre Compra Protegida covers 21 days (Chile example; Argentina 28 days).

**Ratings:**
- Mercado Libre reputation: color thermometer (gray start → green target), metrics: complaints ≤2% for green, shipping time, cancellations; rolling 3-month window; per-country reputation; Mercado Líder tiers (Silver/Gold/Platinum). Users deeply familiar.
- Frontiers study (Peña-García et al., 2024, Mercado Libre Colombia, n=326): fake review perception ↓ trust in rating systems; review quality ↑ all trust forms; trust in rating system mediates CX. Institutional-based trust model (Pavlou & Gefen): reviews as trust transfer mechanism. Verified-purchase ratings more trusted; transparency of algorithms increases trust.
- Gig ratings: one-sided (customer rates worker) in ride-hailing/delivery; Fairwork documents rating systems as algorithmic control; workers penalized; Brazilian court cases show deactivations despite high scores (iFood worker with 98.9 score deactivated).
- Zolvers (Argentina domestic work): platform increased formality/registration.

**Identity verification:**
- Government rails exist in all three: Brazil — SERPRO Datavalid (CPF validation, CNH QR code + face match vs Senatran, liveness/PAD); Receita Federal CPF. Colombia — Registraduría cédula cross-check + biometric face match; Cédula Digital; PPT for Venezuelan migrants (important: ~2.8M Venezuelan migrants; verification must accept PPT). Argentina — RENAPER DNI biometric verification (45M+ records).
- Costs: ~$0.33–0.50 per full KYC check (Didit pricing) — cheap enough for gig onboarding.
- GetNinjas (Brazil): verified profile = document photo + human review; advises clients to check ID; Pix payment guidance; escrow-like "Preço Fechado" holds payment until service complete ("Seu pagamento fica retido até o serviço ser concluído").
- Regulatory: Brazil Law 9,613/1998 AML + BCB Circular 3,978/2020; Colombia SARLAFT 4.0, Ley 1581/2012 data protection, Ley 2294/2023 fintech; Paraguay's draft law mandates identity verification for all platform ecosystem participants (from Fairwork table — shows regional direction).
- Uber in Argentina requires drivers to self-register as formal independent workers (monotributo) — formalization effect (AFD paper).

**Dispute resolution:**
- Brazil: Reclame Aqui as de facto public complaint interface (workers/consumers use it; cited in iFood case); courts frequently order reactivation for unmotivated deactivations (TJRJ 99 case; TJSP iFood cases) — due process (contraditório/ampla defesa) applied horizontally. PLP 12/2024: Art. 6 — exclusion only for fraud/abuse/misuse with guaranteed right of defense; Art. 8 transparency — monthly report with criteria for trip offers, scoring, blocking, suspension, exclusion. Pending but directionally important. Fairwork Brazil 2025: 0/10 for most; no platform evidenced meaningful appeal of disciplinary actions; chatbots prevalent; blocked workers can't access support channels.
- Colombia: SIC (Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio) — SICFacilita free online conciliation chat; PQRFS (peticiones, quejas, reclamos) legally mandated channel with response deadlines; Ley 1480 de 2011 consumer statute; Ley 2466 de 2025 (labor reform covering delivery platform workers — right to file complaints, registration with MinTrabajo).
- Argentina: Mercado Libre's claim system (reclamos) — claims feed seller reputation; Compra Protegida intervention; consumer law 24.240; Fairwork Argentina 2022: only DiDi scored any points (4/10); no platform evidenced fair management.

**Prior experience effects:**
- Pavlou & Gefen institutional trust transfer: users transfer trust from platform institutions (escrow, ratings) to sellers — the Frontiers Colombia study confirms mediation.
- Mercado Libre/Mercado Pago ubiquity = learned mental models: thermometer reputation, Compra Protegida escrow, QR payment. Colombian consumers "generally lacking extensive online shopping experience" but open to adoption (Frontiers).
- Fraud experience creates specific behaviors: Colombians verify transfers in-app due to fake receipt fraud (Colombia Move); Brazilians suffer Pix social-engineering fraud → BCB created MED; Argentines distrust of banks ("colchón bank" — not sourced; avoid).
- Multi-apping (Fairwork Brazil): workers hedge platform risk — indicates low platform loyalty/trust.
- BCB Pix WP600: floods → Pix usage for informal insurance networks — Pix complements rather than substitutes.
- Uber-Ipsos IDB study: 13,722 drivers; 76% joined for income; 52% expectations met; 88% lack financial security; 75% in debt; 30% pension contribution; 19.3 h/week average; education 45% Brazil–74% Colombia tertiary.
- Zolvers Argentina: platform registration increased formalization — platform can be a formality bridge; perceived protection.
- Findex 2025: 79% global account ownership; LAC growth driven by mobile money; 43% opened first account to receive wage/gov payment — relevant: gov transfers (Daviplata CCT, Cuenta DNI IFE) drove first account ownership → trust seeded by state payments.
- BCRA: QR growth; Cuenta DNI grew via IFE (emergency income) — government transfers as onboarding to digital payments.

**Design implications for UX director:**
- Ratings: bilateral but protected (fear of retaliation); show verified-transaction badges; localized norms (Brazilian users expect Reclame Aqui-style public responsiveness; Mercado Libre thermometer mental model); avoid punitive one-sided ratings → court risk in Brazil; appeal UX.
- IDV: tiered KYC using government rails; accept PPT in Colombia (Venezuelan migrants — big share of gig workers; Chile has 28% migrant Uber drivers; Colombia has large Venezuelan population); CPF+CNH or face match in Brazil; DNI+RENAPER in Argentina; show verification badges prominently since interpersonal trust is low (5–25%).
- Escrow: market norm is Mercado Libre Compra Protegida (money held, released on confirmation); Brazil Pix irrevocability means platform must hold funds (can't claw back) — escrow via platform wallet; GetNinjas Preço Fechado model proof in home services; Argentina: Mercado Pago QR + wallet interoperability; Colombia: Nequi/Daviplata disbursement + in-app verification UX to counter fake-receipt fraud.
- Disputes: in-app claim flows modeled on Mercado Libre reclamos; human escalation (chatbot-only fails Fairwork and Brazilian courts); integration with SICFacilita (Colombia), Reclame Aqui responsiveness (Brazil), Defensa del Consumidor (Argentina); transparency dashboards anticipating PLP 12/2024-type rules; deactivation due process UX (notice, evidence, appeal, human review).
- Prior trust experience: leverage learned behaviors (QR scanning, thermometer colors, wallet balances); onboarding via state-payment-linked wallets; design for fraud-savvy users (verifiable receipts, in-app confirmation); word-of-mouth/community trust (low institutional trust → personal referrals, WhatsApp distribution).

Quantitative work: I can show some comparisons: trust levels, informality, Pix adoption numbers, wallet penetration. Maybe compute a comparative table. Show e.g. Pix growth 41.9B→63.8B = +52.2%; QR payments Argentina 278% YoY; cash share Brazil 76.6→40.5pp. These are given. I can do a small computed summary (e.g., informal employment averages, trust deltas).

Uncertainty: Brazil informal employment % not directly sourced — flag. Dates of some sources future-dated (2025/2026) — the dataset includes them; use with care. Mercado Pago 74% share is from a consultancy (Taquion) — flag. Nequi 37.2% reach from a thesis repository — flag moderate reliability.

Structure:
1. Executive summary
2. Market context (informality, trust baselines, payment rails) with comparison table
3. Mechanism-by-mechanism comparison:
   a. Rating systems
   b. Identity verification
   c. Payment/escrow
   d. Dispute resolution
4. Prior trust-system experience → adoption (evidence + mechanisms)
5. Design recommendations per market + cross-market
6. Open questions/uncertainties
7. Sources inline throughout

Length: comprehensive but readable. Write now.
