final.content:
# Autism Diagnostic Criteria: DSM-5 (2013) vs. ICD-11 (2019), With a Focus on Sensory Processing

## Executive summary

DSM-5 and ICD-11 converged on a single "autism spectrum disorder" (ASD) category built from two core domains — social-communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviour (RRB) — and both, for the first time in their respective lineages, elevated atypical sensory processing to a core diagnostic feature. The key differences are in *weighting and architecture*: DSM-5 makes sensory hypo/hyper-reactivity one of four enumerated RRB criteria (of which two are required), uses three domain-specific severity levels, and retains an explicit "early developmental period" onset clause; ICD-11 folds sensory differences into a flexible, non-enumerated RRB domain, replaces severity levels with intellectual-development and functional-language subcategories (6A02.0–6A02.5), and explicitly recognises that symptoms may not manifest until adolescence or adulthood. No published study has directly compared DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria head-to-head for diagnostic accuracy in the same sample; the available evidence consists of DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV/ICD-10 concordance studies and expert/systematic comparisons. That gap is itself a central finding.

---

## A. Side-by-side criteria table

Sources: DSM-5 criteria as reproduced by the IACC (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml) and Autism Speaks (https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5); ICD-11 MMS Chapter 06 (https://faculty.ksu.edu.sa/sites/default/files/icd11_mms-en-06.pdf), ICD-11 CDDR (https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content), and Greaves-Lord et al. 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/).

| Row | DSM-5 (APA, 2013) — 299.00 (F84.0) | ICD-11 (WHO, 2019; effective 1 Jan 2022) — 6A02 |
|---|---|---|
| **Core social-communication criteria** | Criterion A: persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across contexts; **all 3 of 3 sub-criteria required**: (1) social-emotional reciprocity; (2) nonverbal communicative behaviours; (3) developing/maintaining/understanding relationships. Monothetic (all required). | Essential feature 1: "persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and to sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication," with manifestations varying by age, verbal/intellectual ability and sociocultural context. **Polythetic/descriptive** — no fixed number of sub-criteria; clinician judges overall pattern. |
| **Sensory processing: mention & weighting** | **Explicit, enumerated criterion (B4):** "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment" (indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to sounds/textures, excessive smelling/touching, visual fascination with lights/movement). It is **1 of 4 RRB criteria, of which at least 2 are required** — i.e., sensory differences can contribute up to 50% of the RRB threshold but can never suffice alone. New in DSM-5 (absent from DSM-IV). | **Included within the RRB essential feature:** "a range of restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities that are clearly atypical or excessive for the individual's age and sociocultural context"; the CDDR specifies lifelong **persistent hyper- and/or hypo-sensitivity to sensory stimuli** and unusual sensory interests (sounds, lights, textures, odours, tastes). New vs. ICD-10, which had no sensory feature (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/). **Non-enumerated weighting**: sensory differences support, but there is no "2-of-4" arithmetic. ICD-11 deliberately de-emphasises ID-anchored behavioural exemplars (flipping objects, excessive smelling/touching, echolalia) that DSM-5 retains (Greaves-Lord et al. 2022, same URL). |
| **Severity specifiers** | **Three levels, rated separately for each of the two domains**: Level 1 "requiring support," Level 2 "requiring substantial support," Level 3 "requiring very substantial support" (https://www.autismspeaks.org/blog/expert-qa-dsm-5-and-asd). Additional specifiers: with/without intellectual impairment; with/without language impairment; associated genetic/medical condition; co-occurring disorders; catatonia. | **No 1–3 severity levels.** Severity is captured structurally by **subdivision codes**: 6A02.0 (no disorder of intellectual development [DID], mild/no functional language impairment), 6A02.1 (with DID, mild/no language impairment), 6A02.2 (no DID, impaired functional language), 6A02.3 (with DID, impaired functional language), 6A02.4 (without DID, absence of functional language), 6A02.5 (with DID, absence of functional language); co-occurring DID severity (mild–profound) is coded separately under 6A00 (https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02-3/; https://faculty.ksu.edu.sa/sites/default/files/icd11_mms-en-06.pdf). International field studies of the ICD-11 behavioural indicators for DID, including with co-occurring ASD, found good inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.91–0.97) and clinical utility (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35170825/; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jir.13146). |
| **Age/onset requirements** | Criterion C: symptoms "must be present in the **early developmental period**" — but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed capacities, and "may be masked by learned strategies in later life." | Onset "during the developmental period, **typically in early childhood, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities**"; ICD-11 explicitly recognises that overt symptoms can emerge in adolescence or adulthood and "the condition can present clinically **at all ages**" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/). ICD-11 drops ICD-10's requirement of early developmental delay history. |
| **Functional impairment thresholds** | Criterion D: symptoms cause "**clinically significant impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning." Criterion E: not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay. | Deficits "sufficiently severe to cause **impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning**," usually "a **pervasive feature** of the individual's functioning observable in all settings," though varying by context (https://faculty.ksu.edu.sa/sites/default/files/icd11_mms-en-06.pdf). ICD-11 lists a broader, more explicit range of life domains and a pervasiveness expectation. |

---

## B. Evidence synthesis (2013–present)

**Important caveat on scope:** an exhaustive search returned **no peer-reviewed study directly comparing DSM-5 and ICD-11 ASD criteria applied to the same clinical sample for sensitivity/specificity**. ICD-11 ASD field testing occurred within broader WHO field-study programmes (e.g., DID behavioural-indicator studies; child/adolescent reliability studies in Mexico — kappa 0.46–0.81 across disorders; https://www.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.202000830), not as DSM-5-vs-ICD-11 accuracy trials. The five sources below are therefore the closest valid evidence: one systematic review/meta-analysis, one systematic expert comparison of the two manuals, one expert narrative review, and two primary empirical concordance studies (using DSM-IV/ICD-10 as reference standards).

**1. Kulasinghe et al. (2014), "How will DSM-5 affect autism diagnosis? A systematic literature review and meta-analysis," J Autism Dev Disord** — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/
- Design: systematic review + meta-analysis; 14 of 418 screened studies included. Sample: pooled across studies (not single n).
- Key statistics: pooled **decrease in ASD diagnoses under DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV-TR of 31% (95% CI 20–44%, p=0.006)**; Autistic disorder −22% (16–29%, p<0.001); PDD-NOS −70% (55–82%, p=0.01); Asperger's −70% (26–94%, p=0.38, NS).
- Relevance: quantifies DSM-5's tightened net relative to the DSM-IV/ICD-10-era definitions that ICD-11 also replaced; because ICD-11 largely mirrors DSM-5 architecture, similar consolidation is expected under ICD-11 (supported by expert commentary: https://europepmc.org/article/med/33269947).
- **GRADE: Moderate** — pooled effect with statistical significance, but substantial between-study heterogeneity (range of decreases 7.3–68.4%) and reliance on draft/final DSM-5 application to archived data.

**2. First et al. (2021), "An organization- and category-level comparison of diagnostic requirements for mental disorders in ICD-11 and DSM-5," World Psychiatry** — https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825 (accepted ms: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/)
- Design: systematic category-level expert comparison of ICD-11 CDDG "Essential Features" vs. DSM-5 criteria for 103–104 shared diagnostic entities, using a pre-specified 4-level rating system and dual raters.
- Key statistics: **20 disorders (19.4%) major differences; 42 (40.8%) minor definitional differences; 10 (9.7%) minor due to greater DSM-5 specification; 31 (30.1%) essentially identical.** ASD was not among the disorders flagged for major conceptual divergence, consistent with the documented ICD–DSM Harmonization Group process and independent reviews describing the two ASD definitions as highly similar (https://europepmc.org/article/med/33269947; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).
- Relevance: the most rigorous published documentation of where the two manuals align and diverge; for ASD the divergences are in format (enumerated criteria vs. descriptive requirements; severity levels vs. ID/language subdivisions), not core construct.
- **GRADE: Moderate** — systematic methodology with pre-specified ratings, but outcome is expert judgement, not patient-level accuracy data.

**3. Wilson et al. (2013), "Comparison of ICD-10R, DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 in an Adult Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnostic Clinic," J Autism Dev Disord** — https://www.academia.edu/35209341/
- Design: primary empirical, cross-sectional diagnostic concordance study; **n=150 intellectually able adults** referred to a specialist clinic.
- Key statistics: of those diagnosed with ASD under ICD-10R, **only 56% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**; a further **19% met DSM-5 (draft) Social Communication Disorder** instead; of DSM-IV-TR Autistic Disorder/Asperger cases, **78% met DSM-5**. Authors found DSM-5 sensitivity "significantly increased by reducing the number of criteria required… or rating 'uncertain' criteria as 'present', **without sacrificing specificity**."
- Relevance: demonstrates that enumerated DSM-5 thresholds (all 3 social criteria; 2-of-4 RRB) can exclude cognitively able adults — the group ICD-11's flexible wording (later manifestation, camouflaging awareness) was designed partly to recapture; also shows how small threshold changes shift sensitivity/specificity trade-offs.
- **GRADE: Low** — single-centre, clinic-referred sample, no independent gold standard, draft-criteria era context.

**4. Kim et al. (2020), "Autism Spectrum Disorder Diagnosis in DSM-5 Compared to DSM-IV," Psychiatry Investigation (Asan Medical Center, Seoul)** — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7289465/
- Design: primary empirical, retrospective records review with standardised instruments (ADI-R, ADOS, IQ testing); **n=170** (ages 3–23; 140 boys).
- Key statistics: **58/145 (34.1%) of individuals with DSM-IV PDD did not meet DSM-5 ASD criteria; 28 of those 58 (48.3%) had DSM-IV Asperger's disorder.** ADOS/ADI-R algorithm scores were highest in the convergent group; IQ was lower in those meeting both criteria than in the divergent group — i.e., those excluded were disproportionately cognitively able. Concordant with the large Kim et al. population study cited therein (DSM-5 captured 99% of autistic disorder, 92% of Asperger's, 63% of PDD-NOS).
- Relevance: confirms, with gold-standard instruments, that DSM-5's sensitivity loss concentrates in Asperger-like/higher-IQ presentations — a proxy signal for how ICD-11's less enumerated criteria might behave differently, pending direct testing.
- **GRADE: Low** — retrospective, single-site, modest n, though strengthened by standardised ADI-R/ADOS data.

**5. Greaves-Lord, Skuse & Mandy (2022), "Innovations of the ICD-11 in the Field of Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Psychological Approach," Clinical Psychology in Europe** — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/
- Design: expert narrative review/clinical commentary by authors involved in ICD-11 development, integrating biopsychosocial and neurodiversity perspectives.
- Key points (qualitative): ICD-11 includes atypical sensory responses as diagnostic requirements (unlike ICD-10); recognises exceptional-effort compensation (camouflaging) and adult-onset manifestation; intentionally avoids DSM-5's ID-anchored exemplars; recommends diagnosis be used to tailor care rather than as an end in itself.
- Relevance: authoritative statement of ICD-11's intended clinical-utility logic, including the rationale for its sensory weighting.
- **GRADE: Very Low (for accuracy questions)** — no primary data; useful for intended-use interpretation only.

**Counterpoint review (contextual, not counted in the 5):** Bölte et al. (2024), "Autism spectrum disorder in ICD-11 — a critical reflection," Frontiers/PMC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/) argues ICD-11's flexibility risks **false positives**, non-falsifiable diagnoses, rising prevalence, and reduced research specificity — the mirror-image risk to DSM-5's sensitivity loss. GRADE: Very Low (opinion-based perspective), included here because it is the clearest published articulation of over-diagnosis risk under ICD-11.

---

## C. Clinical guideline positions

- **WHO:** The 72nd World Health Assembly adopted ICD-11 in May 2019, effective 1 January 2022 (resolution WHA72, A72_R15: https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA72/A72_R15-en.pdf). WHO's CDDR and MMS place ASD (6A02) in Neurodevelopmental Disorders, include atypical sensory responses within the RRB essential feature, and define severity via DID/functional-language subdivisions. WHO field-study reporting emphasises that ICD-11 trials were "developmental" (guidelines revised iteratively from field data), with internet-based trials across >15,000 clinicians in >150 countries (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11403167/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8751573/). On sensory weighting, WHO positions sensory atypicality as a core (but not independently sufficient) feature, with fewer ID-anchored examples than DSM-5.
- **APA:** Publisher of DSM-5 (2013), which the US uses clinically. APA co-participated in the WHO–APA ICD–DSM Harmonization Group (documented in First et al. 2021, above), indicating institutional support for convergence rather than competition. APA's position is embodied in the DSM-5 architecture itself: sensory hyper/hypo-reactivity is a named, enumerated criterion (B4) with domain-specific severity levels.
- **American Academy of Pediatrics:** The 2020 clinical report "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" (Hyman, Levy, Myers; Pediatrics 145(1):e20193447; reaffirmed October 2025) is explicitly built around **DSM-5 criteria**: it endorses the single ASD category, the two-domain structure, and the inclusion of hyper-/hypo-reactivity to sensory input within RRBs, plus 18- and 24-month standardised screening (https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/145/1/e20193447/36917/; PDF: https://depts.washington.edu/dbpeds/ID.Eval.Mgt.Children.ASD(AAP.2020).pdf). The AAP does not reference ICD-11 criteria for diagnosis.
- **NICE (UK, CG128):** Recommends diagnosis per **either DSM-5 or ICD-11**. The guideline was updated in December 2017 to replace DSM-IV references with DSM-5, and in March 2022 "updated mentions of ICD-10 to ICD-11" (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/evidence/full-guideline-pdf-183228447). NICE's context statement describes DSM-5's two domains including "sensory anomalies" within RRBs and notes diagnoses must have "a significant impact on function" under either system (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Context). NICE treats sensory differences as recognised features but gives no manual preference.

**Summary:** WHO and NICE are dual-manual/ICD-11-forward; APA and AAP are DSM-5-anchored. All four accept sensory processing differences as legitimate core diagnostic features — a position with no remaining guideline-level dissent.

---

## D. Advocacy organization positions

Direct, honest finding: **none of the three organizations has issued a formal position declaring DSM-5 or ICD-11 "more neurodiversity-affirming."** Their documented positions are:

- **Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN):** Engaged intensively with DSM-5 development (2012–2013), not ICD-11. ASAN's joint statement with the Autism Society of America demanded that DSM-5 "ensure that those who have or would have qualified for a diagnosis under the DSM-IV maintain access to an ASD diagnosis," highlighting under-diagnosis among "racial and ethnic minorities, women and girls, adults and… low-income communities" (https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/01/joint-asan-autism-society-statement-on-dsm-5/). ASAN's policy briefs supported the unified spectrum diagnosis, urged greater sensitivity, and explicitly recommended inclusion of motor/movement and sensory issues in criteria (https://autisticadvocacy.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/06/ASAN_DSM-5_2_final.pdf), while opposing the restrictive "3 of 3" social-communication rule (https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/05/asan-talking-points-for-public-comment-on-dsm-5-autism-spectrum-disorder-criteria/). A retrospective scholarly analysis of ASAN's lobbying concludes ASAN "succeeded in substantially influencing the final criteria" but judged them "likely still too narrow and a problematic severity scale" (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13). ASAN's neurodiversity framework is stated at https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/. *Inference (labelled as such):* ASAN's stated values — breadth, sensory inclusion, recognition of marginalised groups — align more closely with ICD-11's flexible, camouflaging-aware framing than with DSM-5's enumerated thresholds, but ASAN has published no ICD-11 endorsement.
- **National Autistic Society (NAS, UK):** NAS's guidance states diagnosis "should be based on criteria listed in… DSM-5 or ICD-11, according to the NICE guidelines," treating them as equivalent while explicitly reframing criteria in neurodiversity-affirming language: "many people (including most autistic people) do not consider autism to be a disorder"; RRBs are described as "self-soothing or self-regulating behaviours, and focused and dedicated interests, including **sensory differences**" (https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment). NAS does not rank the manuals; its neurodiversity-affirming stance is expressed through language and acceptance of either system.
- **Autism Speaks (US):** Publishes and explains the DSM-5 criteria in full (https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5) and its FAQ highlights that DSM-5 "added sensory symptoms as a diagnostic criterion" and created three support-level severity ratings (https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions; https://www.autismspeaks.org/blog/expert-qa-dsm-5-and-asd). Autism Speaks frames these changes clinically (more accurate diagnosis, treatment/service identification, severity assessment) rather than in neurodiversity terms, and has no published ICD-11 position.

**Synthesis:** The neurodiversity community's documented engagement is with DSM-5 (ASAN), where it secured a broader, sensory-inclusive criteria set but criticised residual narrowness and the severity scale. ICD-11's text — co-authored with explicit reference to the "biopsychosocial, neurodiversity perspective" (Greaves-Lord et al. 2022, above), recognising camouflaging and adult manifestation and avoiding deficit-anchored exemplars — is arguably the more neurodiversity-aligned document in design intent, but this remains an analytic judgement; no major advocacy body has formally adjudicated between the manuals.

---

## E. Diagnostic safety risks from DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 differences

**Under-diagnosis (better documented; risk concentrated in DSM-5's enumerated thresholds):**
- Pooled 31% reduction in ASD diagnoses under DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV-TR (meta-analysis above), rising to 70% for PDD-NOS — the subgroup with the most atypical/subthreshold, often sensory-led presentations (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/).
- Only 56% of intellectually able adults with ICD-10R ASD met DSM-5 (Wilson 2013); 34.1% of a Korean ADOS/ADI-R-characterised PDD sample failed DSM-5, disproportionately Asperger-type and higher-IQ (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7289465/). Draft-criteria analyses had already signalled sensitivity of just 0.46 in IQ≥70 groups (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/ — published October 2012, pre-dating the 2013 window; included as context only).
- Excluded individuals may be re-routed to Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder, whose "relation to the autism spectrum remains unclear" as do "the types of services to which an individual might be entitled" — a documented service-access risk (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2040-2392-4-13). ASAN raised the same access-protection concern (cited above).
- Sex/gender: in a Milan adult sample (n=61), **75.4% received their ASD diagnosis on average 8 years after first mental-health contact**; women were "less likely to be correctly diagnosed and more likely to be misdiagnosed," and notably, **women who were misdiagnosed scored significantly higher on the hyper/hypo-reactivity-to-sensory-input domain** — direct evidence that sensory-prominent presentations in women drive misdiagnosis under DSM-5-based practice (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8306851/). Camouflaging is associated with later diagnosis, especially in women (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/aur.3059). ICD-11's explicit recognition of compensation and later manifestation is designed to mitigate this, but mitigation is untested empirically.

**Over-diagnosis / false positives (risk concentrated in ICD-11's flexibility):**
- Bölte et al. (2024) argue ICD-11's high variety of permissible symptom combinations and "vague and subjective concepts… lead to non-falsifiable diagnoses," bearing "a large danger of false positive diagnoses, of further increased prevalence rates, limitations of access to ASD-specific services and of increasing the non-specificity of treatments" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/). This is an expert warning, not empirical measurement.

**Sensory-specific risks:**
- Sensory items had "poor specificity" in DSM-IV field trials, which is why DSM-5 embedded them within a multi-criterion RRB menu rather than as stand-alone features (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2040-2392-4-13). DSM-5-based reviews warn that "overlooking atypical sensory characteristics can cause problems in the diagnostic process" (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK573615/) — i.e., both over-reliance on and neglect of sensory signs are error modes.
- A subtle cross-manual hazard: DSM-5's sensory exemplars (excessive smelling/touching, fascination with lights) are partly ID-anchored; ICD-11's developers caution that such classic exemplars are "mainly observed in individuals with ID," implying DSM-5's examples may under-detect sensory differences in cognitively able people while ICD-11's looser wording may over-include them (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/).
- Intervention pathway risk: formal sensory criterion status can channel families toward sensory-based interventions whose evidence base remains contested; ICD-11 critics explicitly warn of "increasing non-specificity of treatments" if the phenotype broadens further (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/). Direct comparative outcome data on interventions triggered under each manual do not exist.

---

## F. Reimbursement / coding summary

**United States:** Clinically, US providers diagnose using DSM-5, but bill using **ICD-10-CM**; DSM-5 itself lists ASD as "299.00 (F84.0)" (https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml), i.e., DSM-5 ASD maps to a single ICD-10-CM code **F84.0** regardless of DSM-5 severity level (levels 1–3 are not separately reimbursed). The US has **not adopted ICD-11** for morbidity coding; there is no ICD-11-CM in force, so payer coverage, state autism insurance mandates, and Medicaid waiver eligibility continue to key off ICD-10-CM F84.0. Consequently, the choice between DSM-5 and ICD-11 *criteria* has no direct effect on US reimbursement today; criteria affect payment only indirectly, through who qualifies for the F84.0 diagnosis that unlocks ABA and related benefits.

**WHO/EU:** ICD-11 came into effect for WHO member states on 1 January 2022 (WHA72 resolution, above), with ASD coded under **6A02 and its six subdivisions (6A02.0–6A02.5)**. WHO publishes official ICD-10↔ICD-11 mapping tables (listed on the ICD-11 MMS browser: https://icd.who.int/browse/2024-01/mms/en), so dual-coding translation for payers is technically supported. In practice, implementation is staggered: the UK's NICE updated guideline terminology from ICD-10 to ICD-11 only in March 2022 (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/evidence/full-guideline-pdf-183228447), and UK services currently use a mixture of DSM-5(-TR), ICD-10 and ICD-11 — a duality the NAS notes "can really cause confusion… in terms of these labels" (https://acamhlearn.cadmore.media/learning/assessment-and-diagnosis-of-autism-a-guide-for-families/9e83e67e-74b9-41f2-b97c-86a0d5ab4856/b7e30237-5a0d-42e7-b4f1-32520e45aed5). Most EU national health systems were still operating ICD-10-based reimbursement at ICD-11's effective date, with transition timelines set nationally.

**Net effect on coverage:** No evidence identified in this research indicates that adopting ICD-11 criteria, by itself, changes coverage or reimbursement anywhere; both F84.0 and 6A02 denote the same spectrum construct, and expert consensus is that the two criteria sets "show a high similarity… one may expect prevalence rates to be consolidated," with at most modest reductions where "atypical autism" categories disappear (https://europepmc.org/article/med/33269947). The plausible financial risks are second-order: if ICD-11's flexible criteria widen diagnosis (over-diagnosis concern, Bölte 2024), payer costs and service queues expand; conversely, where DSM-5's stricter thresholds deny an F84.0 diagnosis to sensory-prominent or camouflaging individuals, those individuals lose access to diagnosis-gated benefits entirely (ASAN 2012; Wilson 2013). These fiscal impacts are projections, not measured outcomes — a genuine evidence gap.

---

## Overall conclusions

1. DSM-5 and ICD-11 are architecturally convergent on ASD and both weight sensory processing as a **core but non-sufficient** feature; the material differences are DSM-5's enumerated thresholds and severity levels versus ICD-11's descriptive flexibility, ID/language subdivision codes, and explicit accommodation of late-manifesting and camouflaged presentations.
2. The direct DSM-5-vs-ICD-11 accuracy literature does **not exist**; all quantitative evidence is mediated through DSM-IV/ICD-10 comparators, showing DSM-5-style criteria trade sensitivity (−31% pooled diagnoses) for specificity, with losses concentrated in PDD-NOS/Asperger-type, higher-IQ, adult, and female — frequently sensory-prominent — presentations.
3. Guidelines split along jurisdiction (APA/AAP: DSM-5; WHO/NICE: dual or ICD-11), and advocacy organizations have engaged DSM-5 substantively but ICD-11 only tacitly; ICD-11's text is the more neurodiversity-informed by design intent, though no advocacy body has formally declared a preference.
4. Safety risks are symmetric and opposite: DSM-5 risks under-diagnosis and service denial; ICD-11 risks false positives and treatment non-specificity. Both risks are currently supported more by reasoning and proxy data than by direct comparative measurement — the highest-priority research need in this area.

final.content:
# Transitional Justice After Mass Atrocities: A Comparative Analysis of Truth Commissions, Tribunals, Reparations, and Lustration

## 1. Introduction and Evaluation Framework

"Transitional justice" encompasses the set of judicial and non-judicial measures societies use to redress legacies of mass atrocity or systematic repression: criminal prosecutions, truth commissions, reparations, and institutional reform (including vetting/lustration). This report evaluates four families of mechanisms against three criteria drawn from the task: (a) serving victims, (b) enabling democratic transitions, and (c) preventing recurrence. The analysis draws on primary institutional documents (TRC reports, ICC and ICTY records, settlement agreements, German and U.S. legislation) and on the leading cross-national empirical studies (the Transitional Justice Data Base project of Olsen, Payne, and Reiter; the "justice cascade" research of Sikkink and colleagues).

A central finding of the empirical literature frames the whole report: **no single mechanism, used alone, reliably improves human rights or democracy**. Analyzing 91 democratic transitions in 74 countries (1970–2004), Olsen, Payne, and Reiter found that transitional justice overall has a positive effect, but only specific *combinations* work — trials plus amnesties, and trials plus amnesties plus truth commissions — while truth commissions used alone correlate with *worse* human rights outcomes. Their "justice balance" thesis holds that trials supply accountability and amnesties supply stability (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:6e38b8c0-9ddb-419d-b497-6925379e9a92; https://gsdrc.org/document-library/the-justice-balance-when-transitional-justice-improves-human-rights-and-democracy/). The case studies below both illustrate and complicate that finding.

---

## 2. Truth and Reconciliation Commissions

### 2.1 South Africa's TRC (1995–2003)

**Design.** Created by the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act (1995), the TRC investigated gross violations of human rights committed between March 1960 and May 1994. Its innovation was *conditional, individualized amnesty*: perpetrators from all sides received amnesty only upon full disclosure of politically motivated crimes, with the "stick" of prosecution for those who did not apply. Three committees handled human rights violations, amnesty, and reparations/rehabilitation (https://sthp.saha.org.za/memorial/articles/the_truth_and_reconciliation_commission.htm; https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/178073/accountability_and_national_reconciliation_in_south_africa.pdf).

**Outputs.** The commission received roughly 7,116–7,700 amnesty applications; of those adjudicated, 1,167 applicants received full amnesty, 145 received partial amnesty, and 362 were denied. Approximately 22,000 victims made statements; 1,819 testified in public hearings (https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/178073/accountability_and_national_reconciliation_in_south_africa.pdf; https://digitalcommons.du.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1313&context=hrhw).

**Victim service: mixed and ultimately weakened by reparations failure.** The TRC's Reparations and Rehabilitation Committee recommended individual grants of R17,000–R23,000 *per year for six years* (benchmarked to the 1997 median household income of R21,700), a package projected at ~R3 billion for ~22,000 victims (https://www.justice.gov.za/trc/media/1997/9710/s971023a.htm; https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume5/chapter5/subsection8.htm). In April 2003, President Mbeki announced instead a one-time payment of R30,000 (https://iol.co.za/news/politics/2003-04-15-mbeki-announces-payout-for-apartheid-victims/). The quantitative shortfall is stark:

- Recommended total per victim: R17,000–23,000 × 6 years = **R102,000–R138,000**
- Delivered: **R30,000**, i.e., only **~22–29%** of the recommended amount

Victims thus watched perpetrators receive amnesty immediately while their own reparations were delayed years and cut by more than two-thirds — an asymmetry critics call "justice held hostage to truth" (https://digitalcommons.nyls.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2222&context=fac_articles_chapters). Scholars also fault the narrow mandate — gross bodily-integrity violations only — which excluded the socioeconomic machinery of apartheid (forced removals, Bantu education, migrant labor) and gendered crimes, leaving structural inequality largely unaddressed (https://www.csvr.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/South-African-Case-Maxine-Rubin-et-al.pdf; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-modern-african-studies/article/abs/evaluating-the-truth-and-reconciliation-commission/077C3FB04228FA2D56C090A613FACFBA).

**Democratic transition: the strongest dimension.** The TRC was embedded in the negotiated settlement (the 1993 interim constitution's postscript required amnesty) and is widely credited with enabling a peaceful transition without civil war, establishing an authoritative public record, and institutionalizing a culture of truth-telling — including unprecedented hearings on the complicity of business, media, churches, the legal and medical professions (https://digitalcommons.nyls.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2222&context=fac_articles_chapters). The quid pro quo of disclosure-for-amnesty extracted confessions (e.g., to torture and murder by security police) that trials likely never would have produced.

**Prevention of recurrence: weak follow-through.** The government declined systematic prosecutions of those denied amnesty and rejected a wealth tax on apartheid beneficiaries; critics link persistent impunity, unresolved land inequality, and violence to the TRC's unfulfilled remedial agenda (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-modern-african-studies/article/abs/evaluating-the-truth-and-reconciliation-commission/077C3FB04228FA2D56C090A613FACFBA).

### 2.2 Canada's TRC for Indian Residential Schools (2008–2015)

**Design.** Unusually, the Canadian TRC was not a post-regime-change body but a component of a court-supervised class settlement — the 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSA, implemented 19 September 2007), the largest class settlement in Canadian history (https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/indian-residential-schools-settlement-agreement; https://rcaanc.gc.ca/eng/1100100015576/1571581687074). Roughly 150,000 First Nations, Métis, and Inuit children were removed from their families and placed in 139+ schools between the 1880s and 1996; the TRC documented the system as "cultural genocide" (https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/truth-and-reconciliation-commission-by-the-numbers-1.3096185).

**Scale of harm documented.** The TRC took statements from over 6,750–7,000 witnesses. Its Register of Confirmed Deaths records 3,200 children who died at the schools — with no name recorded for 32% of deaths, no gender for 23%, and no cause for 49% — and Chair Justice Murray Sinclair estimated the true toll exceeds 6,000, noting record-keeping was too poor to establish a full count (https://nctr.ca/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Volume_4_Missing_Children_English_Web.pdf; https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/truth-and-reconciliation-commission-by-the-numbers-1.3096185).

**Victim service: substantial material compensation, but slow policy follow-up.** Unlike South Africa, Canada paired truth-telling with large-scale, *actually delivered* reparations under the IRSSA:

- Common Experience Payment (CEP): C$1.9 billion designated; C$10,000 for the first year of residence plus C$3,000 per additional year. By March 2016, **C$1.62 billion paid to 79,309 survivors** (average C$20,457).
- Independent Assessment Process (IAP) for sexual/serious physical abuse: **C$3.18 billion paid to 31,103 claimants** by March 2019 (average C$111,265).
- Plus C$125 million to the Aboriginal Healing Foundation, C$60 million for the TRC, C$20 million for commemoration (https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Residential_Schools_Settlement_Agreement; https://www.residentialschoolsettlement.ca/detailed_notice.pdf).

However, implementation of the TRC's 94 Calls to Action (June 2015) has been slow. Ten years on, tracking organizations converge on a bleak picture: the Assembly of First Nations counts ~13 Calls completed (only two in the last five years; zero in 2024–25); the Yellowhead Institute found zero completed in 2023; a December 2025 assessment estimated fewer than 20 of 94 fully implemented; the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation's count is 14 completed, 42 in progress, 22 stalled, 16 not started (https://afn.bynder.com/m/21a223c344077b7/original/Progress-on-Realizing-the-Truth-and-Reconciliation-Commission-s-Calls-to-Action-September-2025.pdf; https://yellowheadinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/YI-TRC-C2A-2023-Special-Report-compressed.pdf; https://globalnews.ca/news/11579370/under-20-truth-and-reconciliation-calls-implemented-decade-later/). That is a completion rate of roughly **14–20% after a decade**. A National Council for Reconciliation was legislated in 2024 (Bill C-29), though criticized for missing funding and appointment elements.

**Assessment.** Canada's model shows a truth commission can deliver real material redress when embedded in an enforceable settlement — but also that commemorative truth without structural implementation yields diminishing legitimacy. Because Canada was already a stable democracy, the case speaks mostly to victim service and non-recurrence (through education and child-welfare reform), where progress is incomplete; overrepresentation of Indigenous children in care and persistent gaps documented by the Correctional Investigator and Auditor General show the harms' intergenerational continuation (https://afn.bynder.com/asset/36043b91-4f8c-405e-8199-25c886017877/TRC-Report-Card-2024.pdf).

---

## 3. Prosecutorial Tribunals

### 3.1 The ICTY (1993–2017): the accountability benchmark

**Record.** Established by UN Security Council Resolution 827 (25 May 1993), the ICTY indicted 161 individuals; all were accounted for — zero fugitives remained after the last arrest (Goran Hadžić, July 2011). Depending on the snapshot date, 84–93 were sentenced (the ICTY's September 2023 figures list 93 sentenced, including Mladić and Stanišić), 18–19 acquitted, 13 referred to national courts, and 37 cases terminated or withdrawn. It heard 4,650 witnesses over 10,800 trial days, producing 2.5 million pages of transcripts (https://www.icty.org/en/cases/key-figures-cases; https://news.un.org/en/story/2017/12/640022-feature-curtain-falls-un-tribunals-24-year-history-fighting-impunity-former). It convicted the principal architects of the Bosnian war — Radovan Karadžić (40 years, later life) and Ratko Mladić (life) — and was the first tribunal since Nuremberg to try a sitting head of state (Milošević, who died mid-trial).

**Victim service.** The ICTY "gave victims a voice" at scale and established facts beyond reasonable doubt, "shrinking the space for denial" (Diane Orentlicher's phrase). Yet a court in The Hague could not deliver reparations, and outreach to the region was widely judged belated and inadequate (https://www.kcl.ac.uk/warstudies/assets/assessing-the-ictys-legacy.pdf; https://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1043&context=hrbrief).

**Democratic transition and non-recurrence: modest on the ground, transformative globally.** Empirically, the tribunal did *not* reconcile the Balkans: surveys in Serbia show persistently negative perceptions of the court, and genocide denialism about Srebrenica has *risen* despite 2.5 million pages of adjudicated fact — leading scholars (Marko Milanović, Refik Hodžić) to conclude courts establish facts but cannot "persuade target audiences" or reconcile polarized societies by themselves (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-journal-of-international-law/article/abs/impact-of-the-icty-on-the-former-yugoslavia-an-anticipatory-postmortem/CD016D8E8B971AF1F361456AA85EC3AF; https://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2862&context=facsch_lawrev). Its completion-strategy legacy did, however, catalyze domestic war-crimes chambers in Bosnia, Serbia, and Croatia, transferring capacity to national judiciaries (https://www.icty.org/en/features/legacy-conferences/international-conference-2010/background-paper). Globally, it rebuilt international humanitarian law (joint criminal enterprise, sexual violence jurisprudence, command responsibility) and proved international justice viable, spawning the ICTR, SCSL, and ICC.

**Cost critique.** The ICTY cost an estimated **$2.2–2.7 billion** over 24 years (biennial budgets peaked at $286 million for 2010–11) — roughly **$16.8 million per indicted person** or ~$29 million per convicted person at the $2.7B estimate. Defenders note this pales beside the costs of the wars and peacekeeping; critics argue the slowness and expense limited its value-for-money (https://repository.law.uic.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1501&context=facpubs; https://www.cips-cepi.ca/2013/05/29/the-icty-at-20-mission-accomplished/; https://www.icty.org/en/about/tribunal/the-cost-of-justice).

### 3.2 The ICC: Kenya and Sudan — the limits of tribunals without state cooperation

**Kenya (2007–08 post-election violence).** The ICC's Kenya intervention became its most high-profile failure. Charges against Uhuru Kenyatta (confirmed January 2012) were withdrawn by Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda on 5 December 2014: key witnesses died or were "too terrified to testify," others recanted amid bribery allegations, and the Kenyan government refused to surrender financial and phone records. In September 2016 the Trial Chamber formally found Kenya in non-cooperation and referred it to the Assembly of States Parties — with no sanction resulting (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-withdrawal-charges-against-mr; https://www.hrw.org/news/2016/09/19/icc-countries-should-press-kenya-obstruction). The Ruto/Sang case collapsed in April 2016 when charges were vacated after 157 trial days: at least 16–17 of 42 original prosecution witnesses withdrew amid what judges called demonstrated "witness interference and political meddling" (Judge Eboe-Osuji declared a mistrial rather than acquittal) (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/ruto-and-sang-case-icc-trial-chamber-va-terminates-case-without-prejudice-re-prosecution; https://www.hrw.org/news/2016/04/05/icc-kenya-deputy-presidents-case-ends). The accused went on to become President and Deputy President — an outcome arguably *worse* for impunity than no case at all, and one that left victims of the violence (1,100+ killed, hundreds of thousands displaced) with neither accountability nor reparations.

**Sudan/Darfur.** The Darfur situation (UNSC Resolution 1593 referral, 2005) produced the ICC's first arrest warrant against a sitting head of state — Omar al-Bashir, March 2009 (war crimes/crimes against humanity) and July 2010 (three counts of genocide against the Fur, Masalit, and Zaghawa). Bashir traveled openly for years; Sudan refused cooperation; even after his 2019 ouster and the transitional government's custody of Bashir, Harun, and Hussein, none was transferred, and Sudan's 2023 civil war has further stalled prospects (https://www.icc-cpi.int/darfur/albashir; https://redress.org/news/understanding-the-ali-kushayb-trial-qa-on-the-iccs-role-in-crimes-committed-in-darfur/). Yet the case also yielded the ICC's **first Darfur conviction**: Janjaweed commander Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman ("Ali Kushayb"), who surrendered voluntarily in June 2020, was convicted on **6 October 2025 of 27 counts** of war crimes and crimes against humanity after a 134-sitting-day trial — a landmark demonstrating that long-delayed justice remains possible when a suspect loses state protection (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/ali-muhammad-ali-abd-al-rahman-declared-guilty-war-crimes-and-crimes-against-humanity; https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/icc-convicts-first-darfur-militia-leader-war-crimes-2025-10-06/).

**Assessment.** The ICC cases show international prosecutions are hostage to state cooperation: where the accused control the state (Kenya), cases collapse; where the state shields them (Sudan), warrants gather dust for 16+ years. The deterrent and victim-service value is therefore highly uneven, though the cumulative "justice cascade" evidence suggests prosecutions do matter systemically (see §6).

---

## 4. Reparations Programs

### 4.1 Germany's Holocaust Reparations (Wiedergutmachung)

**Structure.** The 1952 Luxembourg Agreements committed West Germany to pay DM 3 billion (~$714 million) in goods and services to Israel (for absorbing ~500,000 survivors) and DM 450 million (~$107 million) to the Conference on Jewish Material Claims Against Germany (Claims Conference), plus an obligation to enact individual compensation legislation (https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany/; https://cms.archivportal-d.de/sites/default/files/media/document/2022-04/1952-09-10_Luxemburger%20Vertrag%20Haager%20Protokolle_BGBl.%201953%20II%2C%2035-97_OG.pdf). Implementing laws followed: the Federal Compensation Act (BEG, 1956) for individual harms (health, liberty, professional and property damage) and the Federal Restitution Law (BRüG, 1957) for property.

**Scale.** This is history's most sustained reparations program. Cumulative payments exceeded **€80 billion by end-2021** (per Chancellor Scholz and the Claims Conference); the Claims Conference reports more than **$90 billion** negotiated and paid to individual victims since 1952. Even in 2023, Germany committed $1.2 billion in a single year; in 2022 over 260,000 survivors in 83 countries received direct compensation; as of mid-2019 some 25,000 survivors still drew monthly BEG pensions (https://www.claimscon.org/2022/09/german-chancellor-and-claims-conference-meet-to-mark-70th-anniversary-of-historic-reparations-agreements-and-announce-negotiations-results-of-over-1-2-billion/; https://apnews.com/article/holocaust-survivor-compensation-fund-germany-0d35aa1cba7756d1b9b6008e9d7841b7; https://teachjewishhistory.org/topic-restitution).

**Assessment.** German reparations succeeded because they were (a) *institutionalized in law* rather than discretionary, (b) *continuously expanded* over 70+ years as new victim categories were recognized, and (c) embedded in a broader Vergangenheitsbewältigung (coming-to-terms with the past) that included trials, education, memorialization, and — in the East — Stasi file access. Reparations alone cannot "make good" (the literal meaning of Wiedergutmachung was contested from the start, and Israel's own debate was bitter), but they materially supported survivors and credibly signaled state acknowledgment, underpinning Germany's democratic reinvention. The obvious caution: this was a wealthy, defeated, occupied state under Allied pressure — conditions rarely replicated.

### 4.2 U.S. Redress for Japanese American Internment

**Process.** The Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians (CWRIC, est. 1980) held hearings and archival research, concluding the internment of ~120,000 people of Japanese ancestry was not military necessity but the product of "racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership." Its findings drove the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (Pub. L. 100-383, signed by President Reagan, 10 August 1988): a formal congressional apology, a public education fund, and **$20,000 per surviving internee** (~$46,000 in 2024 dollars), with payments from 1990. A $1.25 billion trust fund was authorized over ten years (capped at $500 million/year). Ultimately **82,219 individuals received redress checks**, totaling approximately **$1.64 billion** (82,219 × $20,000) (https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/100/hr442/summary; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Liberties_Act_of_1988; https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/public/2021-08/40-461-12013681-OA16204-001-2021.pdf).

**Assessment.** The program is widely regarded as a model of *symbolic-plus-material* redress for a closed historical episode: an official truth commission (CWRIC) → apology → individualized payment → education fund. Its sequencing — payment to *living* survivors with the apology letter in hand — is credited with restoring community dignity. But scholars caution it was "necessary but not sufficient": redress came 46 years late, excluded the dead, property losses were only partially covered (a 1948 act had paid a fraction), and later U.S. policies (post-9/11 detention practices) suggest the "never again" lesson was "ephemeral at best" (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1135&context=hastings_race_poverty_law_journal). Reparations work best for *discrete, bounded* wrongs with identifiable victims — conditions absent in many mass-atrocity settings.

---

## 5. Lustration and Vetting in Post-Communist Europe

### 5.1 Models

Post-1989 Eastern Europe produced a spectrum of vetting approaches:

- **Czechoslovakia/Czech Republic ("semi-retributive").** Act No. 451/1991 (4 October 1991) — the region's first and "most sweeping" lustration law — barred StB (secret police) officers, registered collaborators, People's Militia members, and others from specified state posts for 1948–1989 conduct. By September 1992 the Federal Interior Ministry had issued 168,928 certificates: 153,504 negative (clear) and **15,424 positive (~9.1%)**, with positives (excluding one category) affecting 11,363 persons — about **0.15% of all employed persons**. The Constitutional Court upheld the law in November 1992 while striking some provisions (https://www.usoud.cz/en/decisions/1992-11-26-pl-us-1-92-czechoslovak-const-court-lustration; https://www.ustrcr.cz/data/pdf/clanky/zacek-lustrace.pdf).
- **Poland ("semi-reconciliatory").** Delayed until the 1997 Lustration Act, Poland used a declaration-based, truth-revelation model: public officials filed declarations; a Lustration Court in the Warsaw Court of Appeal adjudicated only *lies* ("lustration liars"), and confessing collaborators received a second chance. A contested 2006 expansion politicized the process further (https://www.shrmonitor.org/assets/uploads/2023/02/To_what_extent_is_lustration_an_effective_mechanism_Zieba1.pdf; https://api.sejm.gov.pl/eli/acts/DU/1997/443/text.pdf).
- **East Germany (archives-centered).** Following citizens' occupation of Stasi buildings, the Stasi Records Act (20 December 1991) created the Gauck Authority (BStU). Within two years, 1.4 million applications for vetting/file access had been filed; roughly **1 in 10 vetted persons** showed evidence of Stasi ties; about **1 in 10 vetted former East Berlin Volkspolizisten** was dismissed. By January 2015, **over 7 million people** had applied to view their own files (https://taz.de/Mit-Stasi-Akten-gegen-die-alte-Macht/!1649515/; https://taz.de/Jeder-zwanzigste-musste-den-Hut-nehmen/!1631775/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stasi_Records_Agency).

### 5.2 Assessment

**Effectiveness for democratic consolidation.** Roman David's comparative study finds the Czech semi-retributive model "relatively successful" in meeting its goals within a few years of adoption, while Poland's semi-reconciliatory model became chronically contested, politically malleable, and weaponized (lustration scandals tainted the 2008 Czech presidential vote and repeatedly destabilized Polish politics) (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-social-inquiry/article/abs/lustration-laws-in-action-the-motives-and-evaluation-of-lustration-policy-in-the-czech-republic-and-poland-19892001/A54F46A5C8E41697959589830750116C; https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/D0651FBE5434D968F2F397C9F1754938/S1574019608004604a.pdf/lustration_and_lapse_of_time.pdf). The East German model is often judged the most rights-respecting because it prioritized *individual access to files* and information provision over collective punishment, leaving employment consequences to case-by-case agency decisions.

**Key pathologies.** (1) *Reliability of files*: secret-police records contain fabrications; the Czech Constitutional Court itself acknowledged this risk. (2) *Guilt by association*: early Czech law sanctioned categories of persons without individualized proof, mitigated only by judicial review. (3) *Instrumentalization*: incomplete files were used for blackmail and electoral attacks in both Czechia and Poland. (4) *Elite continuity vs. expertise*: aggressive purges remove administrative competence; lax ones leave networks intact — Hungary and Russia's weak programs are associated with the region's most severe democratic backsliding, though causality is debated (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0888325405278020; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/hague-journal-on-the-rule-of-law/article/abs/lustration-decommunisation-and-the-rule-of-law/275FDE2E16D12AD1943B3836C2E33D20).

**Victim service.** Lustration is the mechanism *least* oriented to victims directly — its rationale is institutional trust and security ("justice as prevention"). The German file-access model is the exception: millions of citizens learning *who informed on them* served a truth function with real personal significance, arguably more durably than any top-down purge.

---

## 6. Cross-Cutting Evidence: What Actually Works?

**Quantitative findings.**

1. **Combinations beat single mechanisms.** Olsen, Payne & Reiter (91 transitions, 74 countries, 1970–2004; democracy measured by Polity and Freedom House, human rights by Cingranelli-Richards and Political Terror Scale, 10 years post-transition): transitional justice overall improves human rights and democracy; **trials + amnesties** and **trials + amnesties + truth commissions** produce improvements; **truth commissions alone have a negative impact**; no mechanism works alone (https://academic.oup.com/ijtj/article-abstract/4/3/457/2357027; https://gsdrc.org/document-library/the-justice-balance-when-transitional-justice-improves-human-rights-and-democracy/).
2. **Prosecutions deter.** Sikkink & Kim's dataset on domestic and international prosecutions in 100 transitional countries finds human rights prosecutions after transition are associated with *improved* human rights protection, with deterrent effects crossing borders — the "justice cascade" (https://www.iilj.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Sikkink-Explaining-the-Deterrence-Effect-of-Human-Rights-Prosecution-ofr-Transitional-Countries-2009.pdf; https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-lawsocsci-102612-133956). In Latin America, trials did *not* undermine democracy, increase violations, or reignite conflict — refuting the "trial skeptics" (https://fbaum.unc.edu/teaching/articles/J-Peace-Research-2007-Sikkink.pdf).
3. **Sequencing and adoption patterns.** Countries adopt amnesties most often, usually in civil-war endings; trials cluster in Europe and post-authoritarian settings and almost never touch those currently in power — confirming the Kenya lesson that tribunals bite only after perpetrators lose office (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/0022343310382205).

**Qualitative synthesis.** Courts "shrink the space for denial" but do not reconcile (ICTY); truth commissions dignify victims and build national narratives but fail without reparative follow-through (South Africa's 22–29% reparations delivery; Canada's ~14–20% Calls-to-Action completion); reparations work best when legalized, generous, and sustained (Germany) or tightly targeted (U.S.), and worst when promised broadly and delivered minimally (South Africa); lustration guards institutions but is the most easily abused mechanism and the least victim-centered.

---

## 7. Conclusions: Which Approaches Best Serve Each Goal?

**Serving victims.** Ranking by demonstrated victim outcomes: (1) **well-funded, legally institutionalized reparations** (Germany's 70-year, >€80 billion commitment; the U.S. $20,000 payments to 82,219 survivors; Canada's IRSSA paying ~C$4.8 billion to ~110,000 claimants) deliver the most tangible redress; (2) **truth commissions with victim hearings** deliver acknowledgment and truth at scale (South Africa's 22,000 statements; Canada's 6,750+), but victim satisfaction collapses when recommended reparations are cut — South Africa is the cautionary case; (3) **tribunals** serve victims primarily through acknowledgment and voice rather than material repair, and fail them entirely when cases collapse (Kenya). The critical design variable is whether reparations promises are enforceable (court-supervised settlement, statutory entitlement) rather than aspirational (TRC recommendations).

**Enabling democratic transitions.** **Truth commissions with conditional amnesty** are the strongest single tool during fragile negotiated transitions — South Africa avoided civil war precisely because amnesty-for-truth gave outgoing elites an exit. **Lustration** can protect nascent institutions (the Czech model, and Germany's archives model, correlate with durable consolidation; weak de-communization in Hungary/Russia correlates with backsliding), but must have judicial review, individualized proof, and sunset clauses to avoid becoming a partisan weapon (Poland's lesson). **Tribunals** contribute least to the *transition moment* itself but can catalyze domestic judicial reform, as the ICTY's completion strategy did in the Balkans.

**Preventing recurrence.** The empirical verdict favors **prosecution-inclusive combinations**. The justice-cascade evidence links trials to subsequent improvements in human rights protection, and Olsen/Payne/Reiter find accountability (trials) plus stability (amnesties) — with or without truth commissions — is the only configuration that reliably improves human rights and democracy. Truth commissions *alone* correlate with worse outcomes, plausibly because truth without accountability raises expectations and exposes perpetrators' impunity. Structural prevention also requires what none of these mechanisms supplies alone: education, memorialization, institutional reform, and socioeconomic redress — Germany's comprehensive Vergangenheitsbewältigung remains the gold standard, while South Africa's unaddressed economic apartheid legacy and the Balkans' resurgent denialism show the cost of omission.

**Overall judgment.** No mechanism "wins" in isolation; the strongest-performing packages in the record are (a) **Germany's**: reparations + trials + archives + education, sustained over generations; (b) **South Africa's first-order success**: conditional-amnesty truth commission enabling a peaceful transition — undermined by reparations and prosecution failures; (c) **Canada's**: enforceable reparations + truth commission — undermined by stalled structural reform. The weakest records belong to mechanisms deployed without political backing: the ICC in Kenya and Sudan shows international prosecution without state cooperation is easily defeated by witness intimidation and non-surrender (one Darfur conviction in 20 years), and truth commissions whose recommendations are ignored teach citizens that truth-telling is cheap. The practical maxim emerging from both the cases and the cross-national data is the "justice balance": pair accountability with stability, truth with material repair, and courtroom justice with institutional reform — and treat implementation, not design, as the decisive variable.

---

*Key sources: ICTY (icty.org, UN News); ICC (icc-cpi.int press releases, HRW, Reuters); South Africa (justice.gov.za TRC archive, CSVR, Chapman & van der Merwe via digitalcommons.du.edu); Canada (AFN TRC Report Cards, Yellowhead Institute, NCTR, residentialschoolsettlement.ca, The Canadian Encyclopedia); Germany (U.S. State Dept. JUST Act Report, Claims Conference, Bundesgesetzblatt text of Luxembourg Agreements); U.S. (GovTrack text of Pub. L. 100-383, Reagan Library); Lustration (Czech Constitutional Court decision Pl. ÚS 1/92, ÚSTR, Roman David in Law & Social Inquiry, taz/BStU reporting); empirical (Olsen/Payne/Reiter, Transitional Justice in Balance, USIP 2010; Sikkink & Kim, Annual Review of Law and Social Science 2013; Sikkink, Journal of Peace Research 2007). Where figures vary across sources (e.g., ICTY convictions 84–93; ICTY cost $2.2–2.7B; Canada Calls to Action completed 13–20), ranges are reported reflecting different snapshot dates and counting methodologies.*

final.content:
# Farm Management & Traceability Platform Selection for a 5,000-Farmer Coffee Cooperative (Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia)

## 1. Executive Summary

Two findings reshape this procurement before any feature comparison:

**Finding 1 — Olam AtSource cannot be bought by your cooperative.** AtSource is Olam Group's proprietary customer-facing sustainability insights platform, launched publicly in January 2019, built to give *Olam's buyers* (food brands and manufacturers) a traceability and ESG view of Olam's own supply chains. Its farm-level data comes from Olam's internal Farmer Information System (OFIS), collected by Olam-employed enumerators across 550,000+ farmers in 30+ countries (https://www.ofi.com/en-us/sustainability/ofi-farmer-information-system; https://www.atsource.io/atsource.html; https://insights.figlobal.com/food-supply-chain/delivering-supply-chain-visibility-and-meaningful-change). It is not a commercial SaaS product a cooperative can license. It becomes relevant to you only if you sell coffee into Olam/ofi supply chains — in which case data collection happens *to* you, not *by* you.

**Finding 2 — "FairTrace" is two different products, and neither is a farm management platform you can simply purchase.**
- **Fairtrace (FLOCERT/Fairtrade International)** is the mandatory transaction-reporting platform for all Fairtrade-certified supply chain actors. Only FLOCERT-certified organizations get accounts; it records Fairtrade sales volumes, prices, and Premium payments on a "report-and-verify" (virtual handshake) basis, with quarterly reporting obligations (https://fairtrace-account.flocert.net/assets/SAM_FairtraceLoginManual_TR_18_en.pdf; https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf). It has no GPS mapping, no farm management, no offline mobile app — but if you are Fairtrade-certified, you will use it regardless of what else you buy.
- **Trace + Connect (Fairfood, Netherlands)** is a commercial blockchain traceability platform with an offline-capable collector app and NFC "Farmer Cards" that require *no smartphone* for farmers; it was field-tested with two Indonesian coffee cooperatives and has digitized ~15,000 nutmeg transactions in remote Indonesian islands (https://fairfood.org/connect/; https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect).

**Recommendation in brief:** Build a three-layer stack rather than seeking one platform: (a) a first-mile data/mapping layer you control — Farmforce or Fairfood Trace/Connect for commercial deployments, Beyco Farmer Platform (Progreso, free registration, coffee-specific) as the budget floor; (b) the free Fairtrade infrastructure — Fairtrace + Plot Insights — for the Fairtrade-certified portion of your membership; (c) treat Rainforest Alliance geolocation submission (RA Certification Platform) and EUDR due diligence as export-format requirements your mapping tool must serve, not as separate software purchases. Olam AtSource drops out of the competitive set entirely.

---

## 2. What Each Candidate Actually Is

| Platform | Owner / type | Who pays | Available to your coop? |
|---|---|---|---|
| AtSource (+ OFIS) | Olam Group, proprietary | Olam customers (brands) | No — only via selling to Olam/ofi |
| Fairtrace (FLOCERT) | Fairtrade system, mandatory for certified actors | Included in Fairtrade certification | Yes, if Fairtrade-certified; not optional |
| Plot Insights | Fairtrade International + Satelligence | **Free** for all certified coffee/cocoa smallholder producer orgs | Yes, if Fairtrade-certified (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/Press-centre/fairtrade-digital-system-plot-insights-gives-fairtrade-cooperatives-an-eudr-readiness-edge.html) |
| Trace + Connect | Fairfood (Dutch NGO), commercial | Companies/cooperatives, custom pricing | Yes |
| Farmforce (Orbit/Origin/IMS) | Farmforce Inc., commercial SaaS | Sourcing organizations, cooperatives | Yes |
| KoltiTrace (+ FarmXtension, FarmCloud) | Koltiva (Swiss-Indonesian), commercial | Enterprise custom pricing | Yes |
| Cropin (Grow/Trace) | Cropin Technology, commercial | Enterprise, per-license or per-acre | Yes |
| Beyco Farmer Platform | Progreso Foundation (Dutch non-profit) | Free registration; deforestation analysis via OpenAtlas API "at a competitive cost" | Yes — coffee/cocoa coops only (https://beyco.nl/faq?lang=en-us) |
| Enveritas | Non-profit verifier | **Free to farmers** — roasters pay per pound verified | Complement, not a management tool (https://solve.mit.edu/solutions/2884) |

---

## 3. Criterion-by-Criterion Comparison

### 3.1 Usability for farmers with basic phones

The dominant design pattern across all serious smallholder platforms is: **farmers do not operate the software — trained field agents/enumerators do.** The farmer-facing interface, where it exists, is a card, an SMS, or nothing at all.

- **Fairfood Connect** is the strongest fit for basic-phone reality: farmers receive a personal NFC/QR Farmer Card to validate transactions and confirm payments — explicitly "No smartphone needed!" — and can review their transaction history via a digital passbook using the card number. The collector's app is deliberately minimal (enroll farmer, record transaction, photo of receipt if card is forgotten) and was designed with and tested by Indonesian cooperatives (https://fairfood.org/connect/; https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect).
- **Olam OFIS** is enumerator-operated (Android app for authorized data collectors) with an SMS channel to farmers for prices, weather, and agronomy tips (https://www.olamgroup.com/content/dam/olamgroup/files/uploads/2017/07/New-OFIS-Brochure-1.pdf) — but again, not purchasable by you.
- **Farmforce** is field-staff-operated; its farmer-facing app ("Farmforce Connect") is explicitly still a pilot with selected customers. It historically supports two-way SMS communication with farmers (https://farmforce.com/products/farmer-app/; https://bigdata.cgiar.org/digital-intervention/farmforce/).
- **Koltiva** offers a farmer smartphone app (FarmCloud: sales data, transaction authentication, e-wallet KoltiPay) — useful for smartphone-owning Indonesian farmers, less so for basic-phone users in Ethiopia (https://www.koltiva.com/post/transforming-agriculture-supply-chains-a-path-to-achieving-transparency-and-sustainability).
- **Beyco Farmer App** requires Android/iOS — realistically operated by cooperative staff or promoters, not individual farmers (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.beycofarmerapp).
- **Watchlist:** Farmcore (farmcore.io) is building USSD/WhatsApp/SMS channels so members need no smartphone — but it launches first in Tanzania (soft launch Nov 2026) in Swahili only; not yet an option for your geographies.

**Verdict:** Fairfood Trace/Connect best matches the basic-phone constraint today (NFC cards proven in Indonesian coffee). For all other platforms, budget for the cooperative to own the smartphones and employ enumerators — a staffing and device cost that dwarfs software licensing.

### 3.2 GPS plot mapping accuracy in mountainous terrain

This is a hardware/physics constraint more than a software one. Peer-reviewed evidence on smartphone GNSS under canopy and in mountains:

- In mixed forest (leaf-on), smartphone horizontal RMSE ranged **4.96–11.45 m**, versus **1.90–2.36 m** in open areas; survey-grade receivers significantly outperformed all phones (https://exa.ai/library/publication/1qtrdl1yn0k).
- Dual-frequency phones under forest canopy achieved ~2.5 m only with PPP correction and high canopy openness (>0.7); under dense canopy, survey-grade GNSS remains necessary for sub-meter work (https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4907/13/10/1591).
- A 2026 US forest study found 2–6 m typical smartphone accuracy under forest conditions, with sub-meter possible only via an external antenna (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44391-026-00081-9).
- Mountainous terrain specifically degrades accuracy further via slope position and satellite occlusion; handheld receivers were judged "inappropriate for plot establishment" in a mountainous Spanish forest study except where low precision is tolerated (https://sah.borca.ai/papers/53476974).

**Quantitative implication for your cooperative:** A typical smallholder coffee plot of 0.25 ha is roughly 50 m × 50 m. A 5 m boundary-point error (typical under shade-grown coffee canopy) translates to roughly 10% linear uncertainty at the plot edge — area over/underestimation on the order of ±19% (1 − (50/55)² ≈ 0.17; (55/50)² − 1 ≈ 0.21). This matters because:
- **EUDR** requires coordinates to six decimal places (a format precision of ~0.1 m) and **polygons for any plot over 4 ha**; points suffice for smaller plots (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf). Most of your members' plots are almost certainly under 4 ha, so points plus a polygon subset is a viable compliance strategy.
- **Rainforest Alliance (2020 Standard, v1.4)** requires geolocation for 100% of farm units, with **≥35% as GPS polygons by the first certification audit and 100% polygons by the second audit** for group certification; all polygon reference points must be collected *in the field* — desk-drawn polygons from maps are explicitly not acceptable (https://learn.ra.org/mod/page/view.php?id=125526; https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex-v12).

For 5,000 farmers that means: **≥1,750 polygon-mapped farms before audit one; all 5,000 (every farm unit) before audit two.** Walked-boundary polygon capture in Andean (Colombia), highland (Ethiopia), and volcanic (Indonesia) terrain with 5–12 m error under shade canopy is achievable with ordinary dual-frequency Android phones but requires averaging, QA review in GIS software (RA itself recommends QGIS review — https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex-v12), and realistic expectations: these are compliance-grade (~3–10 m), not cadastral-grade, maps.

**Platform mapping capabilities (all broadly comparable at the app level):**
- **Farmforce:** Android GPS polygon mapping, shapefile import, offline-first capture proven "deep inside forest coffee plots with no signal" in Bale/Illubabor, Ethiopia with ECOM/Farm Africa — directly analogous to your Ethiopian membership (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/; https://farmforce.com/solutions/farmers-database-gps-mapping/).
- **Fairfood Connect:** farmer enrollment and transactions; polygon capture is more limited than Farmforce/Koltiva — its focus is transactions and payments (https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect).
- **Koltiva KoltiTrace/FarmXtension:** geolocation mapping, deforestation and GHG layers, field-agent app; active coffee projects in 22 countries and the deepest Indonesian footprint (Swiss-Indonesian, operating since 2013, 1.19M+ producers) (https://www.koltiva.com/koltitrace; https://recatools.com/ai-directory/koltiva-traceability/).
- **Beyco Farmer App:** plot boundary drawing and area calculation that works offline, recently improved GPS accuracy and altitude capture (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.beycofarmerapp). A 2026 EUDR pilot mapped 3,074 farmers / 2,358 ha across five cooperatives with 99.7% of farms classified low deforestation risk (https://www.progreso.nl/openatlas-gosling-coffee-and-progreso-pioneer-eudr-compliance-with-cooperative-data/).

**Verdict:** No platform overcomes phone-GPS physics; differentiate on *workflow* (walked-polygon capture, offline QA, export formats). Farmforce and Koltiva have the strongest mountain/forest field evidence; Beyco is the credible free alternative.

### 3.3 Integration with buyer sustainability certifications (Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade)

- **Fairtrade:** If any of your members are Fairtrade-certified, **Fairtrace use is mandatory, not optional** — quarterly reporting of all Fairtrade sales and direct purchases, plus verification of counterparties' reports (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/09/Chapter-6_Fairtrace.pdf). Plot Insights (free) then handles geolocation validation, Satelligence deforestation risk analysis, and consent-based sharing of plot data with exporters/importers via a "digital handshake" in Fairtrace, with GeoLink API connecting the two (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf). No third-party platform substitutes for this; at best they export data you upload into Plot Insights.
- **Rainforest Alliance:** Certificate holders must upload geolocation (points + polygons) to the RA Certification Platform in specified formats (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex). Farmforce explicitly supports RA with certification registries that "track the mapping status of the fields required for Rainforest Alliance," plus digital survey templates for pre-audit/risk-assessment/audit phases, and also supports GLOBALG.A.P., Organic, and Fairtrade record-keeping (https://farmforce.com/solutions/deforestation-monitoring/certification-process/; https://farmforce.com/products/information-management-system-ims/). Cropin claims compliance/certification management; Koltiva provides EUDR/ESG workflows and "boots on the ground" verification services (https://www.koltiva.com/global-eudr-compliance-tools-for-upstream-and-downstream-businesses).
- **EUDR (increasingly the binding buyer requirement):** compliance deadlines are 30 Dec 2026 (large/medium operators) and 30 Jun 2027 (micro/small), per Regulation (EU) 2025/2650 (https://www.regenesis.ag/compliance-center/eudr-due-diligence-software-coffee-cocoa-cooperatives). Buyers will demand plot geolocation from you; tools that export EUDR-ready GeoJSON include Plot Insights (free, Fairtrade coops), Beyco+OpenAtlas, and numerous commercial platforms (Farmforce, Koltiva, Sylva, OriginTrace).
- **Enveritas** is a different animal: roaster-funded verification, **free to farmers**, operating in 30+ countries with 90,000+ farm verifications in 2024 — if your buyers accept Enveritas verification, it can cover your uncertified members at zero cost to you, though it is an assurance scheme, not a farm management tool (https://www.guidestar.org/profile/81-1681880).

**Verdict:** Fairtrade compliance = Fairtrace + Plot Insights (fixed, free). Rainforest Alliance = any platform with strong polygon management and RA-format exports; Farmforce has the most explicit RA workflow support. Require every shortlisted vendor to demonstrate a live export into RA's platform and EUDR GeoJSON before signing.

### 3.4 Multi-language support

You need, at minimum: Spanish (Colombia), Amharic (Ethiopia), Bahasa Indonesia (Indonesia), plus English for management.

- **Fairtrade Plot Insights:** English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, **Indonesian**, Vietnamese — **no Amharic** (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf).
- **Farmforce:** supports **15 languages** across 32 countries (specific list not published; confirm Spanish/Amharic/Indonesian in procurement) (https://agritechobservatory.review.fao.org/en/farmforce).
- **Olam OFIS:** "multi-language Android OS application" (https://www.olamgroup.com/content/dam/olamgroup/files/uploads/2017/07/New-OFIS-Brochure-1.pdf).
- **Fairfood Connect:** field-proven in Indonesia and Uganda; the app is open-source (React), so localization is technically feasible — but confirm current language builds (https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect).
- **Beyco:** English/Spanish platform heritage (Progreso works in Latin America, Africa, Asia); app deployed with Colombian and Ethiopian farmers (https://www.ionita.nl/projects/farmer-app-for-on-field-data-collection).
- **Koltiva:** Indonesian home market; multi-country deployments.

**Verdict:** Amharic is the gap to probe with every vendor. Demand a demonstration of the enumerator app in all three field languages before contracting.

### 3.5 Offline functionality

- **Farmforce:** offline-first by architecture; collectors "capture data deep inside forest coffee plots with no signal and sync when back in range" (Ethiopia ECOM deployment); Bluetooth scale/barcode scanner/printer integrations for buying stations (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/; https://www.resonanzlab.com/portfolio-items/farmforce/). - **Fairfood Connect:** "operates seamlessly both online and offline," syncing with Trace when connected (https://docs.fairfood.org/trace_connect).
- **Beyco Farmer App:** offline plot area calculation and boundary drawing (explicitly fixed in recent releases) (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_US&id=com.beycofarmerapp).
- **Cropin:** offline capture proven in rural Togo with gebana (https://cropin-tech.medium.com/smartfarm-a-tailor-made-digital-solution-for-plantation-crops-417273b3ecb5).
- **Olam OFIS:** supports data collection "where internet access is limited/non-existent" (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.olam.digital.ofis&hl=en_US).
- **Fairtrace (FLOCERT):** web-only; no offline capability — a known pain point requiring connectivity for quarterly reporting.

**Verdict:** Offline-first is table stakes among credible vendors; only the Fairtrade-mandated web tooling lacks it.

### 3.6 Cost per farmer (5,000 farmers, limited budget)

Published pricing in this market is deliberately opaque; treat all figures below with the stated uncertainty.

| Platform | Published price signal | Modeled cost for 5,000 farmers |
|---|---|---|
| Fairtrade Fairtrace + Plot Insights | **Free** for certified coffee/cocoa producer orgs | **$0/farmer** (for Fairtrade members) |
| Enveritas verification | Free for farmers; roasters pay per pound | **$0/farmer** (if buyers accept it) |
| Beyco Farmer Platform | Free registration; OpenAtlas deforestation analysis "competitive cost" | **~$0 + per-analysis fees** (unpublished) |

## 4. Recommended Architecture for Your Cooperative

**Layer 1 — Compliance backbone (zero cost, non-negotiable):** For Fairtrade-certified members, operate Fairtrace (mandatory quarterly transaction reporting) and Plot Insights (free geolocation validation, Satelligence deforestation risk analysis, EUDR GeoJSON export, buyer data-sharing handshakes).
